I never really looked at this title until it went on sale during the Steam summer sale - and a good friend bringing it to my attention.   I'm very glad he did.  His opinion (and what he heard) plus the trailers really got me excited for this title.
My thoughts about Wolfenstein had been colored a lot by its previous title, which was ok, but nothing more... so I wasn't really interested.
But after playing a couple hours into it... it's reminding me a lot of the somewhat recent Tomb Raider title (without all the crafting nonsense, mind you).  They've made Wolfenstein into a triple A title - worthy of that branding.  It feels like a movie that you play along in.  There are some lengthy cutscenes, but they're pushing a story that you want to see.
[Edit:  The storyline and characters!  Wow!  They did a fantastic job in putting effort into them.  Specifically the characters.  You grow to like them and want to hear more about them.  It's very enguaging and was the primary reason for me to wanting to continue to play to the very end.]
The maps are very well done - complicated enough so that you can explore, but not enough to get lost.  There are parts of the maps where you're given very satisfying power to exploit if you wish.  Then there are others areas where you feel the proper amount of presure pushed upon you, as you would expect in the overwhelming presence of the Nazi army.  Which leads me to my next point...
The stealth system.  They've attempted to put one in this game... but it's rather hallow and not fleshed out.  You CAN be stealthy one some missions, but on others you're simply forced into fighting.  Regardless of your best efforts to go unnoticed, you'll somehow be found and they open fire upon you as any typical AI would - no confusion, no reports going between your foes on your current location.  They simply know where you are, and move towards you like dogs during supper.
There are collectables to search for.  Some unlock more total hit points for you, some for play modes, and some just for simple achievements.  Some of these are well hidden.  During my first play through, I missed a bit more than half of them, and I was actively looking for them as I progressed.
But enough details... in summary... this game has good graphics, sounds, gameplay, and maps.  The only adjustment I would wish for would be smarter AI.
I would give this title 4/5, or 8/10.  Overall the single player was impressive, but lacking in AI (sorry, but Fear kind of upped the bar on this).  I would definately recommend this title due to the other fine things it has to offer.
I purchased this title for $30 (during a sale, if you recall) and I feel it was almost worth that amount.  If you can pick it up for cheaper, you would be wise to do so.  My ideal pricing for this title would be between $15 to $20.
Also, please be aware that if you're looking for multiplayer, this game doesn't have any (which I'm grateful for after the previous Wolfenstein).

The maps are very well done - complicated enough so that you can explore, but not enough to get lost.  There are parts of the maps where you're given very satisfying power to exploit if you wish.  Then there are others areas where you feel the proper amount of presure pushed upon you, as you would expect in the overwhelming presence of the Nazi army.  Which leads me to my next point...
The stealth system.  They've attempted to put one in this game... but it's rather hallow and not fleshed out.  You CAN be stealthy one some missions, but on others you're simply forced into fighting.  Regardless of your best efforts to go unnoticed, you'll somehow be found and they open fire upon you as any typical AI would - no confusion, no reports going between your foes on your current location.  They simply know where you are, and move towards you like dogs during supper.
There are collectables to search for.  Some unlock more total hit points for you, some for play modes, and some just for simple achievements.  Some of these are well hidden.  During my first play through, I missed a bit more than half of them, and I was actively looking for them as I progressed.
But enough details... in summary... this game has good graphics, sounds, gameplay, and maps.  The only adjustment I would wish for would be smarter AI.
I would give this title 4/5, or 8/10.  Overall the single player was impressive, but lacking in AI (sorry, but Fear kind of upped the bar on this).  I would definately recommend this title due to the other fine things it has to offer.
I purchased this title for $30 (during a sale, if you recall) and I feel it was almost worth that amount.  If you can pick it up for cheaper, you would be wise to do so.  My ideal pricing for this title would be between $15 to $20.
Also, please be aware that if you're looking for multiplayer, this game doesn't have any (which I'm grateful for after the previous Wolfenstein).

Age of Empires 2 HD is a great game which takes the original Age of Empires 2 and basically makes it playable more so on the current operating systems of this day and age.
Nothing new is actually added to the core game, but there is an expansion, aptly named "The Lost Expansion" even though I'm sure nothing like it was ever planned in the past at all.
This expansion adds some new factions, units and new campaigns to the story mode, alongside a version of The Conquer's campaign literally named after the expansion.
This "Lost Expansion" is free and is personally a testament to how more content can actually help a game's survival when given for free. It is ofcourse optional.
The game has plenty of new things, added everywhere. There's Steam Workshop support, Achievements, Trading Cards. In the game there are replays, lobbies, pretty much anything one can expect to find in any RTS game.
In my honest opinion, there is not much other than the above that has been added into the game. Anything else, just look up a review explaining everything in the previous version of the game, Age of Empires 2 Gold Edition and you'll find out everything else.
Some Great things:
- The Expansions
- Slightly better AI
- Some simple multiplayer-based aspects added.
- Replays
- Workshop Support for mods and maps.
However... not much else has been changed. If anything the already large amount of content was simply increased a little bit.
Some Things That Suck:
- Unit Pathing is unchanged. It still sucks and when it becomes apparent, it shows just how dated and irrelevant AoE 2 is in today's gaming market where some games have AI players mimicking players almost identically in some ways in terms of strategy. At a minimum.
- There's no real improvement of actual in-game mechanics, nothing added to gameplay worth much mention so as to actually install atleast an artifical sense of change.
- If there were no additional campaigns, there'd be nearly nothing new as lobbies and replays in an RTS are needed and agiven when it ofcourse has the "obligatory" ranked mode.
- Some factions are still almost not worth using in nearly any type of game, just like in the last one, while others are always the best, such as the Huns with the removal of the need of houses.
- Factions have just as much difference between one another as they always have.
Age of Empires 2 HD is simply a port with a tiny bit of stuff added, nothing is really improved save for AI.
Because of that... I'm inclined to agree with the general opinion of this game as it earns a 5/10. What is added to the game, simply causes the game to be worthy of buying as one can easily install the original to play it, just end the explorer.exe process.
If one wants to play the extra content, buy this game, go ahead. you can't really buy it anywhere however, so if you liked Age of Empires 2 and don't have the orignial game+expansion, then feel free to get this one.

This game has long been a childhood favorite. It was the first game I ever bought and owned for the PC. I played a lot of this game, mainly singleplayer back in 2006, but scratched the CD a couple years later. When I found it had been remastered on Steam I was quick to purchase myself a copy and have been playing both singleplayer and multiplayer since. For those of you who used to own a copy like myself, I highly advise purchasing this digital edition, as it offers both the same nostalgic gameplay and a great strategic outlet. The Forgotten DLC also gives you more to explore and adds even greater variety to an already extensive game. I highly recommend this title, as it has quickly (re)become a personal favorite.
For those of you who haven't played Age of Empires before, it was one of the older RTS games dating back to the late 90s / early 21st century. I'm surprised more people don't play it. You are given a wide selection of civilizations with specific perks each, and try to race each other towards an objective, be it a Wonder Race, Deathmatch, or King of the Hill. All of which are great fun! What really stands out with this game is that there are hundreds, if not thousands of ways to win. Granted, the mechanics may seem simple and outdated, but when trying to runn an entire empire with 200+ units against up to seven other players, every click counts as you try to out-maneuver, out-think, and out-micro your opponent. The graphics may take a while to get used to, but what you really should look forward to enjoying is the satisfaction of wrecking the strong defenses of an enemy with allies or alone, and conquering lands one by one. A great title, I also highly advise purchasing this for the newer community.

My first review of this game was just a joke review, but after several patches, hotfixes and another expansion, I think it's time to write a proper one (this review therefore extends over the base game and both expansions).
For starters, something positive: The new Civs added are really well balanced and fun to play! Here definitely lies the strength of the dev team. They insert themselves into the game seamlessly and feel like they were always part of the game. This adds a ton of replayability, because there are a lot of new strategies to explore, both in terms of playing and defeating them.
One of the main features advertised with the HD Edition was the "new and improved AI". Well... this is definitely not the strength of the dev team, in my opinion. The AI definitely is better than the one from the original game and definitely can be challenging, but it's still lacking in a lot of areas. Basically the biggest "improvement" is that it rushes. Really hard and in big numbers. This makes it really frustrating for beginners to get into the game. But when you can fend of the hordes of enemies and the big first attack, it becomes as easy as usual.
Worth a (negative) mention is the multiplayer. It's unstable as ♥♥♥♥ and it doesn't seem to get better. You get unbearable lag and disconnects and when you think the game is running stable for once, you get an Out of Sync.
This, together with the amount of bugs the game has, some of them still from the release years ago, is pretty sad to be honest. I'm sure the dev team is doing their best to fix this... but that's just not enough at this point. I literally never had a multiplayer session without issues with this game.
All in all, I still recommend this game though.
It's still a lot of fun to play and the campaigns are great too. You can still put hundreds of hours into this game without even having to touch multiplayer once and if you don't like the new AI you can still play with the old Conquerors one.
Get the game when it's on sale though, because paying full price is only worth it when multiplayer finally works better than it does right now.

SUMMARY (because we all like it upfront!):
This game is absolutely fun and worth every penny as long as you've got a good PC, enough bandwidth and storage to download ~40gb, and clear expectations about the genre (i.e. single player FPS, just like Wolfenstein has always been). The graphics are fantastic, the gameplay smooth and dynamic, the levels interesting and varied, the AI largely challenging (some exceptions noted below), the story entertaining, etc. If you're on the fence, get it. If you like single player FPS, get it. If you like killing Nazis, get it.
THE DETAILS:
W:NO is a modern twist on a classic FPS game, and for those who enjoy true FPS games (not open world sand-box survival/MMO/RPG/F2P/TDM/etc. shooters), this game delivers in spades. Now, keep in mind the following: it's a brand-new game with a cutting edge engine and it's a single player FPS as Wolfenstein has always been. If you can wrap your head around these two fundamental details, you shouldn't be caught off guard.
What are the implications of these two facts?
1.) The game requires a huge download of ~40gb primarily due to the massive textures used for ultra high-end graphics. If you've got an internet cap or a small hard drive, that's an issue . . . but keep in mind, it's not a problem with the game itself. Modern games are increasingly big (Payday 2, Diablo 3, etc.) because of the increasingly high-end graphics. Better get used to it and buy a bigger drive/switch to a different internet plan. It's the way of things to come, as it always has been.
2.) The game requires a good system to run well. I'm running an i7 4770k, nVidia 770 4gb,, 16gb DDR3 @1866, and a 240gb SSD. The results? I run the game absolutely maxed out on a custom setting that is higher than the "Ultra" setting, plus I force AA and AF through the console, and I get buttery smooth frame rates consistently @ 1080p. So no, this game doesn't run like♥♥♥♥♥♥ Then again, if you're system is♥♥♥♥♥♥ or you've got ♥♥♥♥♥♥ drivers (AMD, I'm looking at you), then it might run poorly . . . but again, that's not the fault of the game. Time for a new system. Note: there are reports of folks w/ AMD having trouble getting this game to play well. Take these with a grain of salt unless you know the exact specs, game settings, and then general health and optimization of the PC that the complainer is using . . . I keep my gaming rig running fast and clean, and I've got zero issues with this game.
3.) This game is focused and designed around a single-player FPS model much like previous Wolfenstein games. Don't buy it expecting an MMO, an open-world, a non-linear game, a multiplayer-centric experience, etc. That's not what this game is . . . expecting something else would be like buying Minecraft and complaining because it's not like Battlefield 4. This game excels at what it does. The story is engaging, it keeps a fantastic momentum that never leaves you bored and frustrated, the characters range from funny to interesting to downright scary, and there's a great blend of sneaking, balls-to-the-wall gun fights, "Gotcha!" scares, and exploration. Fantastic physics, beautiful graphics, varied and interesting maps, awesome weapons that feel and sound great . . . it's a great time. The AI is a little wonky, but most reports of it being terrible are way overblown. I play on the hardest setting, and it's definitely smart and challenging. The AI shows its weakness when you get in CQC and you're sneaking around. At times, you can crouch walk right up to a guard facing you without alarm, or a guard won't become alarmed at seeing another dead guard. This isn't ideal, but it's forgiveable in light of the fact that the game puts you in so many different types of encounters, the majority of which the AI excels at.
So, don't buy all the negative hype going on in the discussions right now. It's certainly worth noting, as it may help you dodge a bullet or make up your mind, but keep in mind that you should take all opinions and observations (including this one) with a grain of salt. Check in with larger review sites as well, both mainstream and indie, so you can get a sense of how the game holds up to people who review things PROFESSIONALLY . . . it can offer a more balanced perspective.
I, for one, love this game, and I'm having a great time playing it. I'm continually taken aback at how damn good it looks, how smooth the combat and movement is, how dynamic they make a linear story feel, and how much fun this is. Then again, I'm familiar with the genre and I have my expectations set accordingly. This isn't Borderlands, BF4, Skyrim, etc. It harkens back to old-school Wolfenstein, but in a very modern, bad-to-the-bone way. I genuinely hope that Bethesda and other publishers will continue to produce these types of game. It's not as if the existance of this game prevents you from playing Borderlands or w/e else . . . it's just another option. And it's an option that I love, and will enjoy for hours on end.

Worth a (negative) mention is the multiplayer. It's unstable as ♥♥♥♥ and it doesn't seem to get better. You get unbearable lag and disconnects and when you think the game is running stable for once, you get an Out of Sync.
This, together with the amount of bugs the game has, some of them still from the release years ago, is pretty sad to be honest. I'm sure the dev team is doing their best to fix this... but that's just not enough at this point. I literally never had a multiplayer session without issues with this game.
All in all, I still recommend this game though.
It's still a lot of fun to play and the campaigns are great too. You can still put hundreds of hours into this game without even having to touch multiplayer once and if you don't like the new AI you can still play with the old Conquerors one.
Get the game when it's on sale though, because paying full price is only worth it when multiplayer finally works better than it does right now.

W:TNO is what Wolfenstein fans have been waiting for! After Raven's monumental flop with their 2009 version of Wolfenstein, Wolfenstein fans were in mourning, but now is the time to rejoice. Blazkowicz is back!
The most obvious changes, at first, are modernized graphics and gameplay. The game plays smoothly, even while rendering a lot of details and effects.
Ducking mechanics are a bit odd. The game decides for you how you lean out, and it varies with your position and the cover you're using, so you don't always get what you expect. But if you go with it, it actally works quite well. There are times when your perspective as you lean out makes you feel exposed, but you are effectively covered. This goes for stealth also, but there, it's even weirder. There are times when you can be crouched right in front of an enemy and you think, &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥ here goes the alarm!" but he doesn't see you and you can take him down. It doesn't feel quite right. It's even worse than hiding behind a box in plain sight in Deus Ex:HR. But it's not a game breaker.
There isn't a lot of variation in the gameplay. You get a mix of stealth and frontal assault, mostly by your choice, but that's it. This is a pure shooter. And it's a good one. No limp noodle weapons in this game. You shoot something, it dies. It might take a few bullets if it's armored, but you don't empty out a clip to kill a guard.
But the real and unexpected gem is the story. I hate cutscenes. I've erased games from my hard disk for shoving one too many cut scenes down my throat (bye, bye, Hydrophobia: Prophecy), But the cut scenes in W:TNO play out like a movie, and not a bad one. The story and characters are interesting. And Blazkowicz has turned into a human, commenting on what's happening with thoughts that a real person might have. The bad guys are still cliché, but they're more brutal, evil, and revolting. You WANT to take them down.
As a warning to parents, this game is really not appropriate for younger or more sensitive children. There are some fairly disturbing scenes.
I highly recommend this for fans of the Wolfenstein franchise and for those who like a good single-player shooter.

Update:
This game has one of the most functional F2P models I have ever seen, if you are wondering I have such little time played, that is because I use the actual independent launcher most of the time, rather than logging on to steam.  There are no features, minus cosmetic, that are behind a paywall.  You can experience anything and everything, without paying a dime.  New players shouldn't immediately change their weapons, and such, as these weapons really are well balanced, and arguably some of the easiest and most effective to use, most of the time.  The reason why you are able to cut the time down and get a membership (it only affects leveling, which after the first 15 levels doesn't mean anything), you get some free points per month, don't have to wait 0-5minutes to get onto a continent that is about to end, and not much more, other than sales (use these with the points granted to save a lot).
The game itself supports many different playstyles, and is changing often.  Personally I am a cosmetic ♥♥♥♥♥, so my wallet is crying, but again, none of it is needed.  I have friends who have literally played since day 1, on the same character, and don't have ANY cosmetics.  The reason why it takes so long to unlock things is because they want to keep you interested in the game for the longhaul.  Same tactic with CoD.
This game is one of the most beautiful, most enjoyable, and also most frustrating of games I've played.  Frustration is important, because if it is only fun, than there is no challenge to it.  At times flying seems pointless, as you'll be MOWED down by people who think they are the Red Baron or something, and it was a hard mindset to get out of.  I eventually realize that it is like anything, a good player is one who has put a lot of time to learn the mechanics.
To some, that is a bad thing, but for those of us that want to be able to sit down and play a game without worrying about having something to do, there is always something to do.  If I want to fight in a massive infantry zerg, I do it.  If I want to play like Ironman with a Minigun and no jets, I do it.  If I want to coordinate a massive aerial invasion, I can do that too.  Ultimately, the game allows you to do what you want, within your abilities.  Teamwork is key, that is true, however if you don't want to work with a team, or only want to work with a few people (friends/family/etc) you can.  Personally, when I grow bored of teamplay, I take a cloaked flash (ATV), behind enemy lines, and just snipe the poor fools while they are facing my team, this way, even if I don't WANT to work with my team, and deal with the various crazy people, I can still be an asset.

The latest in my string of summer games, and what a treat it was. This game has so much going for it's difficult to know where to start. The story is well-written and engrossing. Dark comedy, quick quips and striking metaphors exceptionally voice-acted make this game's dialogue possibly the best I've ever experienced. But the story itself is also unpredictable, well thought-out and emotionally engaging. This is no Michael Bay movie--it's a well thought out drama, a reflective man's tale, and the script is one among many strong pieces in this complete game. The visuals are outstanding. The settings are diverse and colourful; the animations are varied, smooth and solid; and the graphics themselves top notch as expected. In fact, on the whole, the attention to detail in this game--in its script, graphics, sound, voice-acting--and on and on--is simply outstanding. Example: when you pick up painkillers (the game's form of health) you will get a new thoughtful sound clip almost every time.
Last but certainly not least is the gunplay--and "gunplay" is how I would describe it. The formula is simple, but it works. Flying through the air in slow motion putting holes in bad guys' heads doesn't get old. The game is incredibly violent, which isn't always ideal, but in this case it suits the mood and theme of the game and adds to the many jaw-dropping moments throughout. The term "adrenaline rush" comes to mind when thinking of my first few hours experience with this game. There is so much more I could say, but perhaps the best compliment I can pay this game is that as soon as I finished my first play-through, I began another on the SAME day. The only real bad thing I can say about this game is that it had to come to an end. Picking this up at $10 or less is a no brainer if there ever was one. 9.6/10

Age of Empires II HD is a historical real-time strategy game where the player takes on one of a number of civilizations and builds a base using a group of resources (food, wood, stone, and gold) in order to advance technologically and amass an army to attack one (or multiple) enemy bases, who are attempting to do the same to you.
I played the demo endlessly when I was a kid, but never had the opportunity to play the full game. Having come back to it now, mechanically, the game is actually still solid, and individual games can be very pleasant - quick pick-up games are still good. However, when playing strategy games, I prefer to play through the campaign (if one is provided), and this is what I've found difficulty with. A large number of the missions rely overly on already knowing what the map's layout is - knowing where an enemy is based so you can immediately send a surgical strike to take care of someone before they grow too large so you can grow in peace, knowing where fortifications are, etc. So rather, it's a matter of trial an error as opposed to any strategic decisions in order to beat a given level - there's nothing WRONG with this, necessarily, and it was customary at the time, but less so for modern games.
Now, pick-up games where everyone starts from scratch? That's another thing altogether, and the mechanics work fine for that. I just question whether a person who was used to more modern games coming back to this one would find it much of an enjoyable experience without the nostalgia to build off of, as I don't have much myself, and I often found the game to be frustrating.
Ultimately, I'd say the game is worth a look, but for people who didn't play it when it was new, you may run into a similar frustrations.

Splash Damage games always have excellent gunplay and this is no exception. The game is much closer to movement focused FPS games like Quake and the Enemy Territory games, rather than positional games like Couunter Strike. There's enough variety in mercs and maps to make games interesting. The use of loadout cards and rarity is pretty clever and adds a good sense of progression and min/maxing.
The downside is that grinding is very, very difficult. This isn't a game you can just play for free, probably by design. This wouldn't be a big problem if loadouts were so reliant on RNG and crafting and/or if mercs weren't so damn expensive. The game also suffer from a lack of difference inside each weapon class, especially SMGs and rifles. Dirty Bomb has the misfortune of being managed by Nexon, which means apathetic game management, lazy development, and being mined for all the cash it's worth before being cast aside. Competitive mode is currently a wasteland, though that may be due to its status as an alpha test, rather than a fully developed mode.
Since this is free, the game is worth trying. Your time wont be wasted, though unless you're particularly enchanted, I wouldn't waste cash.

Other than that its just the old AOE2.
But the good thing is that it has multiplayer which is no dead and you can easily find a decent amount of people playing online.
In short here are the pros & cons of this version of game-
PROS-
1.Multiplayer reborned

3.For new players I would say you should try playing this best classic RTS game if you want to.
4.Some minor changes like-
-Select more than 40 units in a row(not sure how much, maybe 50 or 60)
-Supports a maximum of 500 population limit in standard game mode.
CONS-
1.Don't buy if you're concerned only with the HD graphics.
2.Its no remastered edition, its just an old AOE2 with steam workshop and steam trading cards available. But yes it has multiplayer to play.
I really don't mind its graphics as I am fine with its old retro style graphics. But they should have improved its graphics as it says "HD Edition" which it is not :C
Finally, I'm happy that it is on steam, and also the developers are releasing new contents for this game.

I initially gave this game my 'Pile of steaming♥♥♥♥♥♥ rating, due to being an obvious console port, buggy/crashy, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 'social' connection/activation process, as well as basically being unplayable using dx9.
All of the above is still true and accurate, but if you actually manage to play the game, it's actually quite a good storytelling experience from a pacing and delivery perspective.  It also helps that it's basically a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for fans of Michael Mann movies and style.
I was a little disappointed in the departure from the film noir presentation (from the previous games), but that's not that big a deal, as in many ways, this is spiritually a modern film noir.  I DO have to ♥♥♥♥♥ about the CONSTANT & obnoxious visual effects to try to convey Max's alcoholism and drug addiction, as it's bad enough that it's nearly a dealbreaker.
The only other thing that needs to be mentioned, is this game could have been called 'Cutscene 3: Rockstar Wants To Make Movies', and while it does add a certain stylistic element to the game that actually adds to the Mann-style presentation, I'm torn by how annoying it gets.
This game could have been ♥♥♥♥ing awesome, but instead, it falls squarely in the 'pretty good' column, mostly because of what I mentioned in the first paragraph.  And the fact that it's 3rd person, but if you're a Max Payne fan, you knew that going into it, so I can't really hold that against it.
From the perspective of the series, this is very much a Max Payne story.  Max's soul and tortured existance comes through exactly the way I would expect from a third installment, and is completely believable that this is where he ends up.
All in all, it's a good game, despite it's problems.

FIrst, there are a ton of technical issues. Memory leaks, intro movies don't like to play, program doesn't properly shut down, and so on. There are some fixes around, but I haven't had any luck with them. Now... All that out of the way, the game itself runs flawless on my system, once I get past the intro movies. From time to time, if I play too long, I need to reboot because of a memory leak from the game, but until that becomes an issue, it's smooth as silk. One MAJOR beef that I have is that there is absolutely no surround sound support. The game has incredible sounds, but it all goes to waste without 5.1 support. Wolfenstein 2009 had -amazing- surround sound support, heck, even RTCW had support, why abandon it now? It -really- detracts from the environment. The graphics are fine, but I wish that Depth of Field could be turned off without console hacks. Ignoring the technical issues, I give the overall presenation a "C+", losing a full letter for the lack of surround support. Now, on to the game itself.
I'm a huge fan of the series, I always have been. Heck, I even loved Wolfenstein 2009. So far, more than halfway thru my first playthrough, I'm very satisfied with the story. I wish they would've acknowledged more of the stories from RTCW & 2009 (Ubersoldat vs Supersoldat, the events of 2009 outside of one major character, and so on). The story has been wildly entertaining, tons of easter eggs, tons of collectibles that add to the environment. I'm kind of torn on the new approach to BJ, however. Voiceless Murder Machine in 3D, Voiceless Polish Murder Machine in RTCW who takes his vacations in warzones voluntarily, Sarcastic Polish Murder Machine in 2009.... Emo reluctant murder machine now, however. I understand the approach in regards to realism, but it did kind of detract from the character to me. Concerning the gameplay, I didn't care for that you can no longer carry heavy weapons with you. Yes, this is a nod to more realistic gameplay, but to me, kind of spits on the older games as a result. Part of the allure of the older games, especially 2009, was a weapon for certain occasions. The cover system they've implemented is perfect to me, though I would've liked dedicated lean keys instead of direction + modifier. All things considered, I'll give the story and gameplay a combined "A".
If I ignore the technical issues, which I'm sure will be fixed in time, I give the game overall a "B". The lack of the surround sound support really detracts from my immersion, but the game is incredibly solid on pretty much all fronts aside from that. It'll definitely get another playthrough even right after I finish it.

A CPU-melting combined arms massively multiplayer online first person shooter. Riddled with bugs, the community is hit-or-miss, and the development pace could be perceived as sluggish to some. However, this game offers a much larger scale than anything currently on the market, which is why it appeals to me.
It's a game with a steep barrier to entry, however. Even now, a free player with little guidance will find himself confused and unable to progress his character at a suitable speed. It's a game that you'll need to watch a fair few videos on, and play hundreds of hours, to understand.
Notable community members such as Wrel have a plethora of videos aimed at helping newbies. I highly suggest checking him out before rage-uninstalling this game.
Also of note: due to the sheer amount of stuff that can happen at once, in a small area, a mid- to high-end cpu is a must if you want to play at a somewhat reasonable framerate. Not for the spud of heart.

Age of Empires II HD is a historical real-time strategy game where the player takes on one of a number of civilizations and builds a base using a group of resources (food, wood, stone, and gold) in order to advance technologically and amass an army to attack one (or multiple) enemy bases, who are attempting to do the same to you.
I played the demo endlessly when I was a kid, but never had the opportunity to play the full game. Having come back to it now, mechanically, the game is actually still solid, and individual games can be very pleasant - quick pick-up games are still good. However, when playing strategy games, I prefer to play through the campaign (if one is provided), and this is what I've found difficulty with. A large number of the missions rely overly on already knowing what the map's layout is - knowing where an enemy is based so you can immediately send a surgical strike to take care of someone before they grow too large so you can grow in peace, knowing where fortifications are, etc. So rather, it's a matter of trial an error as opposed to any strategic decisions in order to beat a given level - there's nothing WRONG with this, necessarily, and it was customary at the time, but less so for modern games.
Now, pick-up games where everyone starts from scratch? That's another thing altogether, and the mechanics work fine for that. I just question whether a person who was used to more modern games coming back to this one would find it much of an enjoyable experience without the nostalgia to build off of, as I don't have much myself, and I often found the game to be frustrating.
Ultimately, I'd say the game is worth a look, but for people who didn't play it when it was new, you may run into a similar frustrations.

During the development of the new Wolf - I was skeptical. Hell, up until release I was skeptical. I feared they were going to CoDify my beloved Wolf and BJ Blazkowicz would never again be the baddest Nazi-killin ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this side of the 4th Reich.
But I was wrong.
Although it starts out slow - Wolfenstein: TNO soon turns into one hell of a game. It looks as good as any modern shooter, plays like the mid 2000's shooters like Soldier of Fortune you remember so well, and tells a story so ridiculous yet so deathly serious you can't help but get caught up in it. Not to mention the characters. Hell, it's been weeks since I beat this game and I can still name all the main characters in this story without hardly even thinking about it. They're all so well realized. So well voiced. They're all important. It's a rare thing in shooters these days.  But it all comes back to Blazko:
One part Lt. Aldo Raine, two parts John McClane and three parts Bear Jew. BJ is back and a better character than he has ever been. Simply put, he IS the baddest Nazi Killin' ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you've ever met. And he's not going down without a fight. Or two. Or three. Or ten. In fact, over the 12-15 hours it'll take you to beat this single player only affair, you'll ask yourself repeatedly - how is this grizzled old ♥♥♥♥ not dead yet?! "Get up, old man. You ain't done yet."
Machinegames did a hell of a job bringing Wolf back for a new generation and as an old school Wolf fan and a champion of old school shooters, I can't say enough about Wolfenstein: TNO. Hell, the best compliment I could give it is that this is the sort of game Raven wishes they could still be making. Equal parts emotional, cinematic, bloody and badass. It's a 2014 FPS ripped right out of 2004's FPS style. You know, back when games like Half Life 2 were what we played, and Call of Duty single player campaigns still meant something.
What else can I say? Get it. And get to killin' some ♥♥♥♥in' Nazis.

Splash Damage games always have excellent gunplay and this is no exception. The game is much closer to movement focused FPS games like Quake and the Enemy Territory games, rather than positional games like Couunter Strike. There's enough variety in mercs and maps to make games interesting. The use of loadout cards and rarity is pretty clever and adds a good sense of progression and min/maxing.
The downside is that grinding is very, very difficult. This isn't a game you can just play for free, probably by design. This wouldn't be a big problem if loadouts were so reliant on RNG and crafting and/or if mercs weren't so damn expensive. The game also suffer from a lack of difference inside each weapon class, especially SMGs and rifles. Dirty Bomb has the misfortune of being managed by Nexon, which means apathetic game management, lazy development, and being mined for all the cash it's worth before being cast aside. Competitive mode is currently a wasteland, though that may be due to its status as an alpha test, rather than a fully developed mode.
Since this is free, the game is worth trying. Your time wont be wasted, though unless you're particularly enchanted, I wouldn't waste cash.

As I entered the armory of the Impact sight, I knew we would soon be overrun by at least two to one. Everyone positioned themselves at the points:
(Next to the Spawn and armory),
(The bridge), and
(On a hill, between alpha and bravo). I stationed myself in between Alpha and Charlie after grabbing a harasser jeep mounted with the G-30 Walker anti-air gun which can make quick work of any enemy, including armored vehicles.
After five minutes have passed, the first New Conglomerate sunderrer APC/Spawn had arrived along with several reapers which were easily taken down. However, several large platoons appeared shortly after annihilating our forces at point Bravo. Charlie, was their next plan of attack and I knew it. It was an essential point of attack if they were to attack Alpha.
I arrived at Charlie after taking care of a sunderrer which made it to a wall behind Alpha. My goal was to take care of an anti-vehicle turret set up in the high cliffs of these edge of the meteor sight. Unfortunately, it did not work out as planned due to a quickly assembled blitzkreig tactic used by several lightning tanks and a squad of infantry units which had destroyed my vehicle yet again, yet I refused to fall without a fight! I had taken down one of the tanks and several of the foot soldiers before they could take me with them!
Resurrecting back inside the armory, I had learned that Charlie has been taken and there was a slim chance of counter-attacking the New Conglomerate forces (which had numbered within a hundred against our twenty-four to forty-eight). I geared up with four other units and a few engineers in order to take the bridge back. There was little resistance until it was ours. Two lightning tanks had discovered us which then forced me to go on a suicide mission with one objective - take out their armor! It worked! I had laid down several anti-tank mines and they did their job as the lightning's rushed us. (I fell off the bridge several minutes later)
Unfortunately, the battle was not going so well for Alpha and Charlie. I went back to the armor discovering that Alpha was the only objective belonging to us due to a Conglomerate counter-attack on our counter-attack at Bravo. I knew immediately to reach high ground as an engineer to set up an anti-infantry turret to at least slow their advance, unfortunately it did not end well, and I was shot in the back. I 'respawned', geared up as a max, and let out a battle cry,
I charged out knowing this was the final stand. I knew, defeat for inevitable.
Rushing out, as many of my fellow comrades were being gunned down, I charged with my grenade launcher and mini-gun annihilating many enemies as they were advancing on Alpha. The Conglomerate menace had taken the objective and the important location was slowing turning to theirs, betraying the original owners of the base. And as I was quickly outgunned, they shot me down. As I fell, the base overturned to the Conglomerate allowing them an almost direct attack on our Warpgate (Main base).
This battle between the Terran Republic, [very few] Vanu Sovereignty, and the New Conglomerate was epic. The Battle of the Meteor Impact Sight lasted two hours. and three more hours after the major battle, we lost the continent.

Used to be a good game at several points, but is currently utter trash on all accounts.
1. Matchmaking - Tiers based on CPU? That's flawed, it can be cheated around as is currently. You see small drones with a single OP weapon and that's even under 500 CPU. New-ish players stand no chance and people with normal bots can't compete with a solid chunk of a weaon taking that makes up for most of the HP of the micro bot yet easily mows down their lower tier water guns. High tier weapons should have a minimum CPU requirement to keep them out of lower tier matches. It's ugly to see a mini bot with a heatseeker or a single leg top-tier laser SMG.
2.Weapon balance -
A) Rocket launcher - any heatseeking weapon in any game will either have a rather easy dodge system, counter measures or low enough stats to be risky. Currently the rocket launcher in lower tiers has vision-range(which puts it on par with the railgun), has perfect heatseeking and wall penetration(no need to aim, can't dodge in the open), can be accessed for lower tiers(allows it to 1- or 2-burst any but the fattest bots), has instant lock-on(shots fired faster than most railguns would produce a 2nd shot if not spammed on a bot). It should be revetred to slower lock-on, MUCH smaller range- a laser barrage should counter it effectively 1 on 1 damage-wise in the open, should be dodge-able from longer ranges by every movement type except hover-only bots and have lower health, so it would force a smarter usage. Heat-seeking is the easy choice and should be the only advantage for the weapon, while everything else should be nerfed to keep the balance.
B) Flak cannon - should be the weapon of choice against smaller flyers, while bigger ones should be countered by railguns. Flak should have deadly damage against annoying small flyers so as to promote more interesting builds, rather than the mellee mosquitoes that run around everywhere.
C) Mid tier laser waepons need more damage, as now I find myself just spamming a bot just to see him barely lose any hp/modules. They are useless vs microbots with high tier weapons.
3. Damage spread- there are ways to avoid it by non-solid blocks and it looks ugly and unrealistic. In reality such a build would fall apart from a single shot and not neutralize the damage. If anything, it should be exactly the opposite from now- solid-built robots should have a bonus in toughness.
4. Reward system - it is a grind fest. Random drops that are trash for the most part and worth nothing to sell. The currency system worked and higher tier parts should be easily accessible so people don't have to invest a ton of time just to have more than 1 higher tier bot. Considering we can have several bots, it's a pain to get the preferred weapons on just one or two if not very active.
Conclusion: Way to destroy a game. I have never seen a bigger downfall in my gaming experience.

After playing this game through I can say with confidence that it is the best story driven game that I have played: The world building, animation and acting all gather to create a compelling storyline filled with poignant and oftentimes touching sentiments in a grimdark yet believable imagining of a world ruled by Nazis.
On top of this, gameplay wise The New Order does not skimp; allowing balls to wall action sequences or tense stealth areas all in the same area. For storyline, beautiful and incredibly varied settings (which I will not spoil) and gameplay this is a game that will be difficult to beat.
However, it does have it's failings, number one being how well it bloody runs. It took me an hour after I had installed the game to get it running as I browsed the support forums trying to get the thing to start. Not a detraction as the game itself is not buggy but be aware it may take a while to get up and running.
The other thing is that the game has a weird interaction system with the difficulty - let me explain. I played the game on 'Hard', it was ok. Died a fair amount of times and I would recommend it for any experienced player - allowing you to stealth well, engage in some cover shooting, but not so much run and gun all the time. But there is SO MUCH ARMOUR AND HEALTH EVERYWHERE. It broke the continuity slightly. Many fights could leave me dead and broken multiple times on the ground, health quickly demolished by some Nazi supersoldiers; but so long as I survived the fight then soon after I would be at 100 HP and probably 100 Armour ready to begin the next fight in the exact same way. At one point in the game it started feeling like I was moving through a series of interactions where I was returned to full health after each one. This was when the game upped the pace however and♥♥♥♥♥♥got real in the ensuing fights, picking up the tension once again.
If you want a decent challenge go hard, because if you're playing on Normal difficulty you better be dual wielding ALL the time as your play style to justify playing it on a lower setting.
In short, this is an awesome game, well worth playing. Don't buy it for 40 quid, don't buy ANY game for that much money - get it on sale or buy a steam key; but this game will give you an emotional, visual and adrenal hit that will leave you hungry for more.

The beginning of this game will raise concern. Within the first few hours of playtime, I could easily picture the gameplay getting stale. It came off as just an average shooter without a solid story line. Once the plot of the game becomes more pronounced, I felt it gripping on to me tighter. My worries faded after about 5 hours in when I realized that I was still having an amazing time. It dove more in depth with strategy playing a big role in the areanas. Enemies surpassed the dumbed down 'put 10 bullets in their chest and they're dead' style of FPS that you see so often today. Different mobs require different weapons, special locational damage, and in some cases, environmental components in order to defeat. The best part? BOSS FIGHTS. Machine Games had a better view on what makes a challenging fight. The developers know that just throwing in overwhelming numbers on enemies to make things tough isn't what you want. Instead, they will strip down the cover system (excellent btw) into something that can only utilized with a strategic mindset and then spawn enemies that have the ability to easily control the room unless you consider their weeknesses and exploit them. The AI's aren't stupid either, it's impossible in this game to just bunker down to one vantage point to wipe out the whole room. They will flank, reposition, and use equipment to bring you out.
Oh, and the dev implemented a stealth system that's actually suprisingly decent. There are three different styles you can follow, each with their own associated chain of perks. Sneak in and take out the squad commanders to eliminate the possibility of them calling in reforcements. You can follow the strategy set, planning out your positioning and setting prioritized targets, or if your in the mood for some quick carnage, go ahead and pick up that second assault rifle/shotgun/pistol and duel wield the ever-living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of anyone who gets in your way : >
I had fun the whole way through. I would reccomend this to anyone who has even slight interest if FPS games.
Overall: 8 / 10 |  Although gameplay is amazing, they may go a little overboard with the theatrics. Narration by the protaganist can get a little cheesy at times, and he's constatly doing it. Story can be more gripping as well. None of this stuff is close to game-breaking, but it prevents it from being a 10/10

Age of Empires II: Age of Kings was originally released in 1999, and it is one of the most influential titles in one of real-time strategy’s most celebrated franchises. It holds a special place within gaming history as a solid, meat-and-potatoes RTS generously drizzled with rich historical gravy.
Age of Empires II: HD’s main changes are updates to the graphics engine, allowing the game to be compatible with modern machines. The game has been overhauled to allow players to take advantage of HD displays and multiple monitors. But one of the strongest elements of the re-release is the score, which has been lovingly remixed. The music now evokes a more sophisticated mood than it did previously, and it’s something that adds greatly to the feel of the game.
This edition of Age of Empires II includes The Conquerors expansion, so fans wanting to replay the campaigns will find hours of familiar scenarios. These haven’t aged particularly well; the scripting system compares poorly with other titles, particularly Blizzard’s Warcraft III and StarCraft II. There are many instances of breaking the fourth wall, where victory and activation conditions are very obviously scripted rather than fitting seamlessly into gameplay.
The new textures added to water, fire, and earth add a nice new look to the terrain. It’s subtle, but the overall impression is refined and almost painterly. The terrain itself has been one of the biggest changes, with a mesh system now used to give a more even natural landscape. Also gone are the 256 colour UI elements, and the icons have been updated to a more rustic feel to go with the softer 32-bit colour scheme.
The only significant change made at all to gameplay is the raising of the maximum population cap to 500. This is a lost opportunity to fix the kinds of problems that even diehard fans consider simple annoyances. The ability to select more than 20 units would have been a worthy addition, and is simply a control flaw rather than a balance or creative issue. Running at 1920x1080 allows for a huge number of units on one screen, which still need to be divided into small divisions to command in battle.
The most positive change – and one that will justify the price tag for most players – is multiplayer. Although alternative matchmaking services have done much to keep interest in the online game alive over the years since the demise of Microsoft’s clunky Gaming Zone, Steam integration puts players back onto a universal ladder system. The platform’s social features and existing framework also mean players can come to the game with their own networks firmly in place.
So for better or worse, Steam has come along and is now selling a game it’s quite possible many gamers already own in some form or other. The changes are subtle, but well-intentioned and admirably executed. Multiplayer is excellent. Those who loved Age of Empires II should happily indulge in some nostalgia with this HD facelift. Anyone new to the game will be frustrated by the lack of modern control systems and responsive hot keys.

Truthfully, this game brings back alot of memories. Memories that i kinda forgot about.
But this isn't about my memories, it's a review.. so let's get started.
(sorry if it's a biit long i want to go in depth with my reviews)
Gameplay.
8/10
Firstly, i must say that Age of empires was and still is one of the games that i enjoyed playing with freinds. the gameply is both simplistic and advanced depending on your skill level ( personally i am not the best :P ) but i have watched gameplay's with 1v3 and the player on his/her own winning. this game is definately worth getting if you have a few freinds that own it, or if you are going to buy it for them aswell, however, personally, i never got into the single player ( hence not giving gameply 10/10 ). Although i can't, it does not mean other players will not enjoy it. Back to the gameplay mechanics being both simplistic and advanced, the player takes control of units within the game. depedning on certain aspects the gamplay can be as advanced as you want it. for example whether using micromanagement skills or not can drastically change how difficult a game can be for both you and the other player. Don't let this draw you away however because alot of players play for fun, which makes it a bit easier for new players. The learning curve is also quite small, a new player could easily compete agains bot's with only a few hours of playing ( human players on the other hand may be a bit tougher, but practice makes perfect). The best part in the gameply howerver is playing against freinds and using deception to trick them. Making them believe you are on their side and siding with the enemy and bringing your freind down makes for some fun times and funny reactions.
visuals
6/10
The remasterd/HD Remake takes playing the old age of empires to a new level, with the implemantation of a few 3D models and Higher textured sprites allows us to enjoy a more better looking game ( not saying the old one looks bad). Also the ability to use texture packs downloaded within the steamworkshop is a plus. :D
Story
3/10
Again i can't really say much for this as i havn't played the single player. and the multiplayer has no story, but i may edit this once i go an complet the campaign.
overall
8/10
This game is not for all people, but if you are a fan of real time strategy games, and or used to play the age of empire series in the old days :P, this this is definately worth the buy.

I've played this a bit so far and it's pretty entertaining. The graphics are pretty, the machines and enemies you fight are interesting, It can be played as an all out Shoot em up or as a stealth game, which ever you prefer. I'm not too far into it but I've already spent 7 hours sneaking around, finding all the collectables, and trying to get either knife or silenced headshot stealth insta-kills. It's not too difficult but it is pretty fun.
The maps have a decent sense of exploration with hidden passage ways and secret item collection eastereggs/health/ammo/collectables. You can ignore all that if you really want but I had fun with it and it's nessecery if you wanna play stealth. I say play stealth but that works like it does in most "stealth"games. You are stealthy for a while, you pick your targets off one by one but then you turn a conor and someone yells for backup, switches on an alarm, and you go into all-out take cover and hold the trigger down mode. Once the you kill the enemies and the alarm goes off things go back to pretending to be stealthy again because apparentlly they didn't bother to phone anyone else.
The perk system is a set of challenges and while there is somewhat of a tree (a few perks require a previous perk) most everything is up for grabs so you don't have to choose one perk tree to focus on.
The storyline and lore is a pile of dung but I don't think a lot of people will be expecting an well done story anyway. Typical action hero finds a lady who falls in love with him instantly for no reason, action hero is fully capable of acomplishing any extreme pysichal task even if the story established that he just got out of a 15 year paralysis, etc. There was one point in the story after waking up from said paralysis that went something like this:
Hero: Where is the resistance?
Old lady: Don't you see? The nazis won! They've been ruling the world for 15 years now! There is no america or resistance left!
Hero: Take me to the resistance!
Old lady: OK.
That's why I think the storytelling is so awful. I wouldn't have minded if there was no story but making such a big deal of it and at the same time making it so bad is a bit of a setback. Still, the gameplay is fun so I can work to ignore that aspect.
All the nazis are treated as if they are literally hitler. There's little newspaper clippings spread throughout the levels which help immerse you in the world but all the clippings are about how evil nazis are. The I-hate-you-because-I-label-you-as-a-nazi thing gets really old and seems a bit shallow. If there was anything to be gained from it, it helps you understand what it's like to be on the losing end of a war where you are completly dominated and invaded and although it's exaggerated I did appreciate that perspective.
Overall so far I have really enjoyed the game and will continue to play it when I want something simple and slightly challenging to occupy me.

I'll address some issues separately:
- This games has the stench of console-optimisation about it, without ever being on any other platform. The game, after the latest major update, eats at my CPU even though the game runs at 120fps. S
- Servers are unstable as ♥♥♥♥, no proper anti-cheat and the Quick Join option is laughably bad. More often than not you'll find yourself all alone on a Russian server (When you're in the EU) or on a server that seems to run on a twenty year old PC.
- The lack of "join as team" outside of competitive mode (read: Cheat City mode) when this game is mostly about dynamics and teamwork is poor thinking on the developers part.
- Menu lag. OH GODS does this game have it? It feels like Hearthstone did when it came out on PC, menu-lag abound which makes it hard to change mercs in the lobby, not to mention navigate the damn menus
(this is a game where you can spend A LOT of time upgrading your loadouts, so this is REALLY not ideal).
- Lack of balance when it comes to mercs is also a think they need to look at. You see the same merc, 2 at the most unless people are going for their missions, within each role constantly.
A tiny, but for me important remark: When you mute someone (say, a 10-year-old child with an extremely loud microphone) he won't stay muted during your next match, even if it's the same server and you both stay IN the lobby between matches. Please free me from prepubescent screeching monkeys.
The good things:
Most mercs are fun as hell, even if they aren't super optimised.
The gamemodes are fun
The maps are cool, though more would be nice
The sound design's great
The core gameplay is exhilarating
The community is, by and large, pretty cool.
That being said, this is NOT a Beta-game. They've had an ingame store for years and it's been in "Open Beta" since before Pacman was created. Remove that freaking tag and stop hiding behind a beta-status.
I would NOT recommend the game in its current state, since it eats away at CPUs like a fat kid at an all-you-can-eat buffet, but when that's fixed I'd say: Give it a shot.

10/10! As you journey through the massive Aperture facility, it becomes clear that Portal 2 does not merely come after Portal. Instead, it radiates outward from its predecessor, simultaneously illuminating the world that gave rise to Portal and continuing the adventure that began there. The sense of novelty is diminished, but the thrill of exploration and puzzle-solving is still intoxicating, and it's amazing how Portal 2 manages to tell a better story with disembodied voices and spherical robots than most games can with full-on humans. Your return to Aperture Science is a joyful one in this immensely appealing, laugh-out-loud funny, and thoroughly satisfying sequel. Immensely clever writing, new characters are hugely entertaining, and the cooperative campaign creates intriguing situations! The only bad thing about this game that I could come up with would be the frequent load times. Valve cuts no corners and finds ways to make you care about everything from the major characters to the cubes used to solve puzzles. From the beginning of the single-player story to the end of the co-op mode, Portal 2 is a novel, unforgettable experience.

I've played this a bit so far and it's pretty entertaining. The graphics are pretty, the machines and enemies you fight are interesting, It can be played as an all out Shoot em up or as a stealth game, which ever you prefer. I'm not too far into it but I've already spent 7 hours sneaking around, finding all the collectables, and trying to get either knife or silenced headshot stealth insta-kills. It's not too difficult but it is pretty fun.
The maps have a decent sense of exploration with hidden passage ways and secret item collection eastereggs/health/ammo/collectables. You can ignore all that if you really want but I had fun with it and it's nessecery if you wanna play stealth. I say play stealth but that works like it does in most "stealth"games. You are stealthy for a while, you pick your targets off one by one but then you turn a conor and someone yells for backup, switches on an alarm, and you go into all-out take cover and hold the trigger down mode. Once the you kill the enemies and the alarm goes off things go back to pretending to be stealthy again because apparentlly they didn't bother to phone anyone else.
The perk system is a set of challenges and while there is somewhat of a tree (a few perks require a previous perk) most everything is up for grabs so you don't have to choose one perk tree to focus on.
The storyline and lore is a pile of dung but I don't think a lot of people will be expecting an well done story anyway. Typical action hero finds a lady who falls in love with him instantly for no reason, action hero is fully capable of acomplishing any extreme pysichal task even if the story established that he just got out of a 15 year paralysis, etc. There was one point in the story after waking up from said paralysis that went something like this:
Hero: Where is the resistance?
Old lady: Don't you see? The nazis won! They've been ruling the world for 15 years now! There is no america or resistance left!
Hero: Take me to the resistance!
Old lady: OK.
That's why I think the storytelling is so awful. I wouldn't have minded if there was no story but making such a big deal of it and at the same time making it so bad is a bit of a setback. Still, the gameplay is fun so I can work to ignore that aspect.
All the nazis are treated as if they are literally hitler. There's little newspaper clippings spread throughout the levels which help immerse you in the world but all the clippings are about how evil nazis are. The I-hate-you-because-I-label-you-as-a-nazi thing gets really old and seems a bit shallow. If there was anything to be gained from it, it helps you understand what it's like to be on the losing end of a war where you are completly dominated and invaded and although it's exaggerated I did appreciate that perspective.
Overall so far I have really enjoyed the game and will continue to play it when I want something simple and slightly challenging to occupy me.

This is an old RTS-classic. Even after 15 years people still play it, and I know why.
Not going to say too much about it. The goal of the game is to build an empire, gather resources and destroy your opponent. You can fight with or against your friends in teamgames. Most people buy because they used to play it, but it is also recommended for people that don't know this title.
There are a few multiplayer platforms. The first one is obviously on Steam itself, the other one is on voobly where the more advanced players play. I recommend starting in the Steam lobbies before going to the Voobly lobbies, because the level tend to be too high for beginners.
Pro:
- Fun campaigns (FE campaigns are quite difficult though)
- Fluent gameplay
- 'Improved' visuals (even though it's not a big difference)
- Multiplayer lobbies (both HD and FE or joined together now)
- Mod workshop (after big update) is user friendly
Con:
- It's pretty much the same version, but with better visuals. 20 dollars isn't really worth it. I recommend buying it during Steam sales.
- Moonwalking soldiers when patrolling
- Lag on Steam platform (more often than on Voobly platform)

I thought, "Damn this is cool!!!" If I was playing DukeNuke'emSide 2, I would have seen the whites of his eyes... and the whites of his teeth... and an assortment of other freely spinning entrails. (BTW, what ever happened to gibbing in video games? We have all these fancy PhysX cards, so the time is nigh to give us our ragdoll physics and flying body parts back!) Most importantly, I was impressed with how lethal I felt in that situation, and also how vulnerable I was, since if he had a split second longer to aim, his fighter's nose cannon would have turned me into mincemeat.
Lethality and vulnerability are two very important concepts in real warfare. In the blink of an eye, a few ounces of metal can transform a soldier from killer to KIA. Taking this discussion back to the digital world, in order for combat focused shooters to impress me, they need "realism". They need to integrate those two powerful concepts (lethality and vulnerability), which when interwoven properly can create a realistic and utterly intense true-to-life battlefield experience.
For an example of my perspective, I've never been satisfied with run and gun arena shooters where the standard measure of making a kill is not bullets spent but, rather frustratingly, magazines spent. Conversely, I am drawn methodical simulations like America's Army. Say what you want about the slow pacing of the great military simulations like that; I will tell you that the intensity and desperation of the firefights that erupt in that style of videogame is second to none. In a game like that, I have to think before I move. In a game like that, I have to utilize cover effectively because no, I'm not Ironman. I'm actually nothing more than a bag of fleshy meat, but when I put a well aimed 3 round burst in your fleshy meaty chest, well... you're dead. In a game like that, I'm very vulnerable, but I'm also very lethal, and (more importantly) my gun feels
.
That brings me to the core of the issue. Guns are powerful. Youtube a video of an AA12 autoshotgun digging a shallow trench in some dirt in 3 seconds with 30 shells of buckshot and you can see the power for yourself. Seriously, that gun could kill a man
! Dat power though! When I play shooters, I want THAT power!
As Day 1 on Auraxium -the homeworld of purple spandex and an eternal 3 faction teabag orgy set in the Planetside universe- continued, I began to realize that the game falls in a weird middle section along the spectrum of realism and well... trashy arcadey nonsense. Sure, my rocket launcher could kick some♥♥♥♥♥ but my guns felt like peashooters. It took 4+ headshots to kill an enemy foot grunt. If I want you dead, I can count myself lucky if 3 three round bursts sends you to the redeployment screen. So no, this game is NOT a simulation; no, realism is NOT a key feature. In that respect I can't recommend this game the way I would do for the Red Orchestra series or the early Ghost Recon games. The gunplay for the most part is disappointingly limp.
And I hate Planetside 2 because of it. But, like a woman in denial and continually drawn back into an abusive relationship, I find myself making excuses for the black eyes and hand-shaped bruises around the neck. No no no, honestly... I fell down the stairs and Planetside caught me by the neck. Totally saved my life, wait what??? Of course I still love Planetside! What kind of question is that!?
So yes I'm a filthy cheating ♥♥♥♥♥ who's forsaken my vows of commitment to the mil-sims I fell in love with, and on the side I'm playing a dirty little arcade shooter with health regeneration. "Why" you might ask?
Well, I'm happy to report that
itself takes centerstage in PS2 and that raw power can still be experienced despite the weak gunplay. This epic power comes from charging a heavily defended enemy installation with 100 other men and women while the Battle of Britain is re-enacted above your head by dozens of fighters and bombers; from when you and 100 other men and women try to hold back a tsunami of flesh and meat that crashes against the walls and gates of your heavily defended installation; from crushing a tank with a bellyflop from a massive troop transport; from putting on a suit of power armor and tearing an objective out of enemy hands in an elegant waltz of blood and death that puts Black Swan to shame; from the thunder of 30 main battle tanks firing a continuous bombardment that rips an infantry formation to pieces; from being part of a well organized Terran Republic platoon that washes that Vanu Sovereignty stain right off the map; from saving the last grenade for yourself when an overwhelming force annihilates your platoon (you always were a prick, Gorman). Raw power oozes from combat on an epic scale that trumps the deficiencies of the one on one combat and weak gunplay.
Also very epic Planetside 2 is the top notch level design. The continents are very well made with plenty of doodads and terrain features that provide cover for infantry and vehicles while assaulting and defending bases. The bases are also much improved upon their original iterations that existed in the months after the game launched. Auraxium and her continents now provide a battlefield that is an active and living character in the ongoing struggles that scar her landscapes.
This is a game with a learning curve. Only after you understand the dynamics of how the different classes and vehicles interact with each other can you truly appreciate Planetside for its strengths. At the core, PS2 is a class-based team shooter. As such, playing a class to a general role is the best way to enjoy the experience. Additionally, you can further tailor your classes to fill more specific roles by purchasing upgrades in a significantly deep character development process. This allows for a rather large variety of playstyles that can fill a wide range of roles in battle. There are right ways to play these roles, and also very wrong ways to play them.
For example, if you select engineer and if you then choose to enter a one-on-one engagement a heavy assault who has max rank body armor and activated overshields, heh. Let's just say that any talk about scoring headshots here is moot; instead, immediately insert your own head between your legs cuz you've played the game wrong and foolishly left yourself very little time to kiss your♥♥♥♥♥goodbye. Next time you see a Uruk-hai Assault you need to listen to Gandalf and fly, you fool! If you wanted to be the spearhead of such an attack you should have built your own Middle Earth superhero. If your character is built to be the tip of the assault, then close the distance and smash the enemy. If you're built for support, then flow in with the second wave and pick off the stragglers and resupply or revive your allies. The point is you can find yourself dying a lot, not gaining xp or otherwise not having fun if you're playing your class outside its scope of operation.
Taken as a whole, this is a game I can recommend if you can stomach the situations where an enemy can eat your whole magazine with his back, then turn after you've taken care of all those itches for him and one-shot your face to death with his pump action shotgun. Prepare for epic frustration, but also prepare for epic fun!

I'm going to start by saying that this game's score form me is 98.5%. If you have played Max Payne 1 (or especially 2) you will be so happy with Max Payne 3 as a fantastic addition to the franchise.
1. Story 95/100: The thought of sending Max to such a different (yet so similar) hive of villainy in Brazil gave the team such creative freedom in making this story. It's visceral, brutal, full of noir and revenge. The frequent inner monologues of Max make a character you play like no other. He's an old boy, almost to mid 40's. You feel it, you hear inside his mind and you become Max in this game; a protagonist and character that you have never felt so uniquely tuned into. Even better than the twists and turns of MP2, never did I feel the story was lacking in any way, and kept me guessing until the last chapter.
2. Grahpics: 85/100: At maximum they look great, still Rockstar is unable to breach the DX11 barrier by themselves, but as a testement to the game engine they have done much to keep the game looking amazing. The slow motion effects, decals and texture details are fantastic. Persistent bullet holes (often through my own limbs and spine). They did a great job on Max, absolutely great.
3. Gameplay: 99/100: Like any sequel (or threequel) it needs to be bigger and better than its former. The gunplay is improved, bullet time is amazing, and innovations like 'last stand' are visceral and hyper-tense. The improvements to dives make it feel real, and feel like it hurts to slam into those walls as you dive dynamically.
My first playthrough was on Hard difficulty and there are 2 unlockable harder than that difficulties that I am going to attempt now.
A lot of great replayability, golden guns to collect (which have tangible benefits) and misc. story clues to find which add to the universe.
3. Sound: Rockstar went to real effort to make each gun have kick and a real thump to them (I hope you have surround sound and bass, holy crap). The final songs are awesome, especially HEALTH - TEARS which you hear towards the end and in the final credits. Also, they stay true to the original haunting film noir piano theme tune for max in this, with very subtle modern changes.
I bought this game for $12.49 on sale, and I would have been happy paying 99.95 for it. It's worth that easily.
Best memories:
- Slow motion office shootouts with sh!t flying literally everywhere
- Watching my final bullet from the milisecond leave my gun and bore itself into the skull of an enemy I was aiming at quite a long distance away.
- Holding down left click whilst the camera zoomed into the face of a criminal I pumped a 42 round machine gun into, seeing the first to the forty second bullet tear through his chest then to his skull (completely dynamic ingame system).
- The game is hard, pretty damn hard, but not impossible and keeps you going and going. I think my record was about 28 deaths in one area (only chapter 3 or so too! But the game kept on encouraging me to punch through it and win. Felt so good to get through that level!
- References to MP1 & 2
- Soundtrack
- Brilliant narration
- Each gun feeling fantastic
- Bullet time dives (super important mechanic to use)
- Collectables
- MULTIPLAYER: It's actually awesome, and the netcode is fantastic, still active and quite deep. What a nice addition they didn't even need to add.

My Personal GOTY TPS for 2012.
If you played the previous installments you'll already have a feel for our anti-hero, Max. He's a moody, drug and alcohol addicted detective...except in this one he is retired, and living in Sao Paulo, Brazil working as a security guard for the wealthy Bronco family.
This game is ultra story-heavy, with top-notch voice and motion capture working seamlessly together throughout the entire game. There is murder, there is mystery, there is heart-pounding suspense, and there is always a rainstorm of bullets being rained down upon you. I guarantee you a good time.
It has a fresh take on gun mechanics, improving upon the franchises already implemented control scheme. You can dual wield two single-handed weapons and carry one two-handed weapon at all times. You have a slow motion gauge that fills up from getting kills and you can use it while you run and gun, duck for cover, dive forward, backward, sideways, down stairwells, you name it - Max can do it if you can.
This installment also gives a new feature called "Last Man Standing" wherein someone shoots you fatally, you have until you hit the ground to find them on screen and shoot them, granting you a painkiller upon success.
Max Payne 3 is a non-stop action thrillride that will have you playing until the end with sweaty palms.
Other features include extra game modes: Score Attack - where you go through completed chapters racking up the most points as possible; New York Minute - you have one minute on the clock to complete each chapter...good luck.

I'm changing my viewpoint after reviewing my previous review. I had become the very thing I loathed: A nostalgia-driven player with no appreciation for positive change. I decided to then re-write my review and give a more solid argument for the game itself.
The inclusion of raw robits in crates is an incredible change. It provides players, paying or not, with a steady, decent supply of in-game currency to use for building robots. It also levels the loot field by counteracting the 3x recycle rate of premium users by effectively replacing most of the low to mid-level parts that you normally get from crates with a fixed amount of currency.
The change to CPU tiers and weapon power is also a good step in the right direction. It gives incentive for building smart at all CPU levels in order to maximize power usage. The ability to define how you deal damage, how long you can deal damage, and how much damage you deal, along with many, many other factors, create a myriad of playstyles.
As a flier main, I can understand some of the hate surrounding the Lock-on Missile Launcher and the Aeroflak weapons. However, without them, planes and other high-altitude fliers would be extremely overpowered. It's also important to note that both can be countered by flying low and close to cover, but that comes with its own risks. Overall, I'd say that they are in a decent spot and have enough good counters. You can also work with your team to identify these weapons and have someone else take them down so they can't bother you.

These days there are not a lot of good FPS games, that get the singleplayer right. They tend to focus on multiplayer of which usually the player base dies within the first month as players are confused as to whether they are playing a part of a story or a deathmatch. By ignoring multiplayer altogether ID has produced a gem of epic proportions.
Within the first few minutes you are treated to an intro played out and not merely watched. With characters you relate to, the game gives you choices that affect those relationships. And if you allow it you feel as the protagonist does. Your hatred towards the Nazi's in this alternate timeline grows more and more. When a game can immerse you not just visually but mentally too then you have a winner.
Now how does it play. Well here we have a classic style gameplay method mixed with modern effects. Like old ID games tou must pick up health and armour. However we have moved on from the walk over you must manually pick up using hotkey to do so.
