im not the type of person who has poured upwards of 1000+ hours in, but i have spent a good 500-650. so take this with a grain of salt i guess.
i think the worst part of RC is the fact that now you can put whatever weapons you want to go with your bot. the whole point of a team based game in which you can pick different classes (or build diff robots) is to pick a playstyle you like, and when that playstyle can't work in a situation, someone else on your team with a different class (robot) who was built for that situation can support you. in otherwords, teamwork. now, although cpu limits prevent people from having very heavy SMG/other weapon tanks, you can still be a plasma/rail/medic walker/flyer, fufilling multiple roles at once. even if said bot doesnt excel at any offensive or movement capabilities it has, it's still NOT something that should exist in a teamplay class based game. robots like that sound like something a child comes up with who bends the rules of a game so they win every time. it's also worth noting about the removal of the pilot seat. it did have a weird damage absorbing mechanic (which nobody bothered to edit), and ejector seats are also kind of annoying. but they gave bots a design aspect in which damage had to be redirected away from it as well as the bot being connected somehow.
there's also the repair on kill feature. conquest would be quite fun and more team based without, due to the fact that nano guns and medics exist. passive repairing, and repairing on kill ruins any need of medics and therefor team support that robocraft once had.
next is how low the rewards for beating a match have gotten. even past the battle arena update with the new gamemode, the rewards were still good enough that you could build a new robot after a few weeks if you were that dedicated to the game. nowadays you barley get anything out of winning a match, and it could take you forever just to get one of the top-tier weapons such as shotguns and missiles.
speaking of which, those weapons look cool and seem fun to use. unfortunately, they're reserved for those who are willing to put up with the grind to be able to buy them. why there isn't even just ONE down-tier version for each of the weapons is a mystery. and if it isn't, its probably a
.
luckily crates are a thing, but due to how long it takes to get a weapon and how much money you need for crates, it seems like more of a cheap way of making money. sure it's not p2p, but with weapons taking around a couple of weeks to accumulate, it seems like fj is trying to force players to give them money. there's also the removal of the tech tree (or its still their but the weird gui makes it hidden), which wasnt even a tree after maybe conquest? the whole point of a TECH TREE is to unlock components that you want for your specific playstyle and bot design. a TECH SPIRAL does not give this freedom, and forces you down a set pathway that results in the stuff that you want taking longer to obtain. to make matters worse, the low rewards mean that you HAVE to rely on random crates. RANDOM CRATES. don't go and actually try and design something, and buy the parts yourself. just let the game give you stuff and you have to try and figure out how to combine that stuff. great choice.
speaking of cheap money, it makes NO SENSE that the ability to color our bots with a wide spectrum, something that people have always wanted (but due to tiered armor being tiered you couldn't really have an artbot in any tier game), is very restricted. they don't even let you buy them once with gc and keep them forever. it just seems like another way of getting cheap money, but it isn't even that well hidden.
lastly. despite all of this, FREEJAM HASN'T DONE JACK. i know there are a whole bunch of people who say that "FJ just has a bit of a listening problem with the community, i'm sure we can send them a clear message somehow." now i hate to shatter your dreams, but this is the exact same thing people have said A YEAR or even TWO years ago. now ill have to admit that i've never had too much of a problem with RC back then. i am by no means a "true veteran," but i have been around before tank treads and after walkers (?) and stayed up until the pit and conquest were restricted. even back then, there were complaints. not great ones, and not too many serious ones. but they were generally about the same thing and even then, FJ probably hasnt read or responded to most. i can only recall 3 things that FJ has ever changed after listening to the community, one of which was weapon damage increases for everything except smgs for balancing, and the rest probably bug fixing. I COULD BE COMPLETELY WRONG SO DONT TAKE MY WORD.
and before someone tells me or anyone that "indie game compaines are small and need money and time quit yapping uwu," freejam has grown from 5 members to around 20-30 in the megabot/conquest update and now they have 40. some bugs have taken a few months to be fixed, despite them being more than an annoyance and posted on the forums atleast 2-3 times a week. which is inexcusable. and i understand that FJ as a bigger indie game company needs more money in order to continue development as well as give devs money for at home stuff. but even then, they could just do this by expanding the previous concepts that made the game excellent, as well as adding more content such as the top tier weapons in a balanced way in order to draw in new players and devs, more money, and speed up development. instead they have watered down the class system in the game in order to appeal to a new audience, who will probably get bored after a while. over time more and more people are going to leave until there's less people playing RC than there are on battleborn.
making an indie game requires extreme dedication to your ideas and community, and feedback+quality must be put before money and more players. FJ has demonstrated that they clearly do not care about feedback or quality. dont download.
tl;dr the denseness of freejam, the watered down importance of bot design, the poorly disguised money making tactics, the long grind, and refusal to listen to feedback, is going to drive FJ's "new audience," and any othere "new audience" that they attempt to aim for every few months, until there's barely anyone left. DO NOT DOWNLOAD.

Planetside 2 started off as your normal generic shooter with a massive world. The game felt like Battlefield but bigger... but then the curse of the 'pay-to-play' struck with the whales (people who spend way to much on a game) dominating all the other sides. Then most players left the game in disgust at what it had become. Destiny was anounced and most people stopped playing, which made the whales get bored so the game died. But now the new owners of Planetside 2 have fixed so many problems, this game now isn't pay-to-win. First off the new owners change the upgrade system, then they balenced the different factions.
Planetside 2 is a large team based game with three diferent factions battling it out for control over the land. If you are getting this game for a story or campaign don't bother, because all we know is there are three factions, (New Conclomerate, who are the rebels. The Terran Republic who are trying to create a new government. And finally the Vanu Sovereignty who are aliens that will do anything to get technology.) This game has no single palyer expirience it is just online only.
The Battles take place on four continents, each with there own climate and landscape. The battles are based on a rock,paper,sissors stratergy. Air beats infintry, and infintry beat tank, tank beats air. There is a big variety of choices in terms of tanks and aircraft. The choices for your class is the standerd, light-assualt, heavy,MAX,engi,medic and the infiltrator a sniper.
This game looks fantastic, with all the playermodels looking almost like real people and the tanks with scratchs on them. It's the little details like that which makes this game look so good. The game mechanics are alright. And the community is generaly easy going and helpful.
I would hive this game 9/10 if they balanced the teams more but until they fix that its 8/10.

As you can see, I played a LOT of this game. It's very fun, and there's not really anything else out there quite like it. And it's free. But honestly, I wish they'd just start charging for it instead of using a pay-to-win system.
Pay-to-win may be a little strong in this case, so let me back up a little bit before I make my accusations.
Robocraft is a game that combines engineering, design, skill, teamwork, and camraderie beautifully. When it's fun, It's really fun.
The game rewards you for designing your robot well, and it rewards you for blowing up other robots with parts to make your robot even better.
This, however, is where it all starts to fall apart. If you pay for 'premium', you get better and more rewards for kills.
Nothing is quite so frustrating as seeing your carefully designed robot be torn apart by someone who just slapped an OP gun on some wheels.
I believe it's technically possible to get all the same weapons in free-to-play, but it's rediculously difficult. For premium members, not so much.
Still, if you're into design (like me), and you don't get frusterated easliy (unlike me) this game might be worth checking out. I just can't reccomend it in good faith until the devs (hopefully) come to their senses and remove the game-breaking pay-to-win system.

Planetside 2 started off as your normal generic shooter with a massive world. The game felt like Battlefield but bigger... but then the curse of the 'pay-to-play' struck with the whales (people who spend way to much on a game) dominating all the other sides. Then most players left the game in disgust at what it had become. Destiny was anounced and most people stopped playing, which made the whales get bored so the game died. But now the new owners of Planetside 2 have fixed so many problems, this game now isn't pay-to-win. First off the new owners change the upgrade system, then they balenced the different factions.
Planetside 2 is a large team based game with three diferent factions battling it out for control over the land. If you are getting this game for a story or campaign don't bother, because all we know is there are three factions, (New Conclomerate, who are the rebels. The Terran Republic who are trying to create a new government. And finally the Vanu Sovereignty who are aliens that will do anything to get technology.) This game has no single palyer expirience it is just online only.
The Battles take place on four continents, each with there own climate and landscape. The battles are based on a rock,paper,sissors stratergy. Air beats infintry, and infintry beat tank, tank beats air. There is a big variety of choices in terms of tanks and aircraft. The choices for your class is the standerd, light-assualt, heavy,MAX,engi,medic and the infiltrator a sniper.
This game looks fantastic, with all the playermodels looking almost like real people and the tanks with scratchs on them. It's the little details like that which makes this game look so good. The game mechanics are alright. And the community is generaly easy going and helpful.
I would hive this game 9/10 if they balanced the teams more but until they fix that its 8/10.

I'm not a really big fan of RTS games. My brain simply can't keep up with managing resources, constructing buildings, and fighting battles...all at the same time! However, I remember playing AoE2 a bunch when I was a kid, so I picked it up for $4 during a sale, not expecting much from it.
I'm glad to say that this was a good purchase!
For a game that was released in 1999, the game holds up well on every front - even the graphics! The game has been marketed as an "HD" release, but aside from the water, everything still looks pretty much the same way it did 15 years ago, which is not a bad thing at all.
Even though I'm not a fan of RTS games, there's something that feels different about AoE2. Typically in an RTS game, I'll be minding my own business and building up my base when suddenly a horde of enemy units will swarm over my base and destroy everything, leaving me wondering how the AI churned out so many units that fast. I don't get this feeling while playing AoE2. Instead, I feel like I have the time to appreciate the different ages and technologies, while still being competitive and in the game.
If you're like me and enjoyed this game way back in the 20th Century, I would recommend purchasing this game again (especially since it's so cheap). Even if you've had no experience with Age of Empires before, I would still recommend it, as it has aged well, and the gameplay is still solid.

Finally, it's here! A true Wolfenstein game.
Yes, unlike Return to Castle Wolfenstein, which actually was Kingpin 2 - Deathshead and Blavatsky: Life of War Crime and Wolfenstein 2009, which in fact was Call of Duty: Occult Warfare, this is real Wolfenstein.
MachineGames came up with a great idea of taking things that made Wolfenstein 3d so great, and build their game on top of it. Remember how knife was a very powerful weapon? It is here, too, complete with stunning melee quick kill scenes. As for "stab enemy repeatedly until he's dead", you'll still find that, but it will make sense and will be used in proper context.
There's still dog food that gives +4 of health, there's still the rule "if you're close to enemies you're as good as dead".
As any great game, Wolf2014 brings innovation to the genre: ability to cut some surfaces - complete with new physical mesh that engine creates in real time, and partial health regeneration.
The gameplay is designed to feel very fair. I played on "I am a death incarnate!", it was hard, but I never had any of those annoying "What the hell?! I pressed the button, but it didn't work!" moments.
The story innovates too - it isn't "How Blazkowicz single-handedly defeated everyone" all the time anymore. The atmosphere is different. It's about living in the world where life is so bad - it isn't worth living. People are eager to risk and even sacrifice themselves to help bring the regime down, because they would not lose anything by doing so.
A few scenes in the game will have you pleasantly surprised, when suddenly things turn out to be totally different from what you originally perceived.
There's one bad thing to say about the story, howewer. The authors couldn't tell some parts of it, so they just skipped them. For example, how Blazkowicz and Anya were getting on the train, then how they were going to the hotel. Those couldn't be simple and smooth, because Nazis are looking for them. I was looking forward to these parts of the story, and authors' inability to tell them is a let down.
Other thing that the story lacked for me is that it didn't show how usual people live in this world. Surely we've seen an asylum and concentration camp, but the game never lets to walk around the city street, see and hear usual people. Eventually we just stop finding out more about life in this alternative history at all, combat operations in some highly guarded important places become everything the game can offer.
Unfortunately, in terms of graphics IdTech5 engine is a disappointment. While at times of Rage we could think that everything will be fixed later, now few years have passed and we still have bugs - texture pop-in, long load times (MachineGames managed to cleverly work around that by making levels load in background during pre-rendered cutscenes), and texture compression artifacts, now even more apparent since a lot of surfaces use bumpmapping and specularmapping. Turning off VT Compression in options menu won't help much - sharp squares will be turned into squares with round corners, that's all.
The engine certainly became worse, because in 64-bit Rage texture pop-ins happen rarely for me, but here they happen almost every time I look around! And from reading about it in Internet it seems like even people with very powerful computers still have the pop-in issue. It also runs less smoothly than Rage does, howewer that's something to be expected since Rage doesn't use dynamic lighting most of the time, and also most its textures don't use bumpmaps and specular.
But, there's one very good thing about the engine: no input lag if FPS is below 60! It is a great feature which makes the gameplay a lot more enjoyable and fun: no matter what FPS you're getting, the controls are still very responsible, thanks to which the game still feels smooth and plays splendidly. Seriously, this great technological achievement in controls makes this game one head taller than many others which do have input lag, such as Lost Planet 2, Battlefield 3, and especially Castlevania: Lords of Shadow.
Speaking of cutscenes, they're all pre-rendered, but it's not as annoying as in Wolfenstein 2009, because it's clear that other way to implement them would be worse. Apart from having to sit through long load time between levels, in-engine realtime scenes show how such way of playback would work - FPS gets decreased, game time gets slower, and sound gets out of sync. The game works with decent FPS everywhere else, but when you get to scripted scene - slowdown happens. Why scripting here is so performance heavy is a mystery.
Some other problems I can remember are DOF which can be turned off only through the console, imperfect collision due to which there's a chance that player will fall through the floor, and lack of 32-bit executable file (and lack of any executable file at all for some players!).
But despite the flaws, overall this is a glorious return of the great Wolfenstein. Beautiful, innovative, enjoyable, true id game. It is saddening that id Software lost the grasp of what makes their games so great, and all they could make is Rage, which, while having great graphics, overall looks like some unfinished open-world techdemo. And now someone else has to make an id game for them.
Play Wolfenstein: the New Order. Because it's more than a good game. It's even more than a great game. It's an id game, which makes it legendary.

Replaying AOEII in glorious HD was a beautiful nostalgic journey in which I could finally overcome a game whose concept enchanted me and whose difficulty hounded me as a child. The game is still complex, the missions long and ardouous, but all of evokes a different type of strategy. These aren't 30 minute missions you can play on a lunch break, you're in for a long haul, fighting to push the English back to their own soil or conquer the world as Kublai Khan. Unlike AOE3, no unit reigns supreme; cannon are weak but can devastate large towers and walls, cavalry are ferocious and swift but can be mown down with enough arrows or a small force of pikes. Each situation requires careful planning and preparation.
If you know you have the time to enjoy it, buy the game, install some extra graphics mods through steam workshop, and settle in for about 120 hours of fun.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is what quality single-player game should be.
The story is set in alternative history 1960s Europe in a world where the Nazis won the Second World War. You play as William "B.J." Blazkowicz from previous Wolfenstein games which surprises me on overall character development. Presentation of each character is really great. The ways BJ talked and thought. I could understand his feeling and motive as the story proceeded. Villains also have great setup and personality. Especially, the cutscenes are very polished which create strong telling and sense of presence. The more you play and discovered its details through notes and news, the more you get supporting details of game world. Only end-game part I feel bit rushed and some characters just hop-in and out to nowhere. However, big thanks to writing and top-notch voice acting. These elements push TNO to be one of most memorable storytelling shooting game.
The gameplay introduces very solid shooting mechanic. The combination of old school (pick-ups, health system, one man arsenal) and modern gunplay (regeneration, cover system, dual-wield) are well implemented. It keeps game fluid without losing its old school feeling. Perk system is like do challenge and unlock your upgrade which add additional gameplay and player’s motive as you can keep your upgrade for higher difficult (but you have to choose from chapter selection).
For gun blazing is very fun as each weapon give strong punch and solid sound. You can expect enjoyment and satisfying shooting as you leave the area with gore and remain of your destruction.
Stealth is great additional advantage to locate the collectables (Yes, TNO has a lot of collectable even most of them are easy to find) and take out high priority threat.
Enemy A.I. is quite challenging with some noticeable frank strategy, but sometimes they just stand and wait for player which makes higher difficult less challenge.
What I love about TNO is timeline based gameplay. Your decision of beginning of the game will effect on your side characters, upgrade, and some pathway. Thanks to map design team that allow player to discover the change and choose their play-style.
What can I say about TNO soundtracks? It’s ROCK and match in each area you encounter or cutscene. OST gives strong taste of both story and gameplay.
IdTech 5 engine is also introduced in TNO with MegaTexture technology. It looks beautiful at the distance and well optimized even my desktop does not match with system requirement. However, the engine requires too much system resource and still gives poorly outcome. About 30 GBs of game space are texture files, but the textures are muddy and blurry in close-up and some texture popping issue like RAGE. I’m quite disappointed in this part.
MachineGames has proved themselves is this Wolfenstein. To be honest, TNO doesn't need to have next-gen elements, but it can provide very satisfying experience and superb storytelling in FPS that I haven’t played for a long time. TNO is considered to be one of my favorite single-player shooting and MachineGames now earn my trust for expectation of future quality game.

Dirty Bomb is a fast paced, objective based shooter that features a cast of 19 mercenaries (as of the time of making of this review) or mercs as the game calls them. Each merc has different abilities, stats and weapons. The game gives you 2 mercs ready to be played, Skyhammer and Aura, a soldier and a medic.
All non-default mercs cost either 30,000 or 50,000 (or 4,50€/7,50€) credits to unlock. Once you unlock them you keep them forever.
When you play the game for the first time, you receive a generous amount of credits. In no time you can already gather the required amount to unlock a merc. This is a one time thing, so don't expect another big credit drop anytime soon.
There is a loadout system that may give different weapons and a certain advantage and it is devided by 6 rarities:
Lead, Iron, Bronze, Silver, Gold and Cobalt.
Lead gives you one ability, Iron gives you 2 and Bronze gives you 3 abilities. These abilities don't give a huge bonus, but they are nice to have. Anything above bronze is purely cosmetical. In my experience, getting the bronze rarity is pretty easy in comparison to the greater rarities such as gold and cobalt.
Depending on your performance and skill, you get a different base reward at the end of each match. You can win either 100 or 500 credits.
You can do missions which will greatly increase your money. They are mostly easy and usually they don't require a merc that you don't have. If it happens, you can simply remove that mission and another one will appear in a couple hours. They can give 500, 750 or 1000 each, depending on the difficulty or "grindiness".
The game also rewards you for a daily play and a daily win. You can win 500 for a daily play in each mode and a single daily win for 500.
Meaning that you can win at least 3,500 credits in 3 matches if you play all the game modes, and do all the existing missions, and win at least one of the match. You can always win much more if you invest more time, obviously.
Using math you can expect to get enough credits to buy one merc in 2 weeks, if you play about 30 minutes per day. If you play 1 hour a day, you can get one in 1 week,
.
You are also rewarded about 1-3+ (low tier) crates a day at the end of a match. Crates offer you loadout cards and it's the cheapest way to get them. You can also buy them at the store for 1000 credits. I think it's a waste of time and money, just open the ones you get for free. You don't get good drops anyway, you'll get lead or iron most of the time.
Store also offers you usual F2P stuff like boosters, better crates and stuff like that.
The game features a crafting mechanic. You can recycle low tier loadout cards for shards which you can then use to craft (a random) high tier cards with a credit fee to make a loadout card for any merc you like. If you happen to get a silver or gold card, I recommend recyclying it, because it will give A LOT of shards which you can use to unlock a lot of cards. Obviously, this is up to you.
The more XP you get, the more score you have, the more credits you receive. Different mercs specialize on a class, giving different type of XP.
There's Combat XP (Kills and damage), Game mode XP (Completing map objectives, winning rounds, etc.) and Support XP (providing ammo, resurecting, giving health, recon, etc.). All are equally important, which I think is great. The game does not focus very much on k/d ratio but on simply how well you are doing in general. Once I played, I had a 6/17 k/d, but was on top of my team because I was the medic.
Some mercs are in a rotation, meaning you can use them as long you want, till the next rotation. This way you can play with almost any character without paying. They usually last a week or so. The only downside is, if you invested a high-tier card into that character, you can no longer use it if you haven't paid for it.
Some mercs are objective specialists, meaning they are better at doing objectives, such as planting/defusing bombs, repearing objectives, etc.
The balancing currently is good. There are no characters which are overpowered or underpowered, each one has its role and it's perfectly capable. There are some characters which are better in 1v1 situations, but that's just the nature of the game. If you see that you are constantly killed by the same merc, you are just playing against a very good player. Not everyone is good at every merc.
You can play in 3 game modes which I refered a while ago. Objective, Stopwatch and Execution. Objective is a short match of about 10 minutes. Attackers play the objective and Defenders must stop them until the time runs out.
Stopwatch is similar to objective mode. It swaps teams on the mid-game. You basically need to complete the objective as fast as possible or prevent the other team from doing it.
The Execution mode is similar to CS: Global Offensive's Classical mode. You have a best of 12 rounds, attackers plant a bomb and defenders must stop them or defuse. This is perhaps the longest game-mode which can last at least 25 minutes, from my experience.
The game says that competitive is in early alpha. I tried many times using it, but the game throws an error everytime so I can't play it, and can't say anything about it. Most likely you won't be able to play it, unless the error was on my side.
There are 6+3 maps. 6 for Objective and Stopwatch mode and another 3 only for execution. The maps have good visiblity and don't have insanely long corridors/open spaces which would be perfect for snipers. It's hard to describe how good a map is, but in my opinion they are decent enough.
THE UI IS SLOW. This is perhaps the biggest downside of the game. It's slow, sometimes unresponsive, laggy and totally unsatisfying. DEVS IF YOU ARE READING THIS, PLEASE FIX THE UI ASAP.
It's also a bit confusing. You will understand if you play the game.
It's a decent game, fun and doesn't give a huge advantage to the people that pay. But it still has a lot of room for improvement, devs get on that, stop adding mercs and improve the god damn game instead.
I would rate it a solid 7.5/10.

Replaying AOEII in glorious HD was a beautiful nostalgic journey in which I could finally overcome a game whose concept enchanted me and whose difficulty hounded me as a child. The game is still complex, the missions long and ardouous, but all of evokes a different type of strategy. These aren't 30 minute missions you can play on a lunch break, you're in for a long haul, fighting to push the English back to their own soil or conquer the world as Kublai Khan. Unlike AOE3, no unit reigns supreme; cannon are weak but can devastate large towers and walls, cavalry are ferocious and swift but can be mown down with enough arrows or a small force of pikes. Each situation requires careful planning and preparation.
If you know you have the time to enjoy it, buy the game, install some extra graphics mods through steam workshop, and settle in for about 120 hours of fun.

Dirty Bomb is a fast paced, objective based shooter that features a cast of 19 mercenaries (as of the time of making of this review) or mercs as the game calls them. Each merc has different abilities, stats and weapons. The game gives you 2 mercs ready to be played, Skyhammer and Aura, a soldier and a medic.
All non-default mercs cost either 30,000 or 50,000 (or 4,50€/7,50€) credits to unlock. Once you unlock them you keep them forever.
When you play the game for the first time, you receive a generous amount of credits. In no time you can already gather the required amount to unlock a merc. This is a one time thing, so don't expect another big credit drop anytime soon.
There is a loadout system that may give different weapons and a certain advantage and it is devided by 6 rarities:
Lead, Iron, Bronze, Silver, Gold and Cobalt.
Lead gives you one ability, Iron gives you 2 and Bronze gives you 3 abilities. These abilities don't give a huge bonus, but they are nice to have. Anything above bronze is purely cosmetical. In my experience, getting the bronze rarity is pretty easy in comparison to the greater rarities such as gold and cobalt.
Depending on your performance and skill, you get a different base reward at the end of each match. You can win either 100 or 500 credits.
You can do missions which will greatly increase your money. They are mostly easy and usually they don't require a merc that you don't have. If it happens, you can simply remove that mission and another one will appear in a couple hours. They can give 500, 750 or 1000 each, depending on the difficulty or "grindiness".
The game also rewards you for a daily play and a daily win. You can win 500 for a daily play in each mode and a single daily win for 500.
Meaning that you can win at least 3,500 credits in 3 matches if you play all the game modes, and do all the existing missions, and win at least one of the match. You can always win much more if you invest more time, obviously.
Using math you can expect to get enough credits to buy one merc in 2 weeks, if you play about 30 minutes per day. If you play 1 hour a day, you can get one in 1 week,
.
You are also rewarded about 1-3+ (low tier) crates a day at the end of a match. Crates offer you loadout cards and it's the cheapest way to get them. You can also buy them at the store for 1000 credits. I think it's a waste of time and money, just open the ones you get for free. You don't get good drops anyway, you'll get lead or iron most of the time.
Store also offers you usual F2P stuff like boosters, better crates and stuff like that.
The game features a crafting mechanic. You can recycle low tier loadout cards for shards which you can then use to craft (a random) high tier cards with a credit fee to make a loadout card for any merc you like. If you happen to get a silver or gold card, I recommend recyclying it, because it will give A LOT of shards which you can use to unlock a lot of cards. Obviously, this is up to you.
The more XP you get, the more score you have, the more credits you receive. Different mercs specialize on a class, giving different type of XP.
There's Combat XP (Kills and damage), Game mode XP (Completing map objectives, winning rounds, etc.) and Support XP (providing ammo, resurecting, giving health, recon, etc.). All are equally important, which I think is great. The game does not focus very much on k/d ratio but on simply how well you are doing in general. Once I played, I had a 6/17 k/d, but was on top of my team because I was the medic.
Some mercs are in a rotation, meaning you can use them as long you want, till the next rotation. This way you can play with almost any character without paying. They usually last a week or so. The only downside is, if you invested a high-tier card into that character, you can no longer use it if you haven't paid for it.
Some mercs are objective specialists, meaning they are better at doing objectives, such as planting/defusing bombs, repearing objectives, etc.
The balancing currently is good. There are no characters which are overpowered or underpowered, each one has its role and it's perfectly capable. There are some characters which are better in 1v1 situations, but that's just the nature of the game. If you see that you are constantly killed by the same merc, you are just playing against a very good player. Not everyone is good at every merc.
You can play in 3 game modes which I refered a while ago. Objective, Stopwatch and Execution. Objective is a short match of about 10 minutes. Attackers play the objective and Defenders must stop them until the time runs out.
Stopwatch is similar to objective mode. It swaps teams on the mid-game. You basically need to complete the objective as fast as possible or prevent the other team from doing it.
The Execution mode is similar to CS: Global Offensive's Classical mode. You have a best of 12 rounds, attackers plant a bomb and defenders must stop them or defuse. This is perhaps the longest game-mode which can last at least 25 minutes, from my experience.
The game says that competitive is in early alpha. I tried many times using it, but the game throws an error everytime so I can't play it, and can't say anything about it. Most likely you won't be able to play it, unless the error was on my side.
There are 6+3 maps. 6 for Objective and Stopwatch mode and another 3 only for execution. The maps have good visiblity and don't have insanely long corridors/open spaces which would be perfect for snipers. It's hard to describe how good a map is, but in my opinion they are decent enough.
THE UI IS SLOW. This is perhaps the biggest downside of the game. It's slow, sometimes unresponsive, laggy and totally unsatisfying. DEVS IF YOU ARE READING THIS, PLEASE FIX THE UI ASAP.
It's also a bit confusing. You will understand if you play the game.
It's a decent game, fun and doesn't give a huge advantage to the people that pay. But it still has a lot of room for improvement, devs get on that, stop adding mercs and improve the god damn game instead.
I would rate it a solid 7.5/10.

The only reason I stopped playing was entirely because of a glitch that kept happening causing it to be impossible to win a match because one side would end up with all the bubbles on their core destroyed, and nothing would happen. I could write a long review detailing everything wrong with the game, but the long story short is this. If they tried to bring the game back towards its roots with some new polish, not only would I play the hell out of it, but I would be able to recommend it and would be willing to pay for premium from time to time. In short. if the developers read any of these, please consider looking back to how the game was in June of 2015. Back in the days where the goal was to destroy the enemy core, robots on both teams kept fairly equal by the tier system, before the days of weapons that run out of energy in seconds. and bring that game back for the community.

The movie comparisons in my review are no accident because if I had to sum up Wolfenstein: The New Order in one word  it would be
. Cinematic in the best way possible. Not the barely interactive cut-scene-and-quick-time-event-pastiche, but the clever artifice of story, art direction, game mechanics, level design, and yes, the well placed cutscene.
This is the Wolfenstein reboot Chris Nolan would have made if he did video games. I haven't enjoyed an FPS this much since HalfLife 2. A large part of that was feeling immersed in an interactive movie; a playable Inglorious Basterds world but with more tech, more soul, and ample homage to Wolfenstein 3D pulled off without seeming silly.
The resemblance to HL2 is unavoidable starting with the fact that Valve deliberately evokes Nazism and the SS in the very look of the combine troops. But Wolfenstein, for its part, incorporates an enemy very reminiscent of HL2's manhacks;
. But Wolfenstein's unique style, voice, and story outshine the passing similarities.
The storyline is expansive. At medium difficulty, through one timeline, I completed the game in 51 hours. I don't feel compelled to replay from the
branch point as I feel the majority of the timeline will play out the same with only minor differences. But I imagine, just as with HL2, I'll get a hankering to play it again and try the alternate branch. Within the in-game statistic page I'm told I've completed 67% and within that I'm quite satisfied with the experience.
The Tech-5 engine shines, even at slightly lower than maximum quality (the most my rig could handle). Yes, occasionally textures "render in" in your field of view, but for me this was uncommon enough to be a fair trade for the gorgeous textures and how the level designers put them to use. I suspect Tech-5 has been optimized since Rage and that level designers have become more astute at using it. Whatever the case, a beautifully realized world in two time periods where the technology mostly did its job invisibly allowing good immersion. Reloading from a checkpoint after death or just wanting a do-over was a tad slow for me. If your rig has an SSD this game would most certainly benefit from being installed on it.
I call it a Nolan-esque reboot for a reason. Wolfenstien: TNO is instantly recognizable as part of the franchise, but also rebooted with that near realism, that almost believability, which Nolan brought to the Batman franchise. Layered on top of that is a cast of NPCs that I cynically assumed were window dressing only to discover as the game crescendoed near the end that I actually cared about them. This was pullled off as expertly as James Cameron made me care for the fate of individual space marines in Aliens or why the ensemble of Ocean's Eleven worked instead of feeling like a bunch of famous faces thrown into a film together.
As deftly as our heroes are portrayed, equaly so are our villains. Most of the time they are disembodied voices, antogonizing prisoners or Blazkowicz himself over the PA system (resemblences to City 17 hard to ignore). But occasional cinematics of up close and personal encounters showed the depth of the enemies' cruelty and sadism and -- displaying the emotional complexity of the writing -- their misguidedness. It is by no accident that Blazkowicz and the resistance are called "terrorists". There is social commentary present; thankfully delivered with subtlety.
Controls -- once I gave up the mouse and keyboard and switched to a controller -- are flippin' fun and amazing. I'm complete♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at aiming with a thumbstick, but a controller was the only sane way for me to manage the amount of gymnastics and vaulting expected of me, so I endured the fact that to an outside observer my aiming looked like I'd strapped a laser pointer to a weeble wobble which I proceeded to kick around a level. I suppose experimentation with various keybind customizations would have allowed me my preferred mousing setup, but once I got the knack of the controller I didn't really look back; it's patently clear the game was designed to be played with a controller. So lots of sprint-sliding, crouch-leaning, stealth-takedowns later I was having a ball.
The combat is good. The AI is adequate. My play style (and thus my perks) tended toward the sneak and takedown or failing that, run back to cover and lure individuals into ranged sniping. Often enough the AI conspired with the level design to have this backfire on me as I got flanked and killed, or nearly so, at close range. I'm not sure how a guns-blazing playstyle works for someone. My few attempts at that had enemies coming out of every corner to mow me down. Still, there's a perk branch for that style of play and the overall quality of the game gives me faith that it was playtested and balanced if that mode suits your fancy. Other than the occasional ambushes, though, the AI, as it must be in comparison to a human players, often falls short. Mostly this takes the form of predictability, where any particular arena becomes a puzzle to solve on how to manipulate the AI opponents into easy targets. Supposedly ominous ubersoldat are the most disappointing. Once their more nimble unaugmented nazis have been dispatched, a giant mecha-nazi is easily befuddled by dancing around an ordinance proof obstacle, or more lamentably
. That aside, the difficulty gradually ramped up as the game neared it's climax, forcing me to expand my playstyle to one of snipe a key enemy alerting others; rush between cover, guns blazing; scavenge quickly for health and armor; thwart a flanking attempt; all the while switching between weapons that were better suited for the next immediate enemy. Although my own gaming skills never allowed such fluidity without several deaths and checkpoint restarts to grok the approach, there were occasional flashes in my mind where I felt like a hero in an epic movie gunfight.

This is going to be more like a Brink-Dirty Bomb review more than just a Dirty Bomb review.
I have been playing random free to play fps games since 2009. From Point Blank (500ish hours) to tens of Asian Counter Strike rip offs. I've played a lot of Modern Warfare 3 on cracked servers (i mean a lot i even prestiged for 10 times like the fat nerd i am) (1000ish hours) and i have been playing shooters since 2007 on different systems. I've spent most of my life, in front of a screen blowing up virtual heads, slaying virtual peoples throats and riding tanks and i can easily say this is my favorite objective-based fps game i have ever played. I played a lot of Brink when it came out. I loved the game because of the free-running mechanics (I grew up watching free-running videos on the internet and had finished Mirror's Edge over eight times. I had to love this game) but people didn't give a flying ♥♥♥♥ about Brink. Soon after it's relase it died, the servers were empty. At least europe east servers were pretty empty compared to other fps games at the time. Brink was an awsome objective-based fps game but free running mechanics made the game too complicated and made some play styles op in a sense. For example the usual smg kid (if he had decent aim) could easily obliterate the whole match by just sliding and jumping around. It wasn't bad or frustrating it was just unbalanced. Brink's story and lore was pretty cliche. Basically it told the story of the poor against the rich, freedom fighters against the government forces but the way that it told its story through the gameplay, that it had a very uniqe graphic style and its atmosphere made the game feel uniqe and made it an unforgettable experience. Dirty Bomb is made by the developers of Brink. They had experience and used it very well. Balanced the game mechanics, removed most of the free running made it a free to play game. They kept polishing the game balancing guns, classes and the maps and overral updated the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the game. These small but important changes turned Brink into a competitive objective based first person shooter. They still do update the game regularly and they still add new quality content to the game. Over the course of only a year they created one of the most fun, challenging and balanced objective based fps experience.Yes it may not be as fast paced as Brink but it is still as good as Brink (If not better).

Best MMOFPS I've played.  I think they have the format down really well.  Good selection of classes.  Nice open maps (no loading between regions, just one open world/continent).  Huge scale.  Vehicles and aircraft are easy to drive/pilot.  Easy to find a whatever kind of FPS play you like.  Easy to find large or small battles.  The way the continents are different is really well done (vegetation, topography, etc).  The connectivity of the regions you battle for are well done (you have to conquer in order, with some that have multiple paths).  The three factions are balanced well, with also having their own technologies and weapons/vehicles/aircraft that there feels like a difference when on the battlefield.
LIke any F2P game, progression can be slow if you aren't good and you don't spend money to get the fancy credits to spend.  But this doesn't bother me and is expected.  Also like any other F2P game I've played, you can do ok, but the guys with the cooler equipemnt seem to do better, but that could be that they also play more and are just better in general.  For this game I rarely feel like I"m not contributing, even at level 1.
If I had to be picky I would complain about the global map.  It doesn't show you everything that's happening across the continent.  It even doesn't show you all of the people in your faction in the continents you control.  I understand why they don't do that, cause that would be 1,000+ people updating each other's position every tick, which would just bog down the network traffic and make the game suck, but I really wish I could make decisions about where I might deploy without having to deploy, then check my map (they show you everyone in your current region), then possibly redeploy instead of running across the map for 10 mins.
My complaint above has minimal impact because:
-respawn/redeploy is like 10 seconds max, usually 5.
-there is usually a vehicle spawn point close to your base spawn, and you can get a 4-wheeler to get across the map fast
-they show you approximately how many ally and enemy units are in a region as you hover over the region with your mouse (just not their location).
Like every other online multiplayer game I've played, your experience will vary depending on the other online players.  Sometimes you will have a good group and work together, other times everyone does their own thing.  But unlike the smaller scale multiplayer games I've played, your chances of finding a decent battle are higher because there are thousands of people playing, so if you don't like one group/region, you can move to another, or even try a different continent.
Other Things I enjoy about this game
-the diversity of weapons and equipment (even in the same class) covers every play style I could ever want.
-how quickly you can be in a battle, and that i can jump in for 30 minutes or less and usually have a good time.
TIPS FOR NEW PLAYERS
-playing as medic and revving/healing will get you the most XP, if you can find people to revive/heal
-engineer seems to be the class that has the most to do other than kill enemies, and is pretty easy to gain XP because there is always a vehicle, terminal, generator, MAX, etc to repair.  Also you can toss resupply boxes for your allies to get ammo (also gives you xp when they resupply)
-the resource you use to get vehicles and MAX's is constantly/automatically resupplying, if you don't use it you are wasting it.
-get a sunderer and drive it close to the front lines, try to hide it behind something, and deploy (pressing the B key when you are completely stopped).  There are two guns on top to help defend your sunderer, and if it's deployed others can spawn there, which also gives you xp.
-jump in a vehicle if you can (pressing the E key enters), to see if you can grab one of the secondary guns.  It makes the vehicle a lot more powerful and you can help keep attackers at bay.
TIP FOR AMD CARDS:  I was having framerate issues at first, but then used the "AMD Gaming Evolved" app and "optimized" PS2 for my computer and now I get 60+ fps with dips into the 40's when things get crazy.  Made the game 1,000% more enjoyable to play.

This is going to be more like a Brink-Dirty Bomb review more than just a Dirty Bomb review.
I have been playing random free to play fps games since 2009. From Point Blank (500ish hours) to tens of Asian Counter Strike rip offs. I've played a lot of Modern Warfare 3 on cracked servers (i mean a lot i even prestiged for 10 times like the fat nerd i am) (1000ish hours) and i have been playing shooters since 2007 on different systems. I've spent most of my life, in front of a screen blowing up virtual heads, slaying virtual peoples throats and riding tanks and i can easily say this is my favorite objective-based fps game i have ever played. I played a lot of Brink when it came out. I loved the game because of the free-running mechanics (I grew up watching free-running videos on the internet and had finished Mirror's Edge over eight times. I had to love this game) but people didn't give a flying ♥♥♥♥ about Brink. Soon after it's relase it died, the servers were empty. At least europe east servers were pretty empty compared to other fps games at the time. Brink was an awsome objective-based fps game but free running mechanics made the game too complicated and made some play styles op in a sense. For example the usual smg kid (if he had decent aim) could easily obliterate the whole match by just sliding and jumping around. It wasn't bad or frustrating it was just unbalanced. Brink's story and lore was pretty cliche. Basically it told the story of the poor against the rich, freedom fighters against the government forces but the way that it told its story through the gameplay, that it had a very uniqe graphic style and its atmosphere made the game feel uniqe and made it an unforgettable experience. Dirty Bomb is made by the developers of Brink. They had experience and used it very well. Balanced the game mechanics, removed most of the free running made it a free to play game. They kept polishing the game balancing guns, classes and the maps and overral updated the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the game. These small but important changes turned Brink into a competitive objective based first person shooter. They still do update the game regularly and they still add new quality content to the game. Over the course of only a year they created one of the most fun, challenging and balanced objective based fps experience.Yes it may not be as fast paced as Brink but it is still as good as Brink (If not better).

B.J. Blazkowicz is back as gun-toting protagonist in this alternate history shooter. His impressive jaw line makes it hard to look at anything else during the excessive third person cut scenes. Years pass in seconds, as you experience the life of a vegetable, before you spring back to life to battle Nazis while you whisper sweet nothings to yourself.
New Order has dreadfully average combat. The pistol, assault rifle and shotgun feel too similar and look the same. You can duel wield all the grey-brown weapons to reload twice as often and walk around like your legs are tied together. The bullet weapons are soulless, but they do the job against standard enemies. When you get your hands on the chain guns, those unlimited ammo bullet-hoses the super soldiers carry, you’ll discover they don’t have unlimited ammo and BJ refuses to drop them once empty. So the laser gun is the main weapon you'll be using against the armoured units because it is order of magnitudes better than anything else you have on hand. It's also used to cut through metal boxes and grates, but not wooden boxes because the Nazis make wooden boxes to much higher standards. In the last third of the game you’ll spend more time looking at the lasergun charge stations than enemies.
So after every battle you have to scurry around and manually pick up ammo and armor. This is absolutely perfect for game designers because they can extend game length by forcing people to hunt for the stuff you should just be able to walk over. It might not be so bad if everything - ammo, health, weapons – weren’t the same shade of gunmetal grey-brown that blends into the environments. This manual collection of items does not suit the style of play New Order occasionally attempts.
New Order is not all about mediocre action though; it has horrible, arbitrary stealth areas too. Stealth suffers mostly because the IQ of the AI is about 100 points below normal. When they get close to you, their heads turn to look directly at you, yet they do nothing. When the AI decides you stood in the middle of the corridor too long, get ready for them to walk towards you with their batons raised. Even auto-turrets firing at you do not attract the attention of nearby patrolling guards. Stealth is mostly optional, but you are essentially deciding between the poor covert approach or weak guns blazing.
New Order includes its fair share of pacing issues, most of them ludicrous for a game that is often trying to replicate ‘old-school’ shooters. When you return to your base between missions, you play errand boy for different characters. New Order isn’t trying to make a joke of games that do fetch quests – it just does them to pad out the already thin shooting. There are other sections with sparse action too, such as the moon base which has so few enemies that it felt like the game forgot to spawn them.  You can sleepwalk through the many linear, hand-holding areas before the game takes half your weapons away for the next combat mission.
Not all is horrible in New Order, but there so few notable positives to talk about. The Wolfenstein 3D Easter egg (top floor of base) is a nice homage even if they couldn’t get the shooting animations correct. Other references to the old games got me a little nostalgic too, like the roast dinner that restores your health. The ghastly RAGE engine is not so bad in New Order, even if it has low-res textures and minimal interactive elements. At least there is decent level variety, small bits of destruction and retro design. New Order is a huge letdown with its mediocre combat, dumb AI, poor pacing and questionable design decisions. 5/10

Type of Game:
First Person Shooter
Version Played:
PC version through Steam
Similar Games:
The new Shadow Warrior, Serious Sam series, and some of the older Wolfenstein games
The Good:
- The tone of this game is a major departure from the uber-serious tone of previous games in this series. The tone is lighter and less bound by reality (and in some of the series, mysticism) than previous Wolfenstein titles. It’s a good reflection of the ultimate source material, Wolfenstein 3D. In summary, it’s really fun and seems to know it.
- You can dual wield every weapon. Even knives and sniper rifles. See the above note.
- Features returning for this game from the original include attack dogs, treasure hunting, and the ability to eat dog food. I can’t stress how fantastic this is for anyone (like me) who grew up with the original.
- The game’s difficulty gradually ramps up, and only rarely does it become stiflingly difficult. It balances its pacing very well.
- The levels are well designed and very creative. Additionally, the easter eggs like treasure, Enigma codes, and scattered articles, are plentiful.
- I don’t normally notice the soundtrack for this kind of game, but this is an exception. I thought the soundtrack for this game was remarkably well done.
- There is no multiplayer, and since I generally don’t invest enough time to get good but still feel obligated to play it, I only ever end up frustrated. So yes, this is a positive.
The Bad (all negatives have to do with the storyline so… SPOILERS):
- There are points during the game in which I believed there was a lack of communication between the voice actors/writers and the director of this game. Particularly when B.J. is growling though his monologue of childhood memories, I had to remind myself that this is a game where I can eat dog food, dual wield sniper rifles, and infiltrate a moon base (in 1960, no less).
- B.J. wakes up in an asylum after his first encounter with Deathshead, semi-conscious but unable to move, and remains unable to move for fourteen years. When he is finally able to get up and start the killing again, he’s still a mass of ripped muscle. I mean, this dude is a beefcake. But after not moving for FOURTEEN YEARS? Were they injecting him with HGH the entire time?!? Come on. Give me a montage where he brings himself back, something. There’s unrealistic, and then there’s this.
While I’m picking nits…
Not much this time. This game is remarkably clean. The only thing I noticed was that sometimes if I turn around quickly the game can’t keep up with which doors are open and which are closed, so there is a split second where there does not appear to be a door, then it appears. This happened infrequently however. No game breakers, no serious bugs. Machine Games QA FTW.
Did I make time to complete it?:
My first playthrough took fifteen hours. I did not get every single unlockable, however, and there is a decision early in the game (it saves one character while killing another) that I would like to change and see the story from that perspective. So this game will probably clock in at 25-30 hours for me.
Recommended Purchase Price:
Not $59.99, but only because I am philosophically against paying the same amount for a digital download as I do for a physical product. I picked it up for $35 and was happy with that, but I’d have gone as high as $45.

A very enjoyable game, although I'm not sure I'd be willing to fork out $60 for it a second time due to some of the cons. I'd say wait for a sale.
Pros
Solid gameplay. Really embodies the old-fashioned run-and-gun gameplay, but brings some newer elements in. The guns are all very fun to use, I never felt like there was one gun to go to, since they were all good at at least one function. The way health was managed also worked very well. The health regen they had was limited enough to make you think twice about taking a lot of bullets, but didn't leave you at 1 health right before a final boss. The health regen puts you to the nearest multiple of 20 health.
Multiple choices. When breaking into a room, you almost always have at least 2 options on how to attack. Do you sneak in and try to take them all out silently? Do you sneak over to the corner with the turret and mow them down? Or do you kick in the door guns blazing? All of them work.
Level design. This is in line with the multiple choices. Very rarely is there one way to navigate around, and I don't feel like I'm being forced to follow along a preset line of paths and cutscenes.
Cons
Length. Finished the story in 10 hours, and I wasn't trying to rush things. There's not much in the ways of replayability, either. You can replay once more to follow both story-lines, but majority of the game is still the same. No multiplayer either - this isn't inherently bad, but with a relatively short campaign, there isn't much to do once you hit that 10-hour mark. This would probably be the biggest reason I would say I wouldn't spend $60 again.
The sex scenes. I'm not against characters having sex in a game, but I really don't see much of a need for having those scenes in there.
The perk tree. I think it's a good addition, but at the same time, a lot of the perks are hard to get to until you are pretty much at the end of the game. You don't get to enjoy a lot of these perks very long, and some of them, like many stealth ones, are rendered useless in the final battles.

This game truly amazed me. In Wolfenstein: The New Order you play as BJ Blazkowicz as in all the other series, but this time you are not just killing Nazis in WWII, no. In this game the Nazis have won the war and it's up to BJ to stop their reign. This game reiterates the series in a way much better than all the other attempts. Unlike the last Wolfenstein (2009), the Nazis in this game do not have supernatural powers but instead they Mech-suits and Kampfhunds, which are killer robotic dogs. I personally find this more enjoyable and more realistic. Also the soundtrack is great and really makes the mood feel as it should. In times when BJ should feel terrified the music fits it perfectly, and in times of vengeance there's an awesome rock beat really getting you into the moment. Graphically the game is great, not as good as some other titles at the current time but still looks very good indeed. The gunplay is spectacular, sure there aren't too many weapons, but what the game does is continuously upgrades the weapons you have and makes them much more interesting and better for different situations. Also, this is a pretty hard game, I felt very challenged on the normal difficulty. But now I can get to the meat of the game, the atmosphere. It truly makes you feel like the Nazis have taken control of the world. I found an article in the game stating that London's official food was forcefully changed from fish and chips to Sauerkraut, or another showing that a band started in Liverpool named The Beatles that was forced to change their names to Die Käfer and have songs with Nazi influences. At times you feel very scared of the world, such as when you and your squad are put into a room with the walls closing in on you, or witnessing an innocent concentration camp prisoner being butchered by a crazed doctor. So far this is my game of the year and would highly recommend it to anyone that is a fan of shooters but especially fast paced action shooters. 10/10

My GOTY of 2014 and it freaking delivers on all aspects and goes even a little further than that.
It refines the classic old FPS style while mixing in some of the more modern FPS elements we all know today. The game is still very linear but never in a bad way. You can simply go all in guns-a-blazing OR use stealth to silently take down commanders to prefent them from calling reinforcements. Though the AI is quite dumb and sometimes run into walls like a blind fool trying to find an entrance to a door but keep bashing into things (still, it doesn't happen all the time, just sometimes).
Weapons feel great and have nice upgrades to dish out more pain to tougher enemies. Dualwielding is probably the coolest addition to this game as you can dualwield almost ever gun in your disposal. Wanna try using an assault rifle in one hand while holding a grenade launcher in the other? Why not use two shotguns at the same time while triggering Scrapnel bullets to completely obliterate every single nazi troop in your way? THE POSSIBILITIES ARE ENDLESS, MY FRIEND. You can also unlock various perks but getting them requires some bizzare ways of playing the game.
Story-wise, it's pretty deep and you can even choose two different timelines for additional rewards and story elements adding some replayability to the game itself. I liked the Fergus timeline more because guys with scottish accents are always a joy to listen to.
In conclusion: Wolfenstein: TNO is a blast to play and well worth your time if you're into killing a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of future nazis.

When a new developer takes over a popular franchise, things don't always go well (Tomb Raider, Silent Hill, etc). Thankfully, Rockstar did a damn fine job with Max Payne 3.
Gameplay is solid, and pretty standard for Max Payne. Shoot-dodging does seem a little sluggish at times though, even without bullet-time. Also, the single-player campaign has far too many cutscenes and not enough gameplay, especially early on. That being said, the game is still fantastic, and the presentation is top-notch.
I love the animation system. Pick up a rifle then swap to a pistol and Max will carry the rifle in his off-hand. Shoot-dodge towards a wall and Max will smack into it and hit the floor. In bullet-time, every bullet is rendered, and you'll see them zip past you (or into you, if you're unlucky).
One last note - the multiplayer, whilst full of great ideas, needed a bit more bugs ironing out. Otherwise, it's a great excuse to keep playing. I LOVE the Gang Wars mode. Hope it makes it into GTA 5!

Max Payne was a game that wowed us back in the day for one reason; bullet time.  A few years later FEAR did the same thing, but both games let us down for the same reason; monotonous level design.
So Rockstar came along with Max Payne 3.  The ballsy developer and Max Payne were a match made in gamer heaven.  A developer not afraid to discard the elements that weren't working, and really explore and develop what made the original games special in their time.
You no longer yawn through cliched 50's style monologues, but instead actually listen to what Max says because it's gritty, funny and relevant to the story, which is simple yet ever twisting.
The thing that's great now about Max as a character is that he's a bas♥♥♥♥♥but not the brightest guy, and as such he's not perfect and you can relate to him more as a result.
The action is intense and fun but the game really excels because it seamlessly links the action with cut scenes into one action packed movie-like gaming experience.

So I just finished the game, and I can't say I didn't like it.  The game really gets you involved, almost indebted to the characters so that you just want to play more and more.  The story line is great, and I don't think anyone will tell you otherwise.  In all the games I've ever played with campaigns, this one, while not the most grandiose or beautiful, is the most incredible.  I don't want to say anything else; if you like good story telling, this is the game for you.
The game play is actually pretty good.  The guns and animations handle just like doom 3, which is to be expected because that engine is ID's bread and butter.  This is not a bad thing, in fact the weapons were quite fun to shoot and each carried with them their own set of uses, pros and cons.  The visuals left a lot to be desired, however.  Doom 3 was the bleeding edge for gaming back in the day, and unfortunately Wolfenstein is not on par with what I would expect from such a big budget title.  They used some sort of blurring effects on things that were far away (or even not so far away).  Even with draw distance maxed out, it didn't seem to matter.  This of course could be an issue with my machine, but it was worth mentioning  that I had trouble tuning this issue out.  The game is also locked in a 60 fps, thanks to IDtec9.  I am a strong believer that in this day and age 60 fps should not be something that we as PC gamers need to settle on.  But I digress.  The game itself does not feel repetitive.  You aren't mowing down endless hordes of the same enemies.  As we would expect from ID, there is somewhat of a diversity in baddies, but I felt it could be more exhaustive.  However, this is only because I hold ID to such a standard.  The stealth parts are A+.  Seriously, in most stealth games, if you are spotted then its game over.  If you are sneaking up on an enemy, and you anticipate that he is going to see you, you can sprint up to him and assasinate him before he finishes calling you out and not break your stealth.  Really, this is awesome and stealth games that are in development should take note. In the event that you lose your stealth, its not really that big of a deal.  A sizable number of reinforcements are called in, and when you take care of them, you move on.  Since the gunplay is actually pretty good, you may even find yourself making no attempt to be stealthy just to be able to waste a few more Nazis.
Would I recommend that you pay $60 for this game?  No.  Simply because no game with only a single player mode should carry this value.  Because the weapons are so much fun to shoot, I wish there was a multiplayer option.  Doom 3 did not have an amazing multiplayer, but they at least attempted it.  I am the type of person who doesn't play a game twice, and even though I'm only "44% Complete," I got my enjoyment and I'm ready to move on.  I came here because I played the original Castle Wolfenstein and Doom games on my windows 95 machine as a kid, and I'm happy to see this title on a game of this magnitude.  I hope for more in the future.

I ran this game on a 4-core i5 and an AMD 7850 and I got good framrates and I was running it on the highest settings. The graphics are a lot better then Rage (which uses the same engine) and I really thought some the sceenery is excellent. And it has excellent coloring so you don't get the cod-esk gray-ish lighting in places that should be colorful. Right now a lot of games that have come out recently are colorless souless cash-grabs that flood the mainstreem, this is as far from that as possible.
Over all It is an excellent game, is it as good as or better then Half-Life 2, probably not. But it is different, so many games are just a cash-grab that is the same as the last one because they are affraid to change it to make it better. This game isn't like that, they put every ounce of work into it. They wern't trying to get it out the door as fast as possible, they wanted to make what came out as good as possible.
Some parts of the game kind of seemed out of place, such as the side quests and the unlocking system (don't worry, you barely notice anyways.) but what they did with this game was wonderful. I can only hope that Doom 4 has some of these people working on it, they know how to do quality.

Although Max Payne series purists might find reason to complain about Max Payne 3, for newcomers or those who are open to change, the game is excellent.
The story is a dark one- a tale of kidnappings, murders, betrayals, conspiracy, greed, and oppression. If you've played Grand Theft Auto IV, the style will be familiar, for this game and GTA4 share the same writer.
On a technical level, the game is polished to a mirror sheen. Rockstar has redeemed themselves when it comes to PC ports- the game has next to no technical flaws, the controls all work as intended, the graphics are beautiful, and the loadtimes are reasonably quick. The framerate remains a smooth 60, and for once, Max Payne 3 takes advantage of multiple cores and other oft-neglected features from day 1. Aim assist defaults to its "off" setting, greatly reducing aiming frustration and making shootdodges and bullet-time a blast.
Overall, I strongly recommend this game for Max Payne veterans and newcomers alike.

So when Portal came out in 2007, it was like revolutionary way of playing a game that consisted of solving puzzles. I mean, the Portal Gun became one of Valve's icons, as well as the characters. So in 2011, a sequel is released. And we have Portal 2.
Whether you think it's more of the same or not... you're not wrong but you're not right either. While Portal 2 is more of the same concept as its prequel, you're not repeating the exact same levels/test chambers/whatever you wanna call them. But I'll get to that in a second.
You play as Chell, once again. Years after you defeated GLaDOS, you wake up and receive instructions on moving, after being in some sort of relaxation chamber for all those years. After that, you're greeted by a core named Wheatley, who tells you he's gonna help you escape from your chamber, only for you to find out you're actually back at Aperture Science and eventually to meet again with GLaDOS in the ruins of her chamber as she wakes up. That's when she throws Wheatly back in the rails he uses to travel and you into new test chambers. So you're once again testing for GLaDOS while you try to get to her. Later in the game, you witness a plot twist, but whether you know about it or not, I won't talk about it.
So as I said before, you're thrown back into Aperture's test chambers, solving puzzles using the Portal Gun and the environment around you in order to advance through the game. Not only that but for some sort of replay value, Portal 2 introduced a co-op mode for you to join forces with a friend to solve a total of 4 different sets of cooperative test chambers, with Atlas and P-Body as your characters. As you progress, you can also unlock items to customize either of them.
New elements were introduced like laser beams that usually have to be worked around with reflecting cubes to point them at their recepticles. Light paths were also added, to either create walls for turrets or new paths. And later on in the game, you're gonna have a lot of fun with the gels. The textures also make the game look like it's actually from 2011 and not like a Portal 1.5.
And if you've already had enough of what Portal 2 has to offer, good news. You can get even more content from Steam Workshop. So there's a lot more than just the game's standard content for you to go through!
I could go on and on about this game, but I think it's time for the score. Portal 2 gets an 9/10. It's an excellent game (I don't call it perfect cuz the concept is not really improved but yet again there's probably not much to improve in Portal's main concept) and a great sequel to an iconic game from Valve. I recommend getting not just Portal 2, but both games!

This game is exactly what it claims to be. A massively multiplayer online mmo fps.... and on such a large scale that it will blow your mind.
Used to the 16vs16 or maybe even 32vs32 large maps?
Well try 100vs100vs100 in one fight on a server with 2k players.
But with that come some setbacks.
Some even call it pay to win, but really it isn't. Yes, you can spend 2-3 days to grind for a new gun or you can buy it right away. This gun wont give you any significant advantage what so ever, but it does save you a lot of time. Evidentally it is flawed.
- Most standard issue weapons really aren't that good. New players suffer a setback for up to 1 week
- This game has RPG elements, so everything you want or need you have to unlock. Getting max lvl is going to take you a year (at least for the average gamer) and even then you will only have unlocked 50%
- Although all vehicles are available to you from the start, any vehicle that isn't upgraded wont pose much of a threat if any at all
- Very low amount of objects (flora, structures, boxes, etc), overall the worlds are very empty
- Poorly optimized, you want to run this game, get a new gamer rig in 2015 to handle ultra settings
- Client side hit detection (you will die even though you make it behind corners or drop to half hp before you even see an enemy player) This works to your advantage as well, but overall this is a truly awful.
- In large fights, making an impact or significance is impossible and that random guy will show up and end your killstreak eventually. It is very hard to make it past 11 kills without dying or super camping.
- The xp gain is extremely slow
- It is next to impossible to recover or counter any attack if you are the first to take a hit (unless you are up against a new player)
- Many items/vehicles are utterly un-balanced
- Lots of glitches and bugs
- A HUUUUUUUGE amount of useless weapons
- Horrible tutorials
In all honesty, this game is still a BETA and needs a lot of work. But the biggest downside to this is how hard it is to find a good fight. Infantry vs Infantry duking it out for hours over a base.
Often one faction will sit in a superior possition and simply farm the other. Should an equal fight actually appear (which is  very rare) it is typically ruined by vehicles or a ZERG.
A zerg in this game is a big amount of players grouping up in a unstopable horde and just capping base after base. The problem is that there is no fighting going on.
Finding a good fight is really really difficult. Sometimes there aren't any. Because it is all about population in the current part of the map.
It doesn't matter how good you are, you will never defend a base from 5 players alone. Let alone more. The community thinks that this is the way it is supposed to be, but sitting in a base, aiming your gun at the enemy spawn room or out of the spawn room then moving on after 5min is super frikken boring.
The game is currently suffering from massive identity issues. As such, as a new player, you will feel like in a real war.
- No idea what the F is going on
- No idea how to get to where you are needed or supposed to be
- Dealing loads of friendly fire and annoying the heck out of everyone
- Feel like everyone's weapons are better than yours (because they are)
- Feel like you don't stand a fighting chance to make an impact on the outcome of a fight
And that's just it. You know those games where you, and YOU alone win this for your team? Well this is never going to happen in Planetside 2.
Be prepared for a lot of frustration.
