When I started playing this game, I expected pure Nazi mayhem, where feels were gone, and guns were in. Oh how I was wrong.
Yes, I still got all the Nazi mayhem I wanted. Duel wielding automatic shotguns, assault rifles, rockets, and heck, even sniper rifles. Is it plausible or nessecary? Nope, but its Wolfenstein so why the hell not? All the run gun fun from older shooters has made it into this game as well as the level design. Most levels allow for a nice amount of exploration, and award the player for exploring secret passageways by gifting them various upgrades and ammo. There is an option of going sneakily, with silenced pistols and knives being present in your inventory for this(and yes, you can duel wield both). Gameplay gets a 9.5/10, the .5 being shot off by a stray shrapnel shot by a shotgun Nazi because he violates everything in the vicinity.
Now... the story. Comming into the gameplay, and remembering this is the Wolfenstein series, one would expect very little justification on why we should kill Nazis, when its the main reason we bought this game. Yet the story takes a very surprising turn when it actually starts depicting the horrors that they have put upon the world, giving you fresh new reasons to brutally murder them. As the story goes on and on, your rage against the Nazis increases further and further, and luckily, the game knows it, because by the end when you reach the final level, ready to shove your knife down the main guys throat, all that stands between him and you is fifty million Nazis and Mechs, giving you plenty of room to work off your feels. And speaking of feels, this game just loves making you feel. All the characters displayed have some sort of personality, have a goal, and are flawed. I really liked each character, and how their story progressed. Without any spoilers, the story progressed in a direction I did not like at all, making me hate the Nazis with an even stronger passion. When I got to the last chapter, I was livid from what happened eariler, and simply couldn't wait to start tearing that place inside out. Once I had finished the chapter and saw the ending, my feels went supernova, and it was quite a heck of a ending for the game. There is the whole dual path thing where you can choose the outcome of a certain choice in the beginning to alter the timeline, but this doesn't change much besides a few paths and dialouge, the story is still intact. Also, being a Wolfenstein game, this game does have some weird spots here and there so that the plot can progress accordingly, while making little sense in the progress. Those are far and few and between though, earning the story aspect a 9.5/10.
Final Verdict: Want some of the funnest old-school gameplay this year has to offer along with a surprisingly well crafted story designed to make you feel and to engross you into the game even more? Pick this up at your next summer sale! One run took me 14-16 hours, and I'm planning on hitting up at least two more runs(alternate timeline, and a custom game mode one).

Okay, after playing the game for an hour, I wrote a sensible review of the game, stating I would not recommend it.
The followling is myy reveiw after 5 whole hours of existing as a miserable soldier in this war.
I likened it being repeatedly kicked in the nuts and then coaxed into giving it another go. The first reveiw was more detailed than that, but that's the gist. I pointed out some sound flaws, and held up the graphics and stability of the engine and server. I basically said it was not my cup of tea. 6 out of 8 people found my review helpful, either saying “Hey, I love games that repeatedly kick me in the balls!” and others who say “Oh, That sounds like a waste of my time and energy.” Either way- helpful.
The 2 people who did not find my review helpful took it upon themselves to say I was being to harsh, and also said I “Couldn’t review the game after only 1 hour.” I did. He was clearly in denial! But I downloaded the game AGAIN, just to be sure.
After 5 hours, I can say, I would not recommend this game to a friend. I just don’t think its fun! How’s that!
Vehicles- they are okay. The controls are messed up on the aircraft though. WAY off weirder than anything I’ve ever played were you fly a plane. But hey, I’ve never piloted an aircraft, what do I know? I know this wasn’t fun.
Character models- They are okay. You can customize them with certificates (or something) you earn or money you pay. Pretty cool. Also hard to tell people apart in various kinds of light. It’s not so clear cut as red dudes shooting blue dudes, when only small elements on a person’s suit are colored so, and the lighting is a hazy beautiful sunset PURPLE. The high tech futuristic  HUD doesn’t know if a guy is friend or foe until its too late. Maybe you can buy an upgrade for that . . . I don’t care.
Controls- they are okay. They are what I would expect. I like 3rd person with cover mechanics better, personally. I say 1st Person Shooter and honestly, you know most of the controls. Nothing special, It gets it done.
Landscape- You are on a planet with some continents divided up into a bunch of hexagons. There isn’t much in the way or realistic geological terrain, overall (like you see in Arma and DayZ- beautiful and realistic). It is more of that sculpty lumpy mountain looking stuff, and here are some really big rocks, trees, a swamp, like that. Some places are better than others. It’s not bad, it’s just nothing special. There is a base every 100 meters or so, no infrastructure, no towns, no cities, no villages, no civilians, no factories, no mines, no wildlife, no nothing. This is a planet full of military bases and there are three factions of really stupid people fighting over it FOR WHAT!?!?   Honestly, I don’t care. I didn’t see anything worth fighting for. That brings us to . . . .
Story- The planet should be a desolate wasteland of craters and corpses. Or maybe one of the factions would have just nuked the whole place from orbit? Basically these three armies are fighting each other with guns and vehicles when they have these machines that just SPEW soldiers into the fight. Put them in vehicles or squads, or drop them unrealistically from low orbit. They run about and die, only to be spewed back out of the machines and given weapons and pointed in the direction of “enemy” like suicidal lemmings!  Why? There are evil republicans, of course, high tech homosexuals, why not, and super awesome rebellious Rock-and-Roll rebels! I don't know what they are fighting for.
The Action- The most fun I had was repairing stuff. I followed some tanks around and repaired them, used their guns until they needed repairs, repaired them. Me and a billion others took a giant mushroom place. Cool. I repaired some guns and shot at tanks and repaired some AA guns and shot at aircraft. Cool. I climbed a mountain and got shot in the face. Disappointing. Most of it is spawn, turn a corner die, spawn run a half mile, die, spawn, grenade, die, spawn, fall, die, spawn, try to repair some shield generator, get shot in the face, die.
Wrap up- This is the longest review I have written. I honestly, just don’t really like wild disorganized hari-kari PVP. This is not a team assaulting a fortified position . . . It is three armies ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at each other as hard as they can, and whoever is standing on the pile at the end . . . wins?
After 30 minutes, I knew it wasn’t my thing. After 5 hours, I feel cheated. I can’t get that time back and I gained nothing as a human. I already know we are insignificant and conflict is ultimately pointless. This game offers me nothing I can’t have somewhere else and have more fun. Does that mean you will not like it? By all means, use that free will, you may love it. I have met plenty of people into S&M. Would I recommend it to a friend? I did, because misery loves company, but I regret it. It was wrong of me in my subjective view of morality as it stands now. I hope he will forgive me one day. NO, I will not recommend this game to a friend. If they ask, I’ll just say “Nah, that’s not my cup of tea.”
Is there anything they could do to change it and make it more palatable to me? No, and I don’t think they should. The game has an audience that loves it. Let it be.

So when Portal came out in 2007, it was like revolutionary way of playing a game that consisted of solving puzzles. I mean, the Portal Gun became one of Valve's icons, as well as the characters. So in 2011, a sequel is released. And we have Portal 2.
Whether you think it's more of the same or not... you're not wrong but you're not right either. While Portal 2 is more of the same concept as its prequel, you're not repeating the exact same levels/test chambers/whatever you wanna call them. But I'll get to that in a second.
You play as Chell, once again. Years after you defeated GLaDOS, you wake up and receive instructions on moving, after being in some sort of relaxation chamber for all those years. After that, you're greeted by a core named Wheatley, who tells you he's gonna help you escape from your chamber, only for you to find out you're actually back at Aperture Science and eventually to meet again with GLaDOS in the ruins of her chamber as she wakes up. That's when she throws Wheatly back in the rails he uses to travel and you into new test chambers. So you're once again testing for GLaDOS while you try to get to her. Later in the game, you witness a plot twist, but whether you know about it or not, I won't talk about it.
So as I said before, you're thrown back into Aperture's test chambers, solving puzzles using the Portal Gun and the environment around you in order to advance through the game. Not only that but for some sort of replay value, Portal 2 introduced a co-op mode for you to join forces with a friend to solve a total of 4 different sets of cooperative test chambers, with Atlas and P-Body as your characters. As you progress, you can also unlock items to customize either of them.
New elements were introduced like laser beams that usually have to be worked around with reflecting cubes to point them at their recepticles. Light paths were also added, to either create walls for turrets or new paths. And later on in the game, you're gonna have a lot of fun with the gels. The textures also make the game look like it's actually from 2011 and not like a Portal 1.5.
And if you've already had enough of what Portal 2 has to offer, good news. You can get even more content from Steam Workshop. So there's a lot more than just the game's standard content for you to go through!
I could go on and on about this game, but I think it's time for the score. Portal 2 gets an 9/10. It's an excellent game (I don't call it perfect cuz the concept is not really improved but yet again there's probably not much to improve in Portal's main concept) and a great sequel to an iconic game from Valve. I recommend getting not just Portal 2, but both games!

Online gameplay is largely stable and it is often not too difficult to find an opponent of your own level, though personally I'd always recommend playing with friends.
The £15 price-tag is reasonable if you're an RTS fan wanting a nostalgia hit. General RTS fans may want to wait for a slightly lower price.

Planetside 2 is a game I have had a very odd relationship with. Every once and a while I'll jump back into it, play for a week and then put it off again.
It's a glorious shooter MMO, with battles comprising of hundreds of players infantry, tanks, aircraft all going after a single point at once. It's a game that can have tactical stake-outs, co-ordinated airstrikes, and these MASSIVE battles where every single unit is an actual player. It's amazing to behold and participate in if your PC can handle it.
However, this game hasn't had the greatest history with updates or well.. "getting better." It's not that there haven't been updates, or there have, lots and lots and lots of updates fixing performance, looks, stability, gameplay, it's just that it's a game that has a tough time improving.
Since Daybreak games has taken over, more patches have been made for performance and stability, and it's become an easier game to get into than when Sony Online was in-charge, but we are likely to get fewer gameplay additions than when Sony was in charge.
Gameplay: As for gameplay, the shooting is pretty "relatively above average". Due to the load on the server, combat isn't incredibly precise. Lag isn't really the issue, it's that firearms by their nature in Planetside 2 are relatively innaccurate. Bullets feel more like physical objects and have actual drop that you have to deal with at the ranges you'll often be fighting at. A lot of combat in planetside 2 takes place at ranges unseen in most games that aren't ARMA, so frequently you'll find yourself having to adjust for bullet drop, even to hit stationary targets as is typically the case, even with the vanilla rocket launcher. (By the way, the stock RPG is one of if not the highest damage dealing weapons in the game.)
Balance: It's also not a perfectly balanced game, and earning new weapons can take a long, long time that you will likely end up spending "certs" on class abilities. The currrent game mitigates this by asking new players what their favorite class would be and then giving them another free firearm for that class.
You are likely to feel a bit useless early on, but just join a squad, stick with your teamates and try to help them out the best you can. I reccomend the Medic class (the only class to use assault rifles), and reviving people when they go down.
The "Free" aspect is questionable. No, you aren't stuck with bush league items if don't spend money, no you aren't at a direct disadvantage if you don't pay for things, but there are quite a few weapons available only with station cash, some of which are exclusive to this.
Despite all that, Planetside 2 is still a very, very fun game and there's still nothing else like it on PC, consoles or well... anywhere. If you have ever dreamed about massive battlefields full of hundreds of players, you should at least give it a try.

Portal 2 is a 2011 first-person puzzle-platform video game developed and published by Valve Corporation. It is the sequel to Portal (2007) and was released on April 19, 2011, for Microsoft Windows, OS X, Linux, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360. The retail versions of the game are distributed by Electronic Arts while online distribution of the Microsoft Windows, Mac OS X and Linux versions is handled by Valve's content delivery service Steam. Portal 2 was announced on March 5, 2010, following a week-long alternate reality game based on new patches to the original game. Before the game's release on Steam, the company released the Potato Sack, a second multi-week alternate reality game, involving 13 independently developed titles which culminated in a distributed computing spoof to release Portal 2 several hours early.
The game retains Portal's gameplay elements, and adds new features, including tractor beams, laser redirection, bridges made of light, and paint-like 'gels' accelerating the player's speed, allowing the player-character to jump higher or place portals on any surface. These gels were created by the team from the Independent Games Festival-winning DigiPen student project Tag: The Power of Paint. In the single-player campaign, the player controls protagonist Chell, awoken from suspended animation after many years, who must navigate the now-dilapidated Aperture Science Enrichment Center during its reconstruction by the reactivated GLaDOS, a powerful supercomputer. The storyline introduces new characters, including Wheatley (Stephen Merchant) and Cave Johnson (J. K. Simmons). Ellen McLain reprised the role of GLaDOS. Jonathan Coulton and The National each produced a song for the game. Portal 2 also includes a two-player cooperative mode, in which the robotic player-characters Atlas and P-Body (both voiced by Dee Bradley Baker) are each given a portal gun and are required to work together to solve puzzles. Valve provided post-release support for the game, including additional downloadable content and a simplified map editor to allow players to create and share test chambers with others.
Although some reviewers initially expressed concerns about the difficulty of expanding Portal into a full sequel, Portal 2 received critical acclaim, particularly for its writing, pacing, and dark humor. The voice work of McLain, Merchant, and Simmons were also praised, as were the new gameplay elements, the challenging but surmountable learning curve, and the additional cooperative mode. Some journalists ranked Portal 2 among the best games of 2011, and several named it their Game of the Year. Portal 2 has since been hailed as one of the greatest video games of all time.

I REALLY want to recommend this game, as it's a good concept and one with potential. But I just can't, and every other review has said just about every shortcoming I could mention. But for the sake of the review, I'll mention them:
Loot system
There used to be a Robopoints system, where even just scouting got you a few points, so you weren't leaving entirely empty-handed if you got one-shotted before doing any damage. Furthermore, if you had a decent match, you could typically afford SOMETHING to build towards the next teir (which I'll mention later). Now that's been done away in favor of loot crates, which are too heavily RPG-influenced, and you can only typically get them in three ways: 1) being the top player in the game (very hard unless you already have Legendary weapons, like the ever-broken LOML), 2) logging in for 6+ days in a row WITHOUT skipping a day, or 3, and what makes the game P2W in my view) buy crates. It's just bad for a game like this and should never have been added.
No tiers
Back in Robocraft's early days, the tier system made things more balanaced. To say the least, the Rail was broken in lower tiers, but due to how many tier points it added to a robot (typically putting a robot at T3 or higher with just the rail alone), you typically couldn't take it into lower tiers without significant sacrifices to durability (to the point where one properly-placed laser shot could destroy your bot in 1 hit). Now that tiers are gone, there are people taking LOMLs against those who are newer/lower CPU robots, with very few things that can reliably counter it.
P2W Environment
In case I didn't point it out clearly enough, this game is HEAVILY PAY2WIN. Recycling cubes gets you ABYSSMAL robits amounts unless they're Epic-tier or higher, everything is severely overpriced in the Forge, to the point where getting Legendary cubes is an needlessly-long grindfest unless the RNG gods deem you worthy of getting one on a non-premium Protonium crate slot (ASSUMING you place first in the match and DON'T LOSE), and the only reliable alternative is to buy large amounts of Protonium crates with, you guessed it, REAL MONEY. Premium isn't THAT big of a deal, but when you can only have up to 3 players in a platoon without it, half of the loot in crates is locked behind Premium, and you have to PRAY that they send out a Premium code if you don't want to spend money for extra loot drops and such, then it doesn't really make things better.
Overall, if there were some MAJOR overhauls, and some of the more questionable decisions were reversed, I'd be more likely to give a good review. But alas, none of those have happened, and the game has continued going downhill (made much worse by how FreeJam handles communications with the community and even tries to snuff out any views that don't put them in a good light), so I'm afraid to say that if you're looking for an experience where you can build your own machine and battle it out against other players, you're better off skipping Robocraft entirely and looking somewhere else.

This is how its done. Some developers just 'get' shooters, ID being one of them. OK this hasn't been developed by them but its running on the ID tech engine and their legacy lives on in this latest installment to the Wolfenstein saga. If you like your shooters old school, you will like this. A muscle bound hero, lots huge guns, tons of ammunition, waves of grunts and big ugly bosses. The gunplay is very reminicent of Rage, in fact there are many elements in this game that are, Thats a good thing as rage got a lot right. Wolfenstein goes further in that the maps are non linear. They are much like the maps of classics like doom, the levels are like a big wide corridor, you have to get from the beginning to the end, and make it through all the enemies. You can choose to play it quiet, using your knife, or go striaght down the middle, all guns blazing - or any combination. Its up to you, and it gives the action a very intersting dynamic. Many games that give you the option of quiet or full on, tend to lean you in one direction, punishing you for taking the 'wrong' option, Thats not the case here and it gives the game a real sense of freedom you dont normally get with shooters these days, even though the maps are actually not that big. Recommended to fans of classic shooters and those looking for a nice single player time sink who are tired of all the modern shooters and are want something a bit different.

An Old Time Player~
I've played my fair share of Robocraft, (More than I'd like to admit). Most of that time was back in 2013-2014. Back then the game was pretty much in it's primme, as all MMO's go through. The game held creative features, and a great fan base. Used to actually come home, and want to play some Robocraft. Was trying new designs, some worked some failed. But my failures i could learn from, make prototypes, test, and improve. The matches were held by a Tier System, this held true word to a balanced game. Not perfect, but good i was always given a chance. Your robot had to cover aspects like; Mobility, weight distrobution, weapon class, tier, weak points, and strong suits. No creation was perfect, and that's where the game was strong. It was creative, and ahead of its time..... It was a biillion dollar idea.... it was one of my favorite games. Now, it's nothing but a beaten horse, the Develpoping, Marketing, and Community all failed through ignorence and greed. So if you happen to read this review and the thought of downloading the game is moving through your head, Please, do.  Try the game out for youreself.... If you like it, good to you. But take it from an old player, the game is empty, dead, and a hollow skeleton of what it once was. I reccommend you try it out, then imagine it 10, 20, 30 times better. Read the other reviews, to tell you about the past and the present.. then decide for youreself wether the game is worth your time or not. Through these recent months of coming back to the game, Iv'e decided to leave it, and tryy to remember it's good years in fondness instead of this.... thing, it is now.

I think I've played enough Planetside 2 to rate it. I rate it 3.5/5. It's pretty good...
but it gets repetitive easily and the game loses interest if you play for free because after an initial few upgrades you can earn it becomes extremely hard to earn further upgrades which leads to a sense of stagnation and some boredom. The graphics are truly beautiful and yet the buildings are all fairly generic with often fairly generic layouts. I wish (and was hoping) this game was more like a massively multiplayer UT2004 Onslaught game but certain game mechanics (such as the general weakness of each individual character) keeps it from being that.
Pros: Great graphics (honestly, some of the most impressive graphics I have seen in a game so far and extremely clean and bright styled graphics too), great controls, good sound, good vehicles types, good number of players, the game world is really big, friendly community, very little lag, good anti-hacking support (I did not notice ANY hacking/cheating), initially interesting and exciting, no bugs, no freeze ups, fun to see random, interesting situations, great chatting abilities, day/night cycle occurs in the game, this is the first multiplayer game I have ever seen which makes it fun to be in a support role (such as a medic or engineer) and as a result there is no lack of them in the game. The game is probably a little more fun (more upgrades, more character abilities, faster upgrades,) if you pay for it and it costs only 10 dollars a month.
Cons: mostly lacks music, air vehicles can be hard to control, generic buildings, the game world is really big, fairly generic (but futuristic looking) weaponry which fails to cover up world war 2 style battle mechanics, most players act like idiots and use poor tactics, not very much sense of accomplishment, very low variety of mission objectives/targets, uses 15gb of hard drive space, terrain is too rugged in many places leading to forced frontal assaults, hard for many players to find vehicles, no way to permanently win makes game seem too pointless, no real plot or story, difficult learning curve for an FPS, extremely noisy game, too easy to get killed, battles don't last long enough for individual players, not enough random interesting situations to keep me coming back for more, not enough players are able to type and game at the same time leading to no one chatting, game world often feels like it is too empty (unless you are in a main battle area) and needs some adventure game elements to fill it up, unable to permanently scar or change landscape in any way, cannot gain character experience in particular skills by simply trying to use those skills but instead uses a standard point system, needs more environments and more weather effects, game needs AI controlled abilities (such as an ability to call in AI airstrikes or artillery from off the map and so forth (as seen in Enemy Territory: Quake Wars), not enough differences between different sides (every side has access to some sort of shotgun, rocket launcher etc. they just look different between sides), no way to pick up other people's weapons (not even from your own team), no side appears to be extremely evil looking (though one side does look a little more fascist than the other two). Game does not appear to provide a whole lot more fun if you pay for it however (only a little more fun). the game makes combat seem too clean and organized. The game still does not manage to depict an appropriate amount of carnage and chaos and the battlefield does not stay strewn (and is not strewn from the outset) with any wreckage whatsoever. The game world is too static.

I had my doubts at first, but getting into the game got me thinking how I have missed the simplicity of an FPS. Dont get me wrong, I am not saying this game is simple. The story is well made and having gotten myself used to approaching games at its highest difficulty all the time, the challenge is there. You can approach it with mindless killing, dual wielding almost all your weapons the whole way or stealthily killing them with your knives -- thrown or not.
I have to admit, I havent had the time to complete the game but as of now, I am really enjoying it.
It was worth my money and I cant wait to see what I can unlock end game. Although linear, the way the game unfolds makes you feel as though the world youre in is bigger than you think. It is both fast paced in action but also delves into critical thinking situations which is a good breaker for all the action.
The story will keep you hooked and the need to kill enemies or find those little collectibles makes playing worth while.
thumbs up for wolfenstein...sadly, lack of multiplayer is its biggest and probably only downside.

Fantastic gunplay is married to a pulpy but enjoyable storyline in the most fun shooter I've played since F.E.A.R. came out nine years ago.  I'm surprised by its thoughtfulness, and by how rewarding it is to take your time here.  Look for secrets, eavesdrop on conversations, and marvel at how intricately considered this turned out to be.  It's an enthralling game, and one that should put MachineGames on the map.  No matter how Doom (4) turns out, I'm confident that good things can still come from id - or at least its back catalog of IP.  HIGHLY recommended.
P.S.  The quoted system requirements are very strange.  They've overspec'ed the CPU requirements (there are YouTube videos of it running agreeably on an i3 with a punchy graphics card) and understated RAM (4 gigs is probably a good *minimum* number), and if you're willing to run below 1080p you'd probably be all right with anything beefier than a Radeon 6670 or its Nvidia equivalent.  Just be certain you've got at least 512 MB of video RAM, and a gig is a much safer bet.  Performance notes follow.
HTPC, Core i5 3570k @ stock, 2048 MB GeForce GTX 750 Ti, 12 gigs DDR3-1333: Performance is grand at 1080p, rarely dropping below 60 fps.
Frankenputer, Core 2 Quad Q6600 @ stock, 2048 MB Radeon R7 260X, 6 gigs DDR2-800: Overall performance is fine at medium detail.  Opening cinematics stutter, but the game itself runs in a fashion that's mostly pleasing.  The CPU seems to be the bottleneck here - in spite of four physical cores, the Core 2 architecture's low-clocked and pokey.
Sooner or later I'll get it installed and running with Wine on my workstation - an AMD FX-8320 with 24 gigs of DDR3-1600 and a GTX 660, running Xubuntu 14.04 x64.  PLAY THIS GAME!

No MP means jack, this game is totally awesome and you should definitely buy it. The gameplay isn't meant to be a realistic military simulation, you are supposed to be runnin' and gunnin' nazis and blowing their faces off with duel-wielding fully automatic shotguns. That is what makes this game extremely enjoyable. The storyline and character development is also very interesting and engaging. The graphics aren't top notch, but it is fun to watch the body parts of the fuhrer's slaves splatter across the walls. The pacing is very thought out, precise, and it comes in just the right amounts. Anyone complaining about how you have to press "e" for every one time they pick up, just learn how to hit "e' fast, it works just fine for me, because there aren't any items that you don't want to pick up. A lot of people don't like the linear aspects, but the game does give you the option to go guns a blazin' or take a stealthier approach, and it does appeal to these playstyles very nicely. Usually when I start a game, I look at the clock frequently to see how long I've been playing, but for this game, I went for 4 hours without even realizing it. So, yes, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who plays video games.

Portal 2 is a 2011 first-person puzzle-platform video game developed and published by Valve Corporation. It is the sequel to Portal (2007) and was released on April 19, 2011, for Microsoft Windows, OS X, Linux, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360. The retail versions of the game are distributed by Electronic Arts while online distribution of the Microsoft Windows, Mac OS X and Linux versions is handled by Valve's content delivery service Steam. Portal 2 was announced on March 5, 2010, following a week-long alternate reality game based on new patches to the original game. Before the game's release on Steam, the company released the Potato Sack, a second multi-week alternate reality game, involving 13 independently developed titles which culminated in a distributed computing spoof to release Portal 2 several hours early.
The game retains Portal's gameplay elements, and adds new features, including tractor beams, laser redirection, bridges made of light, and paint-like 'gels' accelerating the player's speed, allowing the player-character to jump higher or place portals on any surface. These gels were created by the team from the Independent Games Festival-winning DigiPen student project Tag: The Power of Paint. In the single-player campaign, the player controls protagonist Chell, awoken from suspended animation after many years, who must navigate the now-dilapidated Aperture Science Enrichment Center during its reconstruction by the reactivated GLaDOS, a powerful supercomputer. The storyline introduces new characters, including Wheatley (Stephen Merchant) and Cave Johnson (J. K. Simmons). Ellen McLain reprised the role of GLaDOS. Jonathan Coulton and The National each produced a song for the game. Portal 2 also includes a two-player cooperative mode, in which the robotic player-characters Atlas and P-Body (both voiced by Dee Bradley Baker) are each given a portal gun and are required to work together to solve puzzles. Valve provided post-release support for the game, including additional downloadable content and a simplified map editor to allow players to create and share test chambers with others.
Although some reviewers initially expressed concerns about the difficulty of expanding Portal into a full sequel, Portal 2 received critical acclaim, particularly for its writing, pacing, and dark humor. The voice work of McLain, Merchant, and Simmons were also praised, as were the new gameplay elements, the challenging but surmountable learning curve, and the additional cooperative mode. Some journalists ranked Portal 2 among the best games of 2011, and several named it their Game of the Year. Portal 2 has since been hailed as one of the greatest video games of all time.

Great Game.A throw back to old school shooters from the 90's. Been a Wolfenstein fan from childhood.
Machine Games has managed to mix modern shooter features with the old for a very convincing experience. Solid story line and character development, Wolfenstein NO brings the FPS genre backs to its roots with fast pace action based around combat intensity, excitement and less hyper realism that has overtaken the entire genre as of late. No more ducking for cover every five seconds to regenerate your health. Wolfenstein NO makes good use of HP and Armour pick ups that allows the player to feel more apart of the story rather than just a bystander.
I can't rave enough about the gun play in this game, amazing gun selection and design, almost every weapon can be dual-wielded. A good variety of weapons that all have different uses which help foster and encourage different play styles eg. stealth or open combat. This game has put to rest the argument that every FPS must embrace a multiplayer feature. While I hope due to the success of Wolfenstein NO a standalone multiplayer is developed in the future that echos the Enemy Territory model of earlier Wolfenstein games, this game easily stands tall on its singleplayer features alone.
With multiple difficulties, different characters and a meaningful collectibles feature that unlocks four very unique gameplay modes, this game has plenty of replay-ability and could easily be enjoyed for many playthroughs. I don't normally like DLC but I really hope this game gets some side mission or extended story line DLC and fingers crossed a sequel in the coming year or two.
Hats off to Machine Games for crafting an enjoyable singleplayer FPS in an era where everyone is obsessed with multiplayer and for standing by their development goals till completion to produce a solid product. Props also to Bethesda for backing a  studio with great talent and vision. Hope you enjoy this game as much as I did.

I can easily tell you that this is, without a single doubt, the best Max Payne game of the series. And I knew it before even finishing the main story. The narrative breathes relentless intrigue, the gameplay-to-cinematic stylization pulls you in close to the world, Max's self-destructive substance abuse and emotional torment raises the Anti-Hero banner center-stage, and the 90's action movie gunplay and ridiculous heart-pumping pace is addicting.
All of this makes it hard to stop playing the game if you need to go to work, go to sleep, run to the bathroom, or stroll outside to get away from a raging neighborhood fire churning around your computer. All you want is to know what happens next.
Beating the game brings unlocked modes, challenges, and settings (such as unlimited bullet-time, etc.) to make you feel the machismo of being a godlike action movie star when you crave some mindless fun, but it makes you earn many of these perks. Skill is a currency for gameplay modes, which is a hell of a lot better than money. Multiplayer brings a community experience for those who want that sort of thing, and I had a good amount of fun even though I wasn't expecting to; just keep in mind there are some ridiculously-talented and competitive folks running around in MP3's multiplayer, so expect your single-player Godhood Complex to be knocked down a few pegs on the humility ladder.
Worth every penny of it's original $60 price tag when I picked it up at launch, and now that you can find it on supersale much of the time, make good use of that twitchy trigger finger and enjoy Rockstar's take on this classic series.

Having not played any of the previous Wolfenstein games, I was / am completely blown away by Wolfenstein: The New Order.
Theatrically it feels like something akin to "Call of Duty: World at War" (World War II beautiful environments) which is complimented by the Gameplay that takes some cues from "Half Life 2" (think puzzles, exploration, and small but meaningful engagements) and Story Pacing (after the first couple missions it starts to feel like an "Ocean's 11" (2001) movie with its stylishly cinematography). Wolfenstein takes these inspirations and creates something with its own identity that leaves you wanting more.
I've played the game on Uber difficulity, which has taken me about 12 hours to complete. I took my time with a more stealth based approach, but did enjoy a few engagements going full-on guns blazing. Both ways of approaching a situation are carefully crafted making the AI seem very smart than in most games I've played, resulting in some very entertaining combat.
Story wise, the game presents some morally conflicted decisions, sometimes even in very tense situations. MachineGames have done an amazing job at never making you feel like you're being held by the hand of the game designers to do what they want you to do. I've watched walkthrough videos and saw things I didn't expierence, or vice versa. This approach makes your expierence unique when talking with your friends about their expierence encouraging you to go back to play again seeing what else there is.
Another thing that stood out to me was they way they did Quick Time Events (QTEs), or more specifically, how they didn't do them. There are a lot of moments with up close in-your-face gameplay, and you don't get a button prompt on the screen which breaks your believeability of this world you're in. You instinctively start pressing buttons / moving your mouse and you're doing what you thought you'd be doing. They introduce this mechanic in a great (and frantic) way early on in the first level, and continue to effectively implement it in various scenarios that make you feel like "Yeah, I did that on my own".

Portal 2 is a first-person puzzle game developed and published by Valve and released in April 2011. Portal 2 incorporates a campaign that allows you to solve challenging puzzles while treating you to a strong and simple storyline. This review will discuss the campaign, the voice acting, dialogue, and the co-op feature.
Portal 2 is a good and challenging puzzle game that emphasises creativity and excels in the simplicity of telling a story. The story nicely builds to an excellent climax that feels like a satisfying conclusion to the game. The game features beautiful voice acting and some exceptional performances from Merchant and McLain and strongly delivers in the quality of the dialogue. I am new to the puzzle genre so playing Portal 2 felt fresh and different. There are some issues outlined above in the game, but nothing that detracts from the overall experience. At $19.99, I recommend it.
Portal 2 features a quality campaign that emphasises creativity through overcoming puzzles and excels in superb voice acting that includes funny humour. You begin the campaign as Chell, a female character holding a portal gun. Chell completes tests using her portal gun while being monitored by AI computer system Glados, voiced by Ellen McLain. Chell completes these tests while listening to Wheatley, a programming core that is voiced by Stephen Merchant, in which he wants to escape the facility. The puzzles are diverse and I do not grasp the notion they are repetitive. They do in fact become more difficult as the game progresses which is due to new things being added to each level that add a new layer of complexity. For instance, some levels feature turrets that can spray bullets at you, which you must destroy before advancing. Portal 2 has a really good ending that ends the story with an amazing final mission that mixes both emotion and intensity. Furthermore, the ending smoothly transitions into the credits that completely alter the atmosphere into a beautiful light hearted finale, complete with a song sung by Glados. Briefly, the single player experience does have some annoying glitches with freezing when pressing R for the feedback prompt and frequent crashing via alt tabbing. These two issues had minimal impact on my experience of the game.
The dialogue enhances the single player component by incorporating witty humour with dialogue that provides excellent characterisation to the characters. For instance, events showcase characters change of heart and provide some emotion to their robot personalities. This creates a juxtaposition of humans and robots because the game reveals human traits of emotion, self-interest for personal gain, and relationships with other individuals within Glados and Wheatley, both whom are robots. The voice acting in Portal 2 complement the strong dialogue because individually, Stephen Merchant delivers a memorable and excellent performance for Wheatley by striking different voice tones that match different situations within the game. Meanwhile, Ellen McLain provides a good voice line to showcase the personality and character of Glados. The dialogue and voice acting immediately created a sense of whose a protagonist and antagonist in the simple story of hero vs. villain.
The co-op element of Portal 2 provides more levels to lengthen the game. These levels add some exciting fresh dynamics to each level because you have to cooperate with your team mate and depend on the other to complete levels. For instance, I had to stand on a button while my friend flew to the other side of the window to retrieve the block in order to complete the level.
All in All

I played Age of Empires II  extensively back when it was released in 1999 along with every game in the Age of Empires franchise before and after. Age of Empires II is the high water mark for the series and arguably the best overall RTS game of all time. It combines excellent design with solid art direction. The single player campaigns are fun and varied and multiplier is still fun to this day. This is one of the easier RTS titles in which to create your own map and I have made everything from the Great Lakes area of the United States to a large scale map of Middle Earth. Overall you can not go wrong with this purchase, especially for the low price that it is offered for on Steam.
Positives
+Excellent graphics for its time, although they look dated now
+Management of economy units was still important back in 1999 and you win this game with villagers, not with trebuchets.
+Huge maps and many valid play styles.
Negatives
-Dated graphics.
Overall
9/10

Having not played any of the previous Wolfenstein games, I was / am completely blown away by Wolfenstein: The New Order.
Theatrically it feels like something akin to "Call of Duty: World at War" (World War II beautiful environments) which is complimented by the Gameplay that takes some cues from "Half Life 2" (think puzzles, exploration, and small but meaningful engagements) and Story Pacing (after the first couple missions it starts to feel like an "Ocean's 11" (2001) movie with its stylishly cinematography). Wolfenstein takes these inspirations and creates something with its own identity that leaves you wanting more.
I've played the game on Uber difficulity, which has taken me about 12 hours to complete. I took my time with a more stealth based approach, but did enjoy a few engagements going full-on guns blazing. Both ways of approaching a situation are carefully crafted making the AI seem very smart than in most games I've played, resulting in some very entertaining combat.
Story wise, the game presents some morally conflicted decisions, sometimes even in very tense situations. MachineGames have done an amazing job at never making you feel like you're being held by the hand of the game designers to do what they want you to do. I've watched walkthrough videos and saw things I didn't expierence, or vice versa. This approach makes your expierence unique when talking with your friends about their expierence encouraging you to go back to play again seeing what else there is.
Another thing that stood out to me was they way they did Quick Time Events (QTEs), or more specifically, how they didn't do them. There are a lot of moments with up close in-your-face gameplay, and you don't get a button prompt on the screen which breaks your believeability of this world you're in. You instinctively start pressing buttons / moving your mouse and you're doing what you thought you'd be doing. They introduce this mechanic in a great (and frantic) way early on in the first level, and continue to effectively implement it in various scenarios that make you feel like "Yeah, I did that on my own".

The best MMOFPS since the first PlanetSide. Think of it as Halo as an MMO. You get to use tanks, buggies, ATVs, rocket launchers, sniper rifles, machine guns, shotguns, pistols, knives, aircraft, proximity mines, C4, terminal hacking, stealth, jetpacks, and more in this sci-fi themed war game between the three factions TR (Terran Republic), NC (New Conglomerate), and VS (Vanu Sovereignity). As with the first PlanetSide, despite its complexity the biggest problem is the lack of depth since it's really just all about fighting and territories you gain will always eventually be reset or recaptured.
As an example of this lack of depth, buildings are indestructible and there is no way to construct buildings, making it feel like a rather bland, static world at times. If it were inspired by concepts like the (somewhat of a failure) Command and Conquer: Renegade, or games like 10six (which combined MMOFPS+MMORPG with strategy and building), and allowed you to construct and destroy buildings in customizable ways (e.g. nearly any location you want and without the short despawn timers typical of PS2), then it would add a whole new level of depth to the gameplay and make it more dynamic.
If that wasn't bad enough, certain aspects of the game (as a PvP game, of course, there is no real PvE in PS2) have previously been clearly unbalanced but taken weeks or months to correct.
Still, in my opinion this beats nearly every other FPS out there for long-term playability. The complexity of this game and amount of choices are staggering compared to nearly every other FPS because in comparison they have far less players and they seem to be built on a typical FPS template with limited options, especially compared to the plethora of vehicles and vehicle loadouts in PS2.

Portal 2 is a first-person puzzle game developed and published by Valve and released in April 2011. Portal 2 incorporates a campaign that allows you to solve challenging puzzles while treating you to a strong and simple storyline. This review will discuss the campaign, the voice acting, dialogue, and the co-op feature.
Portal 2 is a good and challenging puzzle game that emphasises creativity and excels in the simplicity of telling a story. The story nicely builds to an excellent climax that feels like a satisfying conclusion to the game. The game features beautiful voice acting and some exceptional performances from Merchant and McLain and strongly delivers in the quality of the dialogue. I am new to the puzzle genre so playing Portal 2 felt fresh and different. There are some issues outlined above in the game, but nothing that detracts from the overall experience. At $19.99, I recommend it.
Portal 2 features a quality campaign that emphasises creativity through overcoming puzzles and excels in superb voice acting that includes funny humour. You begin the campaign as Chell, a female character holding a portal gun. Chell completes tests using her portal gun while being monitored by AI computer system Glados, voiced by Ellen McLain. Chell completes these tests while listening to Wheatley, a programming core that is voiced by Stephen Merchant, in which he wants to escape the facility. The puzzles are diverse and I do not grasp the notion they are repetitive. They do in fact become more difficult as the game progresses which is due to new things being added to each level that add a new layer of complexity. For instance, some levels feature turrets that can spray bullets at you, which you must destroy before advancing. Portal 2 has a really good ending that ends the story with an amazing final mission that mixes both emotion and intensity. Furthermore, the ending smoothly transitions into the credits that completely alter the atmosphere into a beautiful light hearted finale, complete with a song sung by Glados. Briefly, the single player experience does have some annoying glitches with freezing when pressing R for the feedback prompt and frequent crashing via alt tabbing. These two issues had minimal impact on my experience of the game.
The dialogue enhances the single player component by incorporating witty humour with dialogue that provides excellent characterisation to the characters. For instance, events showcase characters change of heart and provide some emotion to their robot personalities. This creates a juxtaposition of humans and robots because the game reveals human traits of emotion, self-interest for personal gain, and relationships with other individuals within Glados and Wheatley, both whom are robots. The voice acting in Portal 2 complement the strong dialogue because individually, Stephen Merchant delivers a memorable and excellent performance for Wheatley by striking different voice tones that match different situations within the game. Meanwhile, Ellen McLain provides a good voice line to showcase the personality and character of Glados. The dialogue and voice acting immediately created a sense of whose a protagonist and antagonist in the simple story of hero vs. villain.
The co-op element of Portal 2 provides more levels to lengthen the game. These levels add some exciting fresh dynamics to each level because you have to cooperate with your team mate and depend on the other to complete levels. For instance, I had to stand on a button while my friend flew to the other side of the window to retrieve the block in order to complete the level.
All in All

Good grindy microtransaction FPS game. Tons of people, tons of shooting, tons of vehicles and gear and guns and stuff. But not for me. I lasted a good long week and had a ton of fun.
PRO:
Lots of guns and shooting and stuff.
Fast and furious and deaths don't matter - if you're into that. I'm not. Many if not most FPS players are.
Tried and true concept - see the original. There's a reason for the cult following.
Big worlds and if you don't mind doing some learning you can go places and do stuff. Shooting and dying mainly. Some cool environments (Hossin jungle world).
VERY different classes and vehicles playstyles.
CON:
Deaths don't matter much. You will die a lot and it's just kind of silly quite often, esp. for new players, it's just die die die repeat, even if you know a bit and watch a bunch of videos like
Infantry move too fast and everyone seems to headshot me while I ...I guess I'm just bad.
Tons of vehicles that explode you good. Unless you're into that. They have a bit of learning to them, or a lot.
Takes a lot of fiddling with mouse settings and graphics and whatnot - the default settings for my Razer laptop were way too high for playing in medium-large battles.
Everyone else is now an expert with all the skills and good luck new guy. Die die die repeat.
The basic version of each class/vehicle kind of ...isn't all that. You will die. With some exceptions.
WHY I NO LONGER PLAY:
It's just way too hard to survive unless you really know a lot and you're really good. Watch any good youtuber or Twitcher and you'll see them pull together massive streaks on the regular. Go into game and have fun dying. Repeatedly, for hours and hours. Days on end. There's simply a massive amount of learning to do before you can survive for long. And there are only so many playstyles, and you have to switch from class to class or loadout to loadout to suit the place/time/situation. Not to mention the massive learning curve on many vehicles.
In short, too much skill needed for me, and too much learning required to get there, and too much restriction on how to play (strafe ADAD and constantly jerk around to throw off enemies' aim etc). Everything is jerky and twitchy and respawn. Not fun for me, but maybe for you.

As much as I used to want to, I can no longer reccomend this game.
Back in the day, I had 3 bots, all of which were comfy in the T10 catagory, and 1 was even composed of 90% TX-1 peices. Evetually I scrapped 1 and began construction on a TX-1 bot to play with. At the same time I also made a T4 bot to play with a friend with. It was poorpy put together and basically useless.
I'm sure you would guess which bot is now useful in the new version, even though all 3 have massive drawbacks.
First, let's cover the nano-thingies (medics). Before, a constant stream would come from them, and sustain a steady heaing rate. There was nothing wrong with this, and ship could outgin the healing, and their size and cost meant that most were small hover bots with 4-6 healing turrets on them. Now let's move to today, they fire 1 short burst of "healing", which is not only completely annoying (as you can no longer heal teamates in a controlled way, previously you could heal 2 or more people at once when your beams split), makes the healing gun completely useless (stay out of combat for 10 seconds and you're healed anyways) but also takes all skill out of it, as paying attention to the refresh rate is unused and pointless.
Moving on now to railguns. Which are now 90% less effective than they used to be. I can unload 6 of what used to be T10 rail guns into a peice of robot only 4 cubes thick, and it won't break. I'm no expert, but 6 T10 railguns will mash up even the best unsheilded robot. Even sheilded, 1 hit would disable the shield. Now this no longer works, making railguns completely unviable in later stages, as shields are pretty much a complete defence, and bots in the sky are now big enough to shrug off railguns.
Now onto any bot with wheels. Back in the day maps with ice would actually feel like ice on ice. Now all ground is pretty much dirt. A 4-wheeled bot on earth is pretty much an ice-skater, which makes control around obsticles impossible. The maps are worse, with shrapnel and detial ALREADY built into the map being completely no-clippable through. Even some terrain is clippable.
And now finally for robots overall. The imagination has all been sucked from this game. Robots are all pretty similar, and there is no big benefit to different bots.
And at last, overall, the tiering system needs to be brought back. The 10 teirs made progression seem fun and cool, now I can barely tell where I am other than off my bot rating. In addition it made battles more interesting with 10 fighting classes.
So no, this game has gone from being amazing to crap. Essentially the developers have left the old community out to dry, so if you're looking at coming back, get a new account. If you're new, it's fun for a while, but dedication is not rewarded.
Random loot? Check. Very little progress? Check.  2/10 would not play again.

Portal 2 is a first-person puzzle game developed and published by Valve and released in April 2011. Portal 2 incorporates a campaign that allows you to solve challenging puzzles while treating you to a strong and simple storyline. This review will discuss the campaign, the voice acting, dialogue, and the co-op feature.
Portal 2 is a good and challenging puzzle game that emphasises creativity and excels in the simplicity of telling a story. The story nicely builds to an excellent climax that feels like a satisfying conclusion to the game. The game features beautiful voice acting and some exceptional performances from Merchant and McLain and strongly delivers in the quality of the dialogue. I am new to the puzzle genre so playing Portal 2 felt fresh and different. There are some issues outlined above in the game, but nothing that detracts from the overall experience. At $19.99, I recommend it.
Portal 2 features a quality campaign that emphasises creativity through overcoming puzzles and excels in superb voice acting that includes funny humour. You begin the campaign as Chell, a female character holding a portal gun. Chell completes tests using her portal gun while being monitored by AI computer system Glados, voiced by Ellen McLain. Chell completes these tests while listening to Wheatley, a programming core that is voiced by Stephen Merchant, in which he wants to escape the facility. The puzzles are diverse and I do not grasp the notion they are repetitive. They do in fact become more difficult as the game progresses which is due to new things being added to each level that add a new layer of complexity. For instance, some levels feature turrets that can spray bullets at you, which you must destroy before advancing. Portal 2 has a really good ending that ends the story with an amazing final mission that mixes both emotion and intensity. Furthermore, the ending smoothly transitions into the credits that completely alter the atmosphere into a beautiful light hearted finale, complete with a song sung by Glados. Briefly, the single player experience does have some annoying glitches with freezing when pressing R for the feedback prompt and frequent crashing via alt tabbing. These two issues had minimal impact on my experience of the game.
The dialogue enhances the single player component by incorporating witty humour with dialogue that provides excellent characterisation to the characters. For instance, events showcase characters change of heart and provide some emotion to their robot personalities. This creates a juxtaposition of humans and robots because the game reveals human traits of emotion, self-interest for personal gain, and relationships with other individuals within Glados and Wheatley, both whom are robots. The voice acting in Portal 2 complement the strong dialogue because individually, Stephen Merchant delivers a memorable and excellent performance for Wheatley by striking different voice tones that match different situations within the game. Meanwhile, Ellen McLain provides a good voice line to showcase the personality and character of Glados. The dialogue and voice acting immediately created a sense of whose a protagonist and antagonist in the simple story of hero vs. villain.
The co-op element of Portal 2 provides more levels to lengthen the game. These levels add some exciting fresh dynamics to each level because you have to cooperate with your team mate and depend on the other to complete levels. For instance, I had to stand on a button while my friend flew to the other side of the window to retrieve the block in order to complete the level.

Wolfenstein just might be one of the longest-running game series in existence. Originally conceived as a stealth game in 1981, id Software morphed Wolfenstein into the herald of first-person shooters in 1992, and 2001's Return to Castle Wolfenstein brought along one of the best designed team-based multiplayer FPS experiences. Nowadays, the series is no longer about innovation - the focus has shifted to nostalgia.
And that's not a bad thing at all. Wolfenstein: The New Order is an unashamed throwback to arcadey shooters of the olden days, into the time when enemies were plentiful, cover mechanics were not invented yet and heroes could carry 20 weapons on their backs. Wolfenstein is about action, and lots of it. However, as a nod to the original, stealth is also an option, and a very enjoyable one at that. I think this game is one of the few good examples of how to blend action and stealth seamlessly in an FPS.
The story is surprisingly interesting and even has a bit of depth while keeping true to the popcorn style of the series. Nazis are still the bad guys, are still totally evil and still do their crazy experiments. Only the supernatural elements are a bit more toned down this time since the game concentrates on exploring a new, intriguing what-if scenario not before seen in the series. A highly enjoyable ride, and probably my favorite single-player FPS since Bulletstorm.

Portal 2 is a first-person puzzle game developed and published by Valve and released in April 2011. Portal 2 incorporates a campaign that allows you to solve challenging puzzles while treating you to a strong and simple storyline. This review will discuss the campaign, the voice acting, dialogue, and the co-op feature.
Portal 2 is a good and challenging puzzle game that emphasises creativity and excels in the simplicity of telling a story. The story nicely builds to an excellent climax that feels like a satisfying conclusion to the game. The game features beautiful voice acting and some exceptional performances from Merchant and McLain and strongly delivers in the quality of the dialogue. I am new to the puzzle genre so playing Portal 2 felt fresh and different. There are some issues outlined above in the game, but nothing that detracts from the overall experience. At $19.99, I recommend it.
Portal 2 features a quality campaign that emphasises creativity through overcoming puzzles and excels in superb voice acting that includes funny humour. You begin the campaign as Chell, a female character holding a portal gun. Chell completes tests using her portal gun while being monitored by AI computer system Glados, voiced by Ellen McLain. Chell completes these tests while listening to Wheatley, a programming core that is voiced by Stephen Merchant, in which he wants to escape the facility. The puzzles are diverse and I do not grasp the notion they are repetitive. They do in fact become more difficult as the game progresses which is due to new things being added to each level that add a new layer of complexity. For instance, some levels feature turrets that can spray bullets at you, which you must destroy before advancing. Portal 2 has a really good ending that ends the story with an amazing final mission that mixes both emotion and intensity. Furthermore, the ending smoothly transitions into the credits that completely alter the atmosphere into a beautiful light hearted finale, complete with a song sung by Glados. Briefly, the single player experience does have some annoying glitches with freezing when pressing R for the feedback prompt and frequent crashing via alt tabbing. These two issues had minimal impact on my experience of the game.
The dialogue enhances the single player component by incorporating witty humour with dialogue that provides excellent characterisation to the characters. For instance, events showcase characters change of heart and provide some emotion to their robot personalities. This creates a juxtaposition of humans and robots because the game reveals human traits of emotion, self-interest for personal gain, and relationships with other individuals within Glados and Wheatley, both whom are robots. The voice acting in Portal 2 complement the strong dialogue because individually, Stephen Merchant delivers a memorable and excellent performance for Wheatley by striking different voice tones that match different situations within the game. Meanwhile, Ellen McLain provides a good voice line to showcase the personality and character of Glados. The dialogue and voice acting immediately created a sense of whose a protagonist and antagonist in the simple story of hero vs. villain.
The co-op element of Portal 2 provides more levels to lengthen the game. These levels add some exciting fresh dynamics to each level because you have to cooperate with your team mate and depend on the other to complete levels. For instance, I had to stand on a button while my friend flew to the other side of the window to retrieve the block in order to complete the level.
All in All

I was very surprised by Wolfenstein: The New Order. I expected an average to above average game, but it ended up being my game of the year (so far!). It’s hard to describe how much I enjoyed it but I will try.
Story wise it’s solid. There’s a great cast of characters that you meet throughout the 15 hour campaign. Each has their own story and their own place in the game world. Even the main protagonist BJ, is a much more fleshed out character than his previous depictions in the Wolfenstein games. Also, the cutscenes are incredible. They blended so well into the gameplay and gave me the impression I was watching a film.
In terms of gameplay, this is where Wolfenstein TNO shined the brightest. Every weapon in the extensive arsenal is fun to use, seriously. The weapon sounds, the destruction of the environment and the pure carnage that you can cause is unforgettable. Almost every weapon has alternate firing modes for mixing up the gunplay and making it more than just an average point and click FPS. Dual wielding originally seemed like an unnecessary novelty, but is actually a lot of fun that adds EVEN MORE variety to the way you can play (ex. one assault rifle can shoot rockets while the other fires full auto). Shooting enemies can pop heads, blast off armour, and generally shows a very detailed level of damage. Throughout almost every level there are multiple paths to choose. Because of this, most encounters can be approached with stealth or a more aggressive route.
Wolfenstein the New Order is easily in my top five games of all time. That’s not something I expected in this day and age (especially with all the crap I’ve played lately). This game is a big deal for me and I hope that others can appreciate it as much as I did, because it really deserves the limelight.

It'd been years since I'd played Max Payne 2, years since I'd felt anything but regret. By the time it came out I was too deep in the bottle to remember if it had ever been worth it. Maybe I'd play the game, or maybe I'd be the one who was played; an out of tune deadbeat that's worth nothing more than the 60 bucks in his wallet. I paid the money - what the hell else was I gonna do? They'd gotten me. An overdue port of a washed up franchise, and I'd given in like the sucker they'd pegged me for. I wanted answers. I decided to kill my way to the truth, just like old times.
I wanted to beat the game like a drunk beats his wife - over and over. Then the truth hit me like a double-barreled shotgun straight to the face; unskippable cutscenes. Time seemed to slow down as I hit enter almost as much as I hit the bottle. This is a fun game that recalls a distinct nostalgic memory of older shooters.  There are a lot of nods and nudges towards the classic Wolfenstein 3D in this game, and a lot of older shooter mechanics to take you back to a simpler time.  You are B.J. They feel good and enemies are responsive to their effects, it's satisfying to blow a Nazi's head off, or blow them to chunks and red mist.  The enemies can be challenging, especially in larger numbers, and the Nazi robots, Uber soldiers and dog-creatures all pose unique threats, there's even a classic boss-battle here and there.  Don't expect realism, gritty war simulation or technical feats.  The game looks well enough, the story is fun anything but Shakespear. and the shooting action is as ridiculous and gory as you could ask for with an id property FPS.  I highly recommend it if you're a fan of the older games or like shooting up Nazis in general.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a mixed bag. Is it worth the price? I'll break down what I feel are the strong and weak points.
Pros:
- Definitely worthy as a successor/reboot of the series. Gunplay is solid and the action is responsive.
- No major bugs and zero crashes in my playthrough of the whole campaign.
- Ran very well on my 4+ year old setup (GTX 570 and an older i7, 8 GB of RAM) on a mix of High and Medium settings.
- Not afraid to display the swastika and Iron Cross absolutely everywhere. The cityscapes of a post-German WWII victory look fantastic and memorable. Badass and brutal environment for a FPS.
- Optional newspaper clippings and other documents expose the player to how this alternate history scenario happened.
- Looks very nice and has a surprisingly high standard of voice acting and cinematography.
- The German dialogue is very well done and you'll be hearing a lot of it throughout the game.
Cons:
- Takes an extremely interesting alternate history scenario and doesn't take itself seriously enough to really flesh it out. This is more of a personal opinion and can be seen as a neutral point given the fact that the Wolfenstein series has always been about mowing down Nazis, not elaborating on them. The alternate history is very sci-fi, which is fun stylistic choice and serves the game itself well.
- The newspaper clippings and other lore are nice tidbits, but they feel like they're just teasing the player when you realize that there is never any major exposition. What IS revealed though, is very interesting (Manhattan hit with an atom bomb to force the USA's surrender, the Nazis build a bridge across the Strait of Gibraltar, etc.)
- Oddly disjointed storyline that doesn't feel rewarding to the player due to its sporadic focus and odd jumps in continuity (Minor spoiler: deciding to be purposely captured to be placed into a forced-labor camp with NO decision or setup from the player whatsoever - what?!).
- Little variety in enemy types and overly high margin of difficulty between them (light enemies are trivially easy, heavy enemies can be a slog).
- The unlock system only enables alternate gameplay modes, which doesn't contribute greatly to replayability. Definitely a one-and-done game.
Overall, this is a solid pickup if you are looking for an enjoyable single-player FPS experience, but you may be lefting wanting more in the narrative. Very solid FPS gameplay and OK on the narrative/storyline. This game is worth picking up for at least one playthrough.

To put this game into perspective, it is like a super-sized Battlefield 2142 with a three-way conflict and a seemingly limitless supply of respawn tickets.  Customizable weapons, vehicles, and loadouts allow for players to adjust their gear to suit their needs, whether it would be to quickly repair and deal massive amounts of human tissue damage, or to have the long reach of a good sniper rifle to precisely remove HVTs (High-Value Targets), or to fly high and drop slowly down over a wall, where the enemy least expects opposition, or hook their team up with plenty of ammuntion to keep them in the fight.  There are many other varieties of loadout that I could not hope to cover here.
This game is not infantry-centric, either.  Players have their choice to drive their land vehicles or fly high in various VTOL aircraft, all of which with varying sizes and forms of firepower.  An offensive push with a mix of LAV (Light Armored Vehicle) and MBT (Main Battle Tank) could force an enemy frontline to back off and retreat.  Air strikes and air support would give a team a high angle of attack to rain death on the enemy forces.
A player can be dangerous, when fighting solo and trying to be a one-person-army.  Fighting with a team, however, is deadly.  This game can appeal to the officers and leaders of the real world, as well.  Coordinating a team and leading them to victory, crushing the less-coordinated enemy force in the process, is a rewarding experience, too.
If you happen to be reading this, and Battlefield was a game you enjoyed playing (like me), you should definitely try Planetside 2.  It may surprise you.

Wolfenstein: The New Order  -  A Gamer's Review
This one lives up to genre of "run and gun" FPS games but, for those wondering if it has the feel of Return To Castle Wolfenstein, I'm sorry to say, no.  As I blasted my way through the game, it often felt more like DOOM III than RTCW.  The similarities to RTCW are in name only.  This is quite a departure from the occult-based missions of war torn Germany.  But, some will say, that's as it should be.  "Otherwise, it would just be the same game, only with better graphics."  Although, I'm not sure there's anything wrong with that idea.  I put a couple hundred hours into RTCW and enjoyed every minute of it.  New maps and improved graphics would make the same game replayable for many more hours.  Personally, that's kinda what I was hoping for with this release.  If you are too, try Wolfenstein (PC, 2009) instead.
Initially, after sitting through the makers' logo screens and long drawn out intro scenes, the player is immediately placed into a "panic" situation.  Getting through it is simply a trial and error process.  It would have been nice to have a training mission or at least an easy begining to get used to your movement and action controls but, there's no slow start in this game.  As we progress through the first few chapters, we see more surprises and ambushes by enemies who seem to possess almost psychic abilities to know exactly when you're gonna round a corner or come out from cover and begin walking down a hallway.  Fortunately, there's abundant Health and Armor throughout.
We also are subjected to excruciatingly lengthy cutscenes that often made me feel like I was watching a full length movie, with occassional opportunities to interact with characters and shoot the enemy.
I was surprised to find out that there is no "Quick-save" and "Quick-load" keys!!!  I can't believe they produced this game without them.  We are relegated to the game's Checkpoint Autosave function.  They are fairly frequent but, totally out of the player's control.  If you didn't like how you handled an area or, realized you missed something earlier, your only options are to RESTART LATEST CHECKPOINT, which doesn't take you back very far at all, or RESTART LEVEL, starting the chapter over from the very beginning (including those long cutscenes).
Weapons are mostly geared more for the all out, head on firefight.  Especially when you double them up.  You can dual wield knives, pistols, assault rifles and shotguns to effect more damage in CQB's.  Stealth weapons are limited to the knife and silenced pistol.  Later on in the game, you do get a scoped rifle but there are few opportunities to take your time and use it as a true sniper rifle.  I miss the Snooper Rifle of RTCW.
I've read some reviews that praise the stealth mechanics of the game but, I didn't see anything to applaud.  The few times the player can employ stealth tactics seem like token opportunities that the game sometimes allows. Those who you can sneak up on are dumkoffs who have no situational awareness.  And those watchdogs that just lay there waiting for you to slit their throats...what a joke.  Yet, when you're creeping from cover to cover in the dark, those telepathic soldiers hundreds of yards away zero in on you with amazing acuity.
Then, there are occassional "problem solving" tasks.  For example, a seemingly inaccessable room is right next to a room with three handles.  The idea is to pull the handles in the right sequence, in order to open the secret door to get into the other room.  Not terribly challenging but, a nice change of pace from the hectic  furball usually encountered.  Mostly, the problems I found challenging were progressing from one area to another.  The map you're able to access is not the most helpful aid you have available.  It shows your destination and where you've been but, often, doesn't show the path between the two, until you find it.
The story line is deeper in this release.  Blazkowicz shows more emotion and compassion and, there's more personal bonding, too.  However, some of the the Nazi humanitarian atrocities depicted in several cutscenes really disgusted me.  I understand that the writers really want us to hate the Nazis but, I feel they've gone too far, here, with the choice that  Blazkowicz has to make after being captured by Deathshead or, the carnage at the asylum where Anya works.  And, worst of all, the scene where the Nazi woman is holding a screaming baby up in the air by the leg while beating forced laborers with her whip.  (That's where I quit the game and uninstalled it.)  I think most of us already have enough of a distain for WWII Nazis, that we don't need such disturbing portrayals to motivate us.  Personally, I wonder about the mental wellness of the writers of this game, that they felt it necessary to include scenes like those.  Don't get me wrong here.  I'm not talking about the gore factor.  In many games, graphical depictions of gibs being splattered all over the place is no big deal.  In fact, it's even amusing, sometimes.  I'm talking about the revolting assaults on our moral sensitivities that, for me, ruined what would otherwise be a decent story.
Overall, I'm disappointed and repulsed.  I think it's sad to say that, for me, the highlight of this game was the "Easter Egg" opportunity to play a level resembling the original 1992 release of Wolfenstein 3D.
