I enjoyed the game. Still need to replay once for the second timeline. Started on "Death incarnate" first playthrough. Played a stealth game the first way through and noticed a few things.
- headshots / weakpoints are on every bad guy, and even on the hardest difficulty I only had three spots, all near the end, where I died more than once (37 total deaths in first playthrough, there are stats in the game btw). As far as I can tell, difficulty only increases the punishment they dish out (ill get to this in a second), and how much damage they soak to non-critical areas.
- Cover is over powered in this game. Playing on DI, using cover isn't absolutely necessary, but it completely negates any threat from the enemy as they are unable to hit a melon sized target that isn't moving.
- Never had issues with ammo because they decided to go with a "acquire all your weapons on each level" instead of letting you hold what you have through the end of the last mission.
- Liked the destructible cover (too bad it almost never applied to me), the blind firing of the enemy (even though it was just for show), and the enemy variation.
- Story was good, I felt more interested in the people than anything.
Overall, I'd recommend a buy, maybe wait for the first sale, but definitely worth playing.

First, I want to outline the 3 main reasons I would not recommed this game: The economy, The balance, and the direction which this game has been going. This game had much hope, and was actually my favorite game for a time. However, whe the new changes came around, they ruined what was already a good game.
First of all, The economy is broken. The Devs have made it so that high lvl players have to grind for hours to earn equipment which can compete with other high lvl players on an even lvl. All players get loot caches based upon their performance in a battle providing different Items based upon your performance. However, no matter what your lvl is, the maximum loot cache rewards is the same for all CPu cost units (CPU how many blocks you can place and also how they now determine score.) It take approximately 15 minutes to complete an average game of Battle Arena, earning you 4 random items, their rarity based uponhow well you did. On average, gold and silver crates are the most common, and after testing, I earned about 1000 Robits each match if I sold the Items. Since Epics and Rare Items are about The average Rare Item is about 3000-5000 Robits. and the average Epic item is about 7000-10000. If we do a little bit of math, it would take about and hour or two to get the robits for a single rare Item.  and 3-5 hours to get a singl epic item. However, for epic and rare items to function efficiently, they require multiple items. For example, A plasma decimator (rare) needs 5 for nominal or max dmg. this would compute to about 13000 Robits or about 13 hours of consistent playing. And this is only the weapon! Adding in movement, electroplates or special functions would increase the costs to about 24000 Robits or about a day of consistant work; not even epic lvl items! Also, the newer items such as ion cannons, chainguns, airflak, protoseeker, and other exotic weapons cost a fortune between 75000-150000 alone! about 35.5 hours just for a single legendary. I would agree that a little grinding is necessary for the game to run. (Ppl need to make money). But making certain really expensive items unbalanced just ruins the game.
The next thing that I have a problem with is the balance issues. Legendary Items have lots of HP, Deal high DMG, and are very easy to use. For example, The missile launcher, a legendary, has about 107552 HP alone, costs 275 CPU and deals about 100000 DMG per second for a 1000 Power per second. The average armor block has 2100 HP, so about 53 armor blocks is equal to this one weapon in terms of health. The average electroplate only has about 70000 shields and 2000 armor. however, this items' function is not to protect, but to deal lots of DMG that has a very high chance of hitting, with no effective defense.  Also, most weapons have a CPU ratio of HP to CPU. the most are about 4000 to 3 where the Armor blocks which are DESIGNED to defend, have only 2000 to 1 effectively being only slightly more efficient than regular weapons without the ability for it to do something.
The main problem I have with this game is the fact that the amount of customization is being limited more and more. After removing different lvls of armor cubes, players could no longer change where has the most armor. Also, the ratio of armor to dmg  and the slight Difference in the HP to CPU ratio between 'structure' and armor makes armor only really useful for connecting objects and not for protection. Also, some of the new weapons made it so that certain builds (such as floating snipers) are no longer practical.
I know that the Devs also create polls for people to vote on. My question though is WHERE IS THE OTHER BUTTON! (just wanted to put emphasis on that).  If your poll is something like:
Pls rate each poll on a scale from 1 to 10, using each number once. 1 is for I kind of don't like it and 10 is for I absolutely Hate this.
It doesn't get you anywhere, because its trying to choose which is worse. You can actually see that robocraft has lost players several thousand players ever since it started its updates after the mid 2015s.
The Devs need to learn the important lesson that making ppl play while running under the pretense of 'Free-to-play' does not actually help itself in the long run.

This is an amazing game. I have made a list of pros and cons:
pros:
-massive warfare
-time to kill is less then other shooters, but still fast enough to feel realistic
-class systems fits all playstyles
-graphics are quite nice imo
-vehicles such as tanks and fighters fight alongside infantry
-each faction has its ups and downs both in play and in lore
-open world with no instanced single fight "maps"
-plenty of cosmetics to buy with money to make your character unique
-solo play can be just as good and just as impactful as playing in a group
-active community with competitive events
-4 continents with various terrains forcing changes in tactics
cons:
-steep learning curve (its getting better with more rewards for new players and the new tutorials, along with the upcoming continent Koltyr for new players)
-requires a solid computer (i5 with at least a Nvidia X60 gfx card (or amd equivalents) is pretty much required for decent frames at decent settings)
-lacks the grander strategy it needs, zergs rule the game, and numbers>skill in many cases
-servers can, at times, be bad and give higher pings, but I haven't seen this in a while
-some weapons and abilities are duds, such as the TR striker or the VS Zealot overdrive engine.
-vehicles often farm less experienced players due to skill gaps
-implant system is bland and not very useful (I hardly ever use them)
Overall, most of the cons are fairly minor and are being improved over time. The most recent patch greatly improved multithreading, improving the amount of frames many are getting. I highly recommend this game to all.

I had a lot of fun with this game. I had pretty high expectations going in and they were met in what was a well rounded mix of a modern and classic shooter. Mechanics wise, its mostly old school, mowing down enemies with an impressive arsenal of guns that you can carry all at once (none of that two-weapon swap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t). You can also dual wield most of the weapons in the game, which is great. The health system is mixed as there is partial regeneration. For example, if you fall below 20 health it regenerates up to 20, going below 40 regenerates up to 40, ect. However, you need medpacks to recover completely, which works well. The only downside gameplay wise is the forced stealth sections, which aren't terrible but they do slow down the pace. Most of the game you do get to choose if you want to be stealthy or go guns blazing though.
The story is interesting, set in an alternate 1960's timeline where the Nazi's won WWII and have some crazy future-tech weapons and gadgets. You meet some pretty interesting characters along the way, with some familiar faces returning from previous Wolfenstein games. The story can be a little heavy handed in some instances, but overall provides a compelling narrative. It's also nice to see Blazkowicz get some humanization this time around.
Great game overall, highly recommended. Wolfenstein is back.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is the latest installment in one of the franchises that gave birth to the shooter genre. There's plenty of nostalgia with that, but frankly, there's not much else. The premise of the game is compelling, but the plot is not. Instead of the story playing out naturally, the events that occur seem artificial and too convenient. At times, it's downright hard to believe. It's obvious to me that they decided to focus on action/gunplay over story with TWO, which is fine, but that's the kind of thing I'd expect from games like Call of Duty or Battlefield -- which are not standalone single player games. As for the gameplay, the gunplay is your standard fare; tight and responsive, but also not offering anything particuarly memorable. There are unlockable perks to fit your preferred playstyle; some of them were better than others. The Assault line (dual-wield/heavy weaponry) ended up being my preferred line once I realized how limited and counterintuitive the stealth mechanic was (despite this, my knives still thirst for blood). I won't comment on the graphics because my rig just barely meets the minimum reqs, but even mind-bending graphics would only give the game an extra point or two on its final grade. I do recommend the game, but unless you're playing it for the nostalgia of an old-school shooter, you may want to wait for it go on sale. 6.5 out of 10.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a blast. It really is, it has enough fun, wacky, and bloody moments to make it worth your while. Don't be deceived, this is not an old school game, it is very much modern, with lots of cut-scenes, iron sights, and linear level design to make Call of Duty eat its heart out. Does that make it bad? Not at all, in fact, it is a well done modern FPS well worth your time.
For your first playthrough.
After that, trying to play it again, you realize how much fluff the game has, the amount of cutscenes and gameplay moments where you're not blasting through Nazi scum is astounding. There are intense moments of gameplay that will last from 5-15 minutes, with a level or two dedicated to full blown action or stealth just as you prefer it. In between all that is 30-minutes to an hour of doing a whole lot of nothing. Do you enjoy exploring sewer levels, finding lost toys for a character, or getting a sample of moldy concrete for research? It's all here.
Another big issue is the illusion of stealth vs. action gameplay, this was prominently advertised before the game's release. It implied that you would be able to go as stealth or Rambo First Blood as you wanted. For some levels, yeah, you can do that, but for most, not really. Sometimes your cover is blown right out of the gate, forcing you to go akimbo AR's and mow through lines of baddies. Other times you're so ill equipped to fight you really can't, and you have to go sneaky or face getting your arm ripped off by a genetically mutated robot German shepherd.
Finally, lets talk about the Nazis, there's no Hitler to kill, lets get that out of the gate, and it sucks. The Nazis feel overly evil, and it doesn't give you the proper motivation to kill them. They feel like generic evil-doers that you have to kill in order to progress the story. Instead of an attitude of "business as usual" while committing heinous crimes, it's laughing maniacally as they hold you at gunpoint interrogating you, or flipping tables out of enjoyment as they purge a mental hospital. Don't get me wrong here, they do very much try to give you that feeling of genuine evil, but personally it comes off as a joke.
All in all, I like the game, I think it's fun for that first playthough, but once you see the horrible ending it gives you, and trying to play it again realizing how much fluff you sat through, it just isn't worth owning it. It feels like an awesome weekend rental, with lots of bloody action in between the cutscenes and quiet moments. I cannot recommend buying it for $60 unless you're the kind of person that enjoys watching a movie 4 times in a row.
-Wrap Up-
+Awesome fun at times
+Satisfying and punchy weapons with great gore
+Lots of near death experiences that make you grip your chair
+For a modern FPS, it's a pretty good one
+Moon Nazis
-Lack of weapon variety
-Horrible amount of fluff in cutscenes and quiet moments
-Lots of performance issues and not a single patch as of yet
-Cliche Nazis, with no Hitlers to kill
-Not an old school rebirth of Wolfenstein
-Final Opinion-
Get it at a Redbox or Blockbuster and invite some friends. Treat it like a movie and you'll get the most fun out of it.

Honestly I'm still baffled and I'm clueless how to start this review. I'm still clueless how they set the bar for their prequel this high and even provided with a better sequel. I can't wait to jump into the co-op function honestly since the singleplayer was this good.
Valve literally took a look at Portal and said what could we improve towards the sequel. They added new general features like a loading screen, which I didn't find mandatory, and you can see where your portals are placed through walls. They stuck with similar ideas to complete their puzzles and added loads of new ways to solve puzzles and move along the map. Speaking of puzzles, they added so many, that it seems that the game is twice as long as the prequel. They added lasers and with them you have cubes which you can use to direct the lasers in any way you want.  You have bouncing pads and on walls you see indicators which show where you land. You have bridges to guide you around the map. You also have floating pads which can work in two directions but only when triggered by a button. Finally you have three kinds of gel red blue and white. Red gel gives you a speed boost. Blue gel gives you a jumping boost and white gel allows you to portal on it, mainly for places that you couldn't portal on before.
Obviously the things previously said aren't the ones that baffled me but it is mainly the environment. The story is amazingly well built and it teaches us more about apeture sciences. It also contains a few plot twists here and there. The places you visit are fairly new but you'll visit some well remembered places from portal. Something they also introduced is companions, the most part of the game you'll have a object travelling with you. One of them is a funny little core with a british accent. Aside from entertaining you the bots can help you sometimes to get to certain paths. The jokes are as good as last game so expect a good laugh.
I highly recommend  that you buy this game, and play it for the rest of the day or week. Turn off your notification, because the game doesn't support tabbing, and enjoy this gem for many and many times you want and are supposed to complete the story. (Edit:) You also can choose from many maps from the community to test out so you won't get tired of the story and you can still play.

I had a lot of fun with this game. I had pretty high expectations going in and they were met in what was a well rounded mix of a modern and classic shooter. Mechanics wise, its mostly old school, mowing down enemies with an impressive arsenal of guns that you can carry all at once (none of that two-weapon swap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t). You can also dual wield most of the weapons in the game, which is great. The health system is mixed as there is partial regeneration. For example, if you fall below 20 health it regenerates up to 20, going below 40 regenerates up to 40, ect. However, you need medpacks to recover completely, which works well. The only downside gameplay wise is the forced stealth sections, which aren't terrible but they do slow down the pace. Most of the game you do get to choose if you want to be stealthy or go guns blazing though.
The story is interesting, set in an alternate 1960's timeline where the Nazi's won WWII and have some crazy future-tech weapons and gadgets. You meet some pretty interesting characters along the way, with some familiar faces returning from previous Wolfenstein games. The story can be a little heavy handed in some instances, but overall provides a compelling narrative. It's also nice to see Blazkowicz get some humanization this time around.
Great game overall, highly recommended. Wolfenstein is back.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is the latest installment in one of the franchises that gave birth to the shooter genre. There's plenty of nostalgia with that, but frankly, there's not much else. The premise of the game is compelling, but the plot is not. Instead of the story playing out naturally, the events that occur seem artificial and too convenient. At times, it's downright hard to believe. It's obvious to me that they decided to focus on action/gunplay over story with TWO, which is fine, but that's the kind of thing I'd expect from games like Call of Duty or Battlefield -- which are not standalone single player games. As for the gameplay, the gunplay is your standard fare; tight and responsive, but also not offering anything particuarly memorable. There are unlockable perks to fit your preferred playstyle; some of them were better than others. The Assault line (dual-wield/heavy weaponry) ended up being my preferred line once I realized how limited and counterintuitive the stealth mechanic was (despite this, my knives still thirst for blood). I won't comment on the graphics because my rig just barely meets the minimum reqs, but even mind-bending graphics would only give the game an extra point or two on its final grade. I do recommend the game, but unless you're playing it for the nostalgia of an old-school shooter, you may want to wait for it go on sale. 6.5 out of 10.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a blast. It really is, it has enough fun, wacky, and bloody moments to make it worth your while. Don't be deceived, this is not an old school game, it is very much modern, with lots of cut-scenes, iron sights, and linear level design to make Call of Duty eat its heart out. Does that make it bad? Not at all, in fact, it is a well done modern FPS well worth your time.
For your first playthrough.
After that, trying to play it again, you realize how much fluff the game has, the amount of cutscenes and gameplay moments where you're not blasting through Nazi scum is astounding. There are intense moments of gameplay that will last from 5-15 minutes, with a level or two dedicated to full blown action or stealth just as you prefer it. In between all that is 30-minutes to an hour of doing a whole lot of nothing. Do you enjoy exploring sewer levels, finding lost toys for a character, or getting a sample of moldy concrete for research? It's all here.
Another big issue is the illusion of stealth vs. action gameplay, this was prominently advertised before the game's release. It implied that you would be able to go as stealth or Rambo First Blood as you wanted. For some levels, yeah, you can do that, but for most, not really. Sometimes your cover is blown right out of the gate, forcing you to go akimbo AR's and mow through lines of baddies. Other times you're so ill equipped to fight you really can't, and you have to go sneaky or face getting your arm ripped off by a genetically mutated robot German shepherd.
Finally, lets talk about the Nazis, there's no Hitler to kill, lets get that out of the gate, and it sucks. The Nazis feel overly evil, and it doesn't give you the proper motivation to kill them. They feel like generic evil-doers that you have to kill in order to progress the story. Instead of an attitude of "business as usual" while committing heinous crimes, it's laughing maniacally as they hold you at gunpoint interrogating you, or flipping tables out of enjoyment as they purge a mental hospital. Don't get me wrong here, they do very much try to give you that feeling of genuine evil, but personally it comes off as a joke.
All in all, I like the game, I think it's fun for that first playthough, but once you see the horrible ending it gives you, and trying to play it again realizing how much fluff you sat through, it just isn't worth owning it. It feels like an awesome weekend rental, with lots of bloody action in between the cutscenes and quiet moments. I cannot recommend buying it for $60 unless you're the kind of person that enjoys watching a movie 4 times in a row.
-Wrap Up-
+Awesome fun at times
+Satisfying and punchy weapons with great gore
+Lots of near death experiences that make you grip your chair
+For a modern FPS, it's a pretty good one
+Moon Nazis
-Lack of weapon variety
-Horrible amount of fluff in cutscenes and quiet moments
-Lots of performance issues and not a single patch as of yet
-Cliche Nazis, with no Hitlers to kill
-Not an old school rebirth of Wolfenstein
-Final Opinion-
Get it at a Redbox or Blockbuster and invite some friends. Treat it like a movie and you'll get the most fun out of it.

This used to be one of my favorite F2P games but its fallen into the same trap as World of Warcraft and is bleeding players just like it as well.
They turned a formerly skill based game into a glorified game of rock paper scissors so that even the most casual of players can still do well, and in doing that completely alienated their existing fanbase.
The final nail in the coffin was implementing the "loot crate" system which completely destroyed the games economy.
What used to take a few days of grinding to get now takes weeks and on top of that having to tediously dismantle every piece of crap you get from the crates to get meager amounts of currency instead of just getting the currency to begin with.
Where before you'd be rewarded more currency for being more skilled now its largely a crapshoot where the worst player can get a crate with better stuff than the best player purely based on luck.
The game gets frequent content updates but they're so expensive and currency is so hard to get in the game that the only way to have any hope of getting them is to pay their monthly subscription to get twice as many items in each crate or buy crates outright to gamble in hopes of winning the lottery and getting the new item in one of them.
They used to have a pay for currency called "GC" which you could use to buy these new weapons and skip the grind, but they did away with that all together forcing you to gamble with crates instead.
Where premium used to double the amount of currency you'd get, now it just doubles the amount of items you get from each crate which all too often end up being trash that converts to so little currency that it isn't even worth the effort.
And don't even get me started with the countless balance issues that they refuse to address.
Instead of focusing on balancing whats already in the game they instead focus on adding more and more new stuff to incentivise players spending real money since they have no hope of getting them without it.
"New stuff" sounds good on paper but all it does is make the balance problems even worse, its like trying to put out a house fire by throwing buckets of gasoline at it.
In the end this game is just a reminder that quality is better than quantity and that making gambling the centerpiece of your games economy is an awful idea.

Honestly I'm still baffled and I'm clueless how to start this review. I'm still clueless how they set the bar for their prequel this high and even provided with a better sequel. I can't wait to jump into the co-op function honestly since the singleplayer was this good.
Valve literally took a look at Portal and said what could we improve towards the sequel. They added new general features like a loading screen, which I didn't find mandatory, and you can see where your portals are placed through walls. They stuck with similar ideas to complete their puzzles and added loads of new ways to solve puzzles and move along the map. Speaking of puzzles, they added so many, that it seems that the game is twice as long as the prequel. They added lasers and with them you have cubes which you can use to direct the lasers in any way you want.  You have bouncing pads and on walls you see indicators which show where you land. You have bridges to guide you around the map. You also have floating pads which can work in two directions but only when triggered by a button. Finally you have three kinds of gel red blue and white. Red gel gives you a speed boost. Blue gel gives you a jumping boost and white gel allows you to portal on it, mainly for places that you couldn't portal on before.
Obviously the things previously said aren't the ones that baffled me but it is mainly the environment. The story is amazingly well built and it teaches us more about apeture sciences. It also contains a few plot twists here and there. The places you visit are fairly new but you'll visit some well remembered places from portal. Something they also introduced is companions, the most part of the game you'll have a object travelling with you. One of them is a funny little core with a british accent. Aside from entertaining you the bots can help you sometimes to get to certain paths. The jokes are as good as last game so expect a good laugh.
I highly recommend  that you buy this game, and play it for the rest of the day or week. Turn off your notification, because the game doesn't support tabbing, and enjoy this gem for many and many times you want and are supposed to complete the story. (Edit:) You also can choose from many maps from the community to test out so you won't get tired of the story and you can still play.

This used to be one of my favorite F2P games but its fallen into the same trap as World of Warcraft and is bleeding players just like it as well.
They turned a formerly skill based game into a glorified game of rock paper scissors so that even the most casual of players can still do well, and in doing that completely alienated their existing fanbase.
The final nail in the coffin was implementing the "loot crate" system which completely destroyed the games economy.
What used to take a few days of grinding to get now takes weeks and on top of that having to tediously dismantle every piece of crap you get from the crates to get meager amounts of currency instead of just getting the currency to begin with.
Where before you'd be rewarded more currency for being more skilled now its largely a crapshoot where the worst player can get a crate with better stuff than the best player purely based on luck.
The game gets frequent content updates but they're so expensive and currency is so hard to get in the game that the only way to have any hope of getting them is to pay their monthly subscription to get twice as many items in each crate or buy crates outright to gamble in hopes of winning the lottery and getting the new item in one of them.
They used to have a pay for currency called "GC" which you could use to buy these new weapons and skip the grind, but they did away with that all together forcing you to gamble with crates instead.
Where premium used to double the amount of currency you'd get, now it just doubles the amount of items you get from each crate which all too often end up being trash that converts to so little currency that it isn't even worth the effort.
And don't even get me started with the countless balance issues that they refuse to address.
Instead of focusing on balancing whats already in the game they instead focus on adding more and more new stuff to incentivise players spending real money since they have no hope of getting them without it.
"New stuff" sounds good on paper but all it does is make the balance problems even worse, its like trying to put out a house fire by throwing buckets of gasoline at it.
In the end this game is just a reminder that quality is better than quantity and that making gambling the centerpiece of your games economy is an awful idea.

Played this to death as a kid and it is exactly how I remember it.
AoE2 is the quintessential medieval base builder that has you conquering your opponents through four "Ages", with progressively stronger and better units. Best part was they released an expansion after more than a decade because this game has such a cult following.
The game has you gather resources, build structures, amass units and go trapsing over maps of all kinds. These range from tiny islands to pretty decent sized representations of European climates that have you seek out and destroy your enemies or win by several other not-so-total conquest game types. The new expansion allows those maps to be massive and adds even more civilizations to play with, making the total 23. These civilizations span from all corners of Europe, Asia and the Middle East. All units have voice clips in their native languages to help with the feel of every faction being truly different in addition to visually unique buildings and units depending on the cultural locale of your civilization.
With its migration to Steam AoE now has great multiplayer support, achievements, and Steam Workshop capabilities that will allow the sharing of user-created content to be spread much easier than having to download things like scenario  maps from a third-party webpage over dial-up as I did back in the day.
If you played this game in the past, it is well worth picking up again if nothing more than for nostalgia goggle syndrome because you know just how fun this was. If you somehow missed the boat in the past and are a fan of games like this there is literally no reason you should not own this game. It has been improved and will more than likely be considered one of the fine wines of gaming; Better with age and enjoyed even more with friends.

INGREDIENTS
•  2 pounds mahi mahi (skinned, boned and cleaned) cut into 1-ounce strips
•  2 cups all-purpose flour
•  3 eggs, lightly beaten
•  4 tablespoons water
•  2 cups panko bread crumbs
•  Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
•  Vegetable oil, for frying
•  1/2 head savoy cabbage, finely shredded
•  1 bunch cilantro, leaves picked
•  1 bunch chives, chopped
•  3 limes, cut into wedges for garnish
PINK CHILE MAYONNAISE:
•	1 cup sour cream
•	1 cup mayonnaise
•	3 chipotles in adobo, plus 2 tablespoons of adobo sauce
•	1/2 lemon, juiced
•	Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
MANGO-RADISH SALSA:
•	2 limes
•	2 mangoes, diced
•	4 to 5 red radishes, diced
•	1 red onion, diced
•	1 tablespoon chili powder
•	1/2 bunch fresh cilantro, leaves chopped
•	1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
•	Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
DIRECTIONS
Prepare the fish. Cut the pieces of fish into 1-ounce strips. Set up abreading station of flour, lightly beaten eggs with water, and seasoned panko bread crumbs. Season all with salt and pepper.Dredge the pieces of fish in flour, egg then bread crumbs. Once all the fish is breaded deep-fry in small batches in (375 degrees F) oil.Drain on paper towels and season with salt. Keep warm until ready to serve.
Prepare the pink chile mayonnaise. Put the chipotles in a blenderand puree until smooth. Add the sour cream, mayonnaise, adobo sauce and lemon juice and continue to process until the mixture is consistent and creamy. Season with salt and pepper and refrigerate until ready to use.
Prepare the mango-radish salsa. Remove the peel and pith from the limes and cut between the membranes to remove the segments. Put these "supremes" into a bowl and squeeze over the juice from the membranes. Add the remaining ingredients and mix. Season and refrigerate until ready to use. You can also place all of the ingredients into a food processor and puree for a smoother salsa.
To serve, set up the tacos "family-style". Assemble the fish in a pile on a plate; the pink chile mayonnaise in a bowl; and mango-radish salsa in another. Set a pile of shredded savoy cabbage, cilantro leaves, chopped chives and lime wedges next to the fish. Toast the corn tortillas lightly over an open flame (on your stove top) and serve.

Playing this game has been the most fun and entertaining experience I've had with the FPS genre in a long while.
Sure, at first and deep down this game is a linear, run-and-gun game, same as most FPS. However, the way it's been setup for it completely changes the feel of the whole thing. Quite literally, after some thought, it's a literall run-and-gun game. But not quite simply running and gunning as in most FPS; this game is stupidly immersive, combat is fluent, non-repetitive and incredibly dynamic. Combat AI is incredibly well developed in NPCs; on the harder difficulties this game more than presents a challenge. Common enemy soldiers will try to flank you whenever you find a good vantage point, they'll lob grenades at you if you try to take too much advantage of good cover, they'll corner and keep you pinned down while a heavy soldier with an auto shotgun rushes at you if you try to don't change positions. Not only that but it's stupidly easy to run out of ammo and get yourself in a tight situation.
This game does not spoon feeds you anything. It's not for those who are accustomed to the usual FPS style single-player campaign. There are no pauses to gather medkits and ammo, there's no health stations or power-ups, nor OP friendly NPCs that will bail you out of tight spots or perfectly timed cutscenes or events that will eliminate the difficulty of a firefight or cut a level in half.
Combat is constant, if you want ammo, you'll need to run your♥♥♥♥♥out into the line of fire and get it where it was dropped, all the while the enemies open fire on you. Forget about NPCs dropping medkits, or fully loaded weapons, you are lucky if you get half a clip because they deplete their ammo same as you, and whatever armor piece they might drop is minimal. Scavenging is essential. Overcharging health items is a must for prolongued firefights (these are located around the map and it's up to you to find them; only some times will the enemy drop a small medkit.)
This game brings back the feel of FPS games of old. The feel one gets out of this game is stupidly reminiscent of that one would get out of the old Wolfenstein 3D and the old Doom games, yet incredibly innovative in it's own way.
Levels were designed in a fashion that, while linear, allows for a certain degree of exploration. You are not always forced to approach every level or enemy in the same way either. It's up to you to decide if you want to go in guns-blazing, being a murder machine and death incarnate, or instead, be a sneaky infiltrator quietly elliminating all that stands in your way. Or both.
The storyline is amazing and well developed, characters have depth and dialogue is pretty good. The main character himself breaks away from the trend of the silent protagonist, often dropping his own thoughts in the middle of a mission or firefight and allowing the player a peek into his mind. Other characters display their own internal conflicts, or share unique dialogue, making it pretty easy to immerse yourself in the story.
Overall, this is a great game. I highly recommend it and advise everyone to play in the two highest difficulty levels for a better experience. There are minor glitches of course, but nothing as overly exagerated as some reviews make it out to be. The only things I experienced were a minor sound delay glicth during the short train mission where B.J meets Frau Whatshername for the first time, and another glitch where the ambiance suddently stopped out of the blue during a cutscene.
My PC setup isn't the greatest,  yet ran this game smoothly on the "High" setting with decent FPS rate.
The lack of multiplayer is no excuse to give this game a low-rating, as there is more to gaming than killing 12 year olds  and♥♥♥♥♥♥talking on team chat. Those looking exclusively for multiplayer would do well to stay away from this game. Even if the multiplayer mode was featured in this game, those who played it exclusively would miss out the great experience provided by the single-player campaign.
Apologies for any grammar or sintax error. Typed this review rather quickly.

This is a bad game. Even after coming back to this game that fact still stands and it stands tall. Here are just few reasons why.
1. The games fps is normally quite low even if you have a decent pc and that fact rings true with a lot of players and in a fast paced fps you can't have that but the developers have not yet seemed to address this.
2. Obviously players who have played a game for longer will have an advantage over newer players, this is how to should be, but the difference should be skill based and not perk based like it is in dirty bomb. If you dont know how the gae play works then basically you can unlock cards which give a certain class different weapons, skins and perks. New players don't get these perks and and whilst you wouldn't think that a extra clip of ammo or a medic pack health boost would help you that much then you need to think again.
3. Like I said before the cards change a merks weapons and some of these cards are alot better than others. For example one merc called Aura is a medic who uses a shotgun. Having her use a shotgun makes her balanced because it means that she has to get close to an enemy before she can kill them, so people can shot her from far away without much difficulty, killing the teams medic. Now lets say that she has a card which gives her a sub machine gun extra healing power and a couple of extra clips for good measure, congrats you just made a tank who can revive team-mates and kill from all ranges.

Dirty Bomb uses a merc rotation system which allows players to use mercs that they don't own, whilst at first this make the games seem varied, it just makes all the matches the same for a week and sometimes everyone having the same merc is a bad thing. For example one week the merc Kira was on rotation and her ability is to summon a lazer from the sky to kill the enemys and also damage objectives. In modes where you have to push an objective she is hard to beat as she can destroy the objective meaning you have to repair it, normally this would be fine but when everyone can be kira,♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down. This has to be my favorite shooter of 2014 so far. It's a blast!
This is a run and gun (or a paced stealth hunt) game where you play the now 54 year old B. J. Blazkowicz. The story is very strong (which is rare for a Wolfenstein game) and the way they tell the story is good. I found the sharp changes into the cut scenes to be off putting at first, but after a while I got used to it.
The shooting in this game is spot-on. Every gun in this game has a sense of power behind it and any gun can be wielded akimbo (including the knives). You lose the ability to zoom into the scope (or use iron sights) but you gain the ability to shoot twice as fast or have one gun set to primary fire mode and the second set to the alternate fire mode.
I did run into the awkward situation when trying to stab an enemy from too far away. I would throw my knife instead (because the takedown button is the same as the knife throw button). This usually would take them down anyway, but sometimes I would accidentally throw my knife and would have to go looking for it (since you can only hold 3-5 knives).
The levels are vast. There were many times when I would clear out an area only to find that there were three or four other ways to run an attack. This can cause some confusion since you'll get lost going back an alternate route, but it's not that annoying. In general I welcome this over endless corridors that only go to the primary objective.
The graphics are good. I had issues with texture popin (similar to Rage). It doesn't look bad by any stretch and it serves the purpose of telling the story.
The enemies in this game are interesting. Most of the SS that you encounter are pretty easy to kill (I played on "Normal" difficulty) but there are the panzerhounds which take a lot more firepower. Most of the time your only option is to run.
The story, as previously mentioned, is a main star in this game. It's smart and is well thought out. The voice acting is superb and by the end of the game you will be wanting more. The story, oddly, adds to the replay-ability since a choice you're forced to make early on changes how the game plays out. I've yet to completely replay the game so I don't know what all changes.
If you are sensitive to violence obviously stay away from this title. There's plenty of blood and guts and it is focused on being visually striking.
If you are sensitive to nudity, there are two sex scenes in the game which would bother you.
I still think this is a great game and will enjoy playing it again soon.

Team-based, objective-focused multiplayer with lots of different classes, weapons, abilities, etc. It's fairly balanced and has skill progression - real skill as in you get better as you play and the gameplay becomes more rewarding as you do that. Most imporantly it's a lot of fun. There's a very interesting merc customization system with loadout cards that modify the base loadout of a merc to change its playstyle in a certain way without allowing great deviations from its original idea.
On the downside, not all mercs (classes) are unlocked and you have two options to do so: pay real money, or grind in-game credits. Believe me when I say that the second option is *extremely* time-consuming. The customization loadout cards are timed/random drops cases in-game, which you can also purchase with real money. Unfortunately, you cannot chose what to customize because what you get from the cases is based on 'luck'.
Imagine a more serious version of TF2 where team play matters more than individual kills. Also with all the Overwatch overhype, this game has and delivers most of what Overwatch promises right now, not sometime in the future. And it's been around for almost two years in alpha and beta form. Of course it doesn't have the production quality of Blizzard but why should it matter? Just try it and see for yourselves - you have nothing to lose.

Playing this game has been the most fun and entertaining experience I've had with the FPS genre in a long while.
Sure, at first and deep down this game is a linear, run-and-gun game, same as most FPS. However, the way it's been setup for it completely changes the feel of the whole thing. Quite literally, after some thought, it's a literall run-and-gun game. But not quite simply running and gunning as in most FPS; this game is stupidly immersive, combat is fluent, non-repetitive and incredibly dynamic. Combat AI is incredibly well developed in NPCs; on the harder difficulties this game more than presents a challenge. Common enemy soldiers will try to flank you whenever you find a good vantage point, they'll lob grenades at you if you try to take too much advantage of good cover, they'll corner and keep you pinned down while a heavy soldier with an auto shotgun rushes at you if you try to don't change positions. Not only that but it's stupidly easy to run out of ammo and get yourself in a tight situation.
This game does not spoon feeds you anything. It's not for those who are accustomed to the usual FPS style single-player campaign. There are no pauses to gather medkits and ammo, there's no health stations or power-ups, nor OP friendly NPCs that will bail you out of tight spots or perfectly timed cutscenes or events that will eliminate the difficulty of a firefight or cut a level in half.
Combat is constant, if you want ammo, you'll need to run your♥♥♥♥♥out into the line of fire and get it where it was dropped, all the while the enemies open fire on you. Forget about NPCs dropping medkits, or fully loaded weapons, you are lucky if you get half a clip because they deplete their ammo same as you, and whatever armor piece they might drop is minimal. Scavenging is essential. Overcharging health items is a must for prolongued firefights (these are located around the map and it's up to you to find them; only some times will the enemy drop a small medkit.)
This game brings back the feel of FPS games of old. The feel one gets out of this game is stupidly reminiscent of that one would get out of the old Wolfenstein 3D and the old Doom games, yet incredibly innovative in it's own way.
Levels were designed in a fashion that, while linear, allows for a certain degree of exploration. You are not always forced to approach every level or enemy in the same way either. It's up to you to decide if you want to go in guns-blazing, being a murder machine and death incarnate, or instead, be a sneaky infiltrator quietly elliminating all that stands in your way. Or both.
The storyline is amazing and well developed, characters have depth and dialogue is pretty good. The main character himself breaks away from the trend of the silent protagonist, often dropping his own thoughts in the middle of a mission or firefight and allowing the player a peek into his mind. Other characters display their own internal conflicts, or share unique dialogue, making it pretty easy to immerse yourself in the story.
Overall, this is a great game. I highly recommend it and advise everyone to play in the two highest difficulty levels for a better experience. There are minor glitches of course, but nothing as overly exagerated as some reviews make it out to be. The only things I experienced were a minor sound delay glicth during the short train mission where B.J meets Frau Whatshername for the first time, and another glitch where the ambiance suddently stopped out of the blue during a cutscene.
My PC setup isn't the greatest,  yet ran this game smoothly on the "High" setting with decent FPS rate.
The lack of multiplayer is no excuse to give this game a low-rating, as there is more to gaming than killing 12 year olds  and♥♥♥♥♥♥talking on team chat. Those looking exclusively for multiplayer would do well to stay away from this game. Even if the multiplayer mode was featured in this game, those who played it exclusively would miss out the great experience provided by the single-player campaign.
Apologies for any grammar or sintax error. Typed this review rather quickly.

Wolfenstein: The New Order surprised me.  Not only because the game actually turned out good, but it's most redeeming factor is the story.
Who would've thought Wolfenstein would have transformed from a extremely linear 2D classic shooter to this?  The graphics look very nice, the audio is well done, the guns feel very good and the story is amazing.
The story see's the player take control of William "B.J." Blazkowicz, which anyone who has played Wolfenstein before will be familiar with. Blazkowicz suffers a critical head injury and this is where the main story point kicks in - Blazkowicz wakes up in 1960, 14 years after the start of the game, inside a insane asylum.  In this alternate universe, the Nazi's won World War II and there is not a stretch of land on the planet that is not under their control.  They have amassed a huge amount of futurisitic technology which will see the player engage with not only Nazi soldiers but armoured dogs, robots and drones.
The story of the game also tackles the grim reality of World War II and what the Nazi's in particular were trying to do.  Without going in to too much detail some of the issues that the game tackles are; Concentration camps and PoW's, experimention and the brutality of war.  Some of it is eye opening and some of it is genuinly just good story telling.
The gunplay feels great, the guns feel very meaty and as if you are firing your bullets with a lot of power behind them.  Just like you would expect from a game like Wolfenstein.
Wolfenstein: The New Order surprised me and I thuroughly enjoyed my time with the game.

AoE2 is the quintessential medieval base builder that has you conquering your opponents through four "Ages", with progressively stronger and better units. Best part was they released an expansion after more than a decade because this game has such a cult following.
The game has you gather resources, build structures, amass units and go trapsing over maps of all kinds. These range from tiny islands to pretty decent sized representations of European climates that have you seek out and destroy your enemies or win by several other not-so-total conquest game types. The new expansion allows those maps to be massive and adds even more civilizations to play with, making the total 23. These civilizations span from all corners of Europe, Asia and the Middle East. All units have voice clips in their native languages to help with the feel of every faction being truly different in addition to visually unique buildings and units depending on the cultural locale of your civilization.
With its migration to Steam AoE now has great multiplayer support, achievements, and Steam Workshop capabilities that will allow the sharing of user-created content to be spread much easier than having to download things like scenario  maps from a third-party webpage over dial-up as I did back in the day.
If you played this game in the past, it is well worth picking up again if nothing more than for nostalgia goggle syndrome because you know just how fun this was. If you somehow missed the boat in the past and are a fan of games like this there is literally no reason you should not own this game. It has been improved and will more than likely be considered one of the fine wines of gaming; Better with age and enjoyed even more with friends.

This is probably one of the most well-placed steps in the right direction for single-player FPS design I've seen since the turn of the "Seventh-Gen" Consoles and Call of Duty's arrival. There's a very cohesive mixture of the classic mechanics with a few of the newer staples added into the mix to really flesh out the shooter experience in Wolfenstein: The New Order. You can carry as many weapons as there are & dual-wield most of them, you have a classic health & armour system with an added touch of 10-20% health regeneration (Subject to upgrades, perhaps difficulty too, but I can't be certain of the latter yet), you can move & sprint very fast, you can aim-down sights while maintaining a classically accurate & reliable hipfire, and you can sprint & crouch-slide at quite some speed, whilst having a peek around cover mechanic for those occasions you choose not to perform the bulletstorm dance.
And one of the most shining traits of the gameplay is the ability to choose between complete stealth or complete carnage or even both for the majority of the game's chapters! The fantastic level design allows the player to formulate a plan or find alternate routes to silently take down the humourously, but not tension-breaking awareness-lacking Nazis, kill Communications Officers to allow you to go loud without them able to call for backup, or just plain throw brains out the window and run around guns fully blazing at whatever dares throw themselves at you.
Otherwise, the game sports:
- A very fine-controlling shooter for both mouse & keyboard and controller (especially the former) with fully rebindable keys & several controller layouts
- An FOV-Slider that goes from 80-100 (so no fear for those who suffer with low FOV).
- A fantastic aesthetic design which makes better use of the grey & brown colour palette than many whom have made that colour palette notorious
- Many secrets & collectables to further encourage & reward exploration including Nazi gold, Enigma Codes that unlock additional game-modes such as Hardcore, Ironman & Walk in the Park mode when solved, written letters, weapon & armour upgrades and even German-covers of classic music including The Beatles & The Animals
- An interesting yet disturbing world where the Nazis won World War II
- A story far better written & constructed than I'm sure any Wolfenstein fan would expect from a Wolfenstein game that can last you 8-14hrs (depends on how little or much you like to explore or interact with other characters), even if it doesn't exactly fly high in standards among other games.
- A surprisingly more human BJ Blazkowicz along with a potentially likeable cast of characters, even if a majority lack significant development or interest.
So even with the game having confusing graphical settings and currently being subject to performance problems for a small number of people, which I have personally not encountered, I fully recommend this game to any shooter fans out there with 50GBs to spare on their hard-drives looking for a real good time with a single-player first-person shooter.

Like several of the games Crunch has previously reviewed, he came into this franchise without having played any of the previous games. So his expectations are likely different from those that have.
The game started off in 1946 with assault on Deathshead's compound (Chapter 1), likely picking up shortly after the prior games. This allows you to get used to some of the game mechanics and early versions of some adversaries and weapons. Also, it forces you to pick one of two timelines (not sure what the difference is other than the lock picking mini-game or the health/armour bonus drops). So, you will have to playthrough twice to find out. Chapter 1's final moments also provide the good and reasonable explanation why you, as Blazkowicz, ends up in an insane asylum for such a long time (not going to spoil it).
The story progression from chapter to chapter was compelling and draws you in to find out what happens next. While not necessary, there are collectibles of several types spread throughout each chapter and finding all of one type in  a chapter provides a bonus. Also performing certain actions unlocks perks you can use and also allows you to work on unlocking the next perk in the chain. This can be tedious especially in the action needed is not something you do often (e.g. sprint slides are one for Crunch).
The reason provided as to why the Nazis were able to get such advanced technology was a bit contrived and formulaic. Some more thought should have gone it that part. As well, some parts did not allow for alternative approaches. One section where Crunch died repeatedly, you are forced to engage in a firefight. No option to sneak around to a better position. Nope, you have to drop down from a vent and every guy in sight with a gun starts banging away (see below)
Though Crunch has not finished it (end boss fight has stymied him) yet, he has been having a very good time. There have been near rage quit moments (Sure! Drop Crunch in the middle of room full of Nazis with heavy body armour & autoshotguns. I am Troll. Crunch can take 'em ... ack!!!). Dual wielding almost anything from knives to autoshotguns is fun however burns the ammo so is best saved for when you need to take something down hard and fast.
On the subject about no multiplayer, Crunch is very glad there is none. In his experience, games that add multiplayer tend to focus on it too much and the single player suffers, a lot. There are exceptions (Mass Effect 3, and Space Marine come to mind). He feels too many games are trying to get part of the multiplayer action making it difficult to do well unless you have an established franchise (and they are close to being milked dry) or unique and compelling multiplayer.
All in all, having a good time. 9.0 out of 10 from Crunch. Might change once he has finished the game.

I played this game about a year back (i stopped shortly after they released legs) And came back now to see what happened to the game in the meantime. For someone who really enjoyed how the game used to work, it's a big disappointment now. The removal of blocks with different durabilities might have been a defendable change, since some might argue that it turned the game into a bit of a grind, but replacing it with a system built on loot crates with random contents and weapons as different rarity drops makes no sense in this kind of game. The "healing" of damage dealt to your robot (at least in the gamemodes where you can actually find a game in a reasonable time) might be nice if it happens to you, but is utterly frustrating when a fast enemy just escapes from your view to return unharmed a few seconds later. For me the fun in the early stages of robocraft was in building a robot with multiple propulsion systems and failsafes to make sure i can still fight after taking damage, it was in batteling a crippeled enemy while trying to angle my weapon with my one remaining leg. Of cause it takes away waiting time from the game, but the cost is a lot of what made robocraft unique.
It seems like someone decided to take the regeneration of a modern shooter (without taking into account how little sense that makes for robots), the lootcrate system of Overwatch (with the difference that the crates actually contain stuff that changes the gameplay, making it almost pay to win) and the slow progression of Warframe (which is worse since the game is PvP not PvE so the loadout actually matters).
I can see how players like some of these changes and i can see how players that played a lot and dont mind to spend some money from time to time will still enjoy the game, but i would not pick it up as a new player, there are better f2p games out there and i would not come back to it if you enjoyed it when it first started. First, a word about the so called "minimum" requirements: HORSEPIß
By that I mean they're massively overblown. They're massively overblown because a bunch of stupid schits in the gaming journalism industry took Bethesdas spec recommendation for playing the game at max settings in 1080p as the "minimum requirements", and then it got plastered everywhere. Bethesda never bothered addressing it, possibly because they couldn't figure out the actual minimum specs themselves, or possibly because the difference between "ultra" and "low" settings in TNO is almost nothing.
Still, TNO's engine has a myriad of technical issues, and even if you surpass the games overblown requirements, there's no guarantee you'll run the game well or at all. Whether or not the game will work on your system seems to be entirely up to the whims of RNGesus. With that in mind though, if you have any sort of quadcore cpu or better, and atleast a 1GB videocard (preferably NVidia), you'll probably be able to run the game with a playable frame rate. Probably. The problem with TNO is it is a colossal memory hog. I tested the game on low settings at 720p in one of the least detailed areas in the game and it was taking up in upwards of a GB of vram. So for best results you'll want atleast a 2GB card, else you may suffer major dips in FPS or severe texture pop in.
So anyways about the game. After ~25 hours, 2 playthroughs (one for each timeline), obtaining every collectable, gruelingly unlocking every perk and bonus mode, I can safely say this game...is not worth $60, and I definitely wouldn't of dropped $60 on the preorder if it wasn't for the Doom 4 beta. HOWEVER, it is a solid FPS with a blend of oldschool and modern shooting mechanics. Once the sales start a few months down the line, it will definitely be worth a pickup.
The most important part of any FPS is the gunplay, and TNO nails it for the most part. Movement is smooth and fluid. Weapons handle appropriately and have a satisfying impact. You can dual wield almost every gun and mow down nazis like a maniac, or you can fire from cover with the nifty leaning mechanics and meticulously pick off nazis, or in some areas you can stealthily pick off nazis one by one dual wielding silenced pistols or throwing knives.
The graphics are, well...fairly average for the most part. There are plenty of pretty postprocessing and lighting effects to be had, but they're countered by terrible looking textures in the world that look like they came straight from the year 2000. Weapon and character textures look fine for the most part however. Textures will noticeably pop in at times even on higher settings, but can be alleviated by setting the FOV to 100. There's no option for anti-aliasing, but it can be forced on through launch commands.
A special mention goes for the depth-of-field effect, which looks absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥ing awful and turns BJ Blazkowicz into the most near-sighted war hero in the history of the universe. You can't turn it off through the options menu, but again can be forced off through launch commands or the console. I suspect the devs didnt want you to turn it off to help hide the bad texturing, texture pop in, and lack of an AA option. Why blur just edges when YOU CAN BLUR THE WHOLE ♥♥♥♥♥ING SCREEN AMIRITE BlTCH!?! Uh.. ehrm...sorry.
For me, TNO only has 2 significant negatives. First, there is a disappointing lack of content, considering the absence of multiplayer. The 2 timelines have only slightly different stories, and the occasional different path options throughout the game. You're essentially playing the exact same game in either timeline. The weapon variety leaves much to be desired. While you'll unlock alt-fire modes for each gun throughout the game, you'll be using the same guns for 3/4 the campaign. Nazi variety isn't much better. You'll be fighting essentially the same soldiers, heavy soldiers, super soldiers, and occasional dogs and robots through 99% of the game. The bonus modes you can unlock are simply novelty difficulties that you'll likely not want to bother with if you've played the game twice already. Supposedly if you obtain every collectable there is another mode that unlocks that, in the words of the devs "will keep people coming back to the game", however this mode apparently hasn't been put into the game, yet.
Secondly, the game is far too easy, even on the hardest standard difficulty. There are a few points where you'll get overwhelmed from time to time, but other than that any experienced FPS player should have little issue tearing through the game in 10-12 hours on Uber. This isnt necessarily because the AI is stupid, but because there aren't enough enemies around to put up a serious fight, or there aren't enough tough enemies. The AI is competent in a shootout, capable of suppressing fire and flanking attacks, but in stealth mode it is full on retärded.
Stealthable areas in TNO are universally trivial because the AI is so massively gimped that a toddler could clear them without alerting a single nazi. The AI is completely deaf being unable to hear the whelps of the nazi dog 3 feet behind them as you stab it in the chest, is incapable of recognizing his dead nazi retärds lying in pools of blood right infront of them, and has to stare at the player in full view for a solid 5 seconds before being alerted. Just about the only thing that will alert the nazis is an unsilenced gunshot. Thankfully, you're never really forced into stealthing any part of the game, so I would recommend just going loud at all times for full enjoyment.
So, in conclusion, if you love shooting things, nazis in particular, and TNO is around $40 or less, I would highly recommending picking it up.

Game played on 'I am Death Incarnate', campaign lasted a solid 16.5 hours.
The Good:
The emotions and thoughts evoked by the first half of this game struck me as almost a spiritual successor to Half-Life 2. A challenging and desperate undermanned undergunned fight against a malevolent power that rules the entire world. There is no backup to be had, you are the last best hope for humanity. With puzzles, platforming, secrets, a solid stealth mechanic, and more than one way to approach most areas, it gives you a sense of freedom to play the game your way. Bethesda have once again done what they do very well: Make a game with extremely solid gameplay mechanics, that is fun and beautiful, full of emotional atmosphere. The game starts out incredibly strong with a rivetting story, gut-wrenching choices, and an absolutely perfect emotional buildup to the mid-point showdown.
The Bad:
The sense of scale, time and distance was very difficult to follow in the second half, due to a complete lack of appropriate cutscenes. There are no sweeping vistas or wonder as the hero discovers new and interesting locations (and there are some that REALLY REALLY REALLY deserved some), travel of hundreds to thousands of miles are reduced to a black screen fade. Your view of the Nazi world is rather limited to back alleys and dungeons with the occasional glimpse of the backstory via newsclippings that you can find to read. It's not even very clear who's in charge of the worldwide Nazi regime.
Unfortunately, the game also suffers from less than fleshed out story and character development. The first half of the game was stunning in all respects. Cutscenes were appropriate, you began to care about characters, and to delve into their backstories. Where it breaks completely appart is the second half. In some ways it's as if the writing team got laid off halfway through, and some hapless intern was charged with trying to tie up the plot.
Character stories that had started to be explored, the angst, the horror, the regrets, they all suddenly dry up, from one interaction to the next. As an example, one character blames you for the death of another, yells 'Get out!', slams the door in your face, then 5 minutes later they are talking to you again as if that interaction had never happened, and it never once comes up again for the rest of the game. Characters that have very little to do with the story are given backstory cutscenes, while main characters that you are supposed to care more about are not even given more than a passing mention.
The Verdict:
I really enjoyed this game overall, and I would thoroughly recommend it on gameplay mechanics alone, as well as the rivetting story of the first half. If the solid writing had been maintained through the second half, this would definitely be one of my favorite games of all time. Despite this, it is a lot of fun and I am working on a second playthrough. It is possible that my perception of the plot will improve.

Wolfenstein: The New Order has provided me the single-player shooter I've waited a long time to see.
This is probably one of the most well-placed steps in the right direction for single-player FPS design I've seen since the turn of the "Seventh-Gen" Consoles and Call of Duty's arrival. There's a very cohesive mixture of the classic mechanics with a few of the newer staples added into the mix to really flesh out the shooter experience in Wolfenstein: The New Order. You can carry as many weapons as there are & dual-wield most of them, you have a classic health & armour system with an added touch of 10-20% health regeneration (Subject to upgrades, perhaps difficulty too, but I can't be certain of the latter yet), you can move & sprint very fast, you can aim-down sights while maintaining a classically accurate & reliable hipfire, and you can sprint & crouch-slide at quite some speed, whilst having a peek around cover mechanic for those occasions you choose not to perform the bulletstorm dance.
And one of the most shining traits of the gameplay is the ability to choose between complete stealth or complete carnage or even both for the majority of the game's chapters! The fantastic level design allows the player to formulate a plan or find alternate routes to silently take down the humourously, but not tension-breaking awareness-lacking Nazis, kill Communications Officers to allow you to go loud without them able to call for backup, or just plain throw brains out the window and run around guns fully blazing at whatever dares throw themselves at you.
Otherwise, the game sports:
- A very fine-controlling shooter for both mouse & keyboard and controller (especially the former) with fully rebindable keys & several controller layouts
- An FOV-Slider that goes from 80-100 (so no fear for those who suffer with low FOV).
- A fantastic aesthetic design which makes better use of the grey & brown colour palette than many whom have made that colour palette notorious
- Many secrets & collectables to further encourage & reward exploration including Nazi gold, Enigma Codes that unlock additional game-modes such as Hardcore, Ironman & Walk in the Park mode when solved, written letters, weapon & armour upgrades and even German-covers of classic music including The Beatles & The Animals
- An interesting yet disturbing world where the Nazis won World War II
- A story far better written & constructed than I'm sure any Wolfenstein fan would expect from a Wolfenstein game that can last you 8-14hrs (depends on how little or much you like to explore or interact with other characters), even if it doesn't exactly fly high in standards among other games.
- A surprisingly more human BJ Blazkowicz along with a potentially likeable cast of characters, even if a majority lack significant development or interest.
So even with the game having confusing graphical settings and currently being subject to performance problems for a small number of people, which I have personally not encountered, I fully recommend this game to any shooter fans out there with 50GBs to spare on their hard-drives looking for a real good time with a single-player first-person shooter.

Like several of the games Crunch has previously reviewed, he came into this franchise without having played any of the previous games. So his expectations are likely different from those that have.
The game started off in 1946 with assault on Deathshead's compound (Chapter 1), likely picking up shortly after the prior games. This allows you to get used to some of the game mechanics and early versions of some adversaries and weapons. Also, it forces you to pick one of two timelines (not sure what the difference is other than the lock picking mini-game or the health/armour bonus drops). So, you will have to playthrough twice to find out. Chapter 1's final moments also provide the good and reasonable explanation why you, as Blazkowicz, ends up in an insane asylum for such a long time (not going to spoil it).
The story progression from chapter to chapter was compelling and draws you in to find out what happens next. While not necessary, there are collectibles of several types spread throughout each chapter and finding all of one type in  a chapter provides a bonus. Also performing certain actions unlocks perks you can use and also allows you to work on unlocking the next perk in the chain. This can be tedious especially in the action needed is not something you do often (e.g. sprint slides are one for Crunch).
The reason provided as to why the Nazis were able to get such advanced technology was a bit contrived and formulaic. Some more thought should have gone it that part. As well, some parts did not allow for alternative approaches. One section where Crunch died repeatedly, you are forced to engage in a firefight. No option to sneak around to a better position. Nope, you have to drop down from a vent and every guy in sight with a gun starts banging away (see below)
Though Crunch has not finished it (end boss fight has stymied him) yet, he has been having a very good time. There have been near rage quit moments (Sure! Drop Crunch in the middle of room full of Nazis with heavy body armour & autoshotguns. I am Troll. Crunch can take 'em ... ack!!!). Dual wielding almost anything from knives to autoshotguns is fun however burns the ammo so is best saved for when you need to take something down hard and fast.
On the subject about no multiplayer, Crunch is very glad there is none. In his experience, games that add multiplayer tend to focus on it too much and the single player suffers, a lot. There are exceptions (Mass Effect 3, and Space Marine come to mind). He feels too many games are trying to get part of the multiplayer action making it difficult to do well unless you have an established franchise (and they are close to being milked dry) or unique and compelling multiplayer.
All in all, having a good time. 9.0 out of 10 from Crunch. Might change once he has finished the game.

Well, Age of Empires II was one of the big classics of RTS. After the first part which played in the Antique and tought the player much about european history if he was willing to read all those history-parts in the scenario descriptions, AoE2 chose a different approach. The game now played in medieval times and the history was told by a narrator on the beginning and on the end of every scenario in the main campaigns, so that even the lazy ones got their education.
Now, what to expect on the HD-Edition? Well, of course some better graphics. If you have the original game (and "the Conquerors"-AddOn) and don't think higher resolutions are worth the money, you might still want to buy the game to get the "The Forgotten" DLC. It's a new set of campaigns about some historical persons who are well less known then those in the original game. For example Vladimir Tepesh, also known as Dracula (who was not a real vampire but a very bloodthirsty military leader who fought the osman Empire). And you will get some new nations to play.
So is everything well with the game? Not entirely. The developpers revised the random maps and some bugs still don't seem to be fixed. For example some AIs seem to have problems with a nomadic start which results in doing nothing at all. And the scenario intros on the "forgotten" campaigns are not narrated as players of the original campaigns are accustomed.
Still it's AoE2 and hey - if you missed this game you can't understand the history of the RTS genre.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is the best entry in the Wolfenstein franchise since Wolfenstein 3D. I am loving the id tech 5 engine because of all facial modeling in the game. It's all wonderfully rendered without raching that uncanny valley point. The action is quick and visceral.

The story was new and fun. It even plays a tad on the prior Wolfenstein game, and the continuation of that universe is great. The events and locations get more ludicrous as the game progresses, but holy hell, it's a lot of fun. Stealth helicopters, trains, submarines, underwater hold outs, the moon, and so much more. I saw ludicrous lovingly because Wolfenstein has never prided itself on being realistic, and for that I love it. It's a nice break from all these "Real world" shooters, and I had a great time.

is a great blend of oldschool and modern FPS mechanics.
Wolfenstein is a gory, over the top murderfest. It evokes a familiar feeling and makes you smile with a great arsenal of weapons and its witty dialogue. But that's not all this game is, MachineGames put effort into their story and it stands out. The story begins with a fairly lighthearted approach but as the final cutscene fades into black you are left with quite a somber tone... enjoyed it thoroughly.
The alternate reality fiction is put together with impressive detail and the world offers some of the most memorable characters I've seen, especially Frau Engel & Bubi. The game has great sound design across the board but the superb voice acting and soundtrack are worth a special mention.
The best part of the game is the gunplay, it is sublime. The guns have weight and they sound fantastic. You can dual-wield anything and killrooms tend to turn into quite a mess. If you're the stealthy type, don't worry, you're still in for a treat. The stealth mechanics are solid and offer a great alternative for people who want to take the quiet approach. Most missions offer a great balance for different playstyles. The campaign is lengthy but doesn't overstay its welcome. Your first playthrough will probably clock around 12 hours.
One of the more oldschool mechanics in Wolfenstein is the health system. As a welcome change, healthpacks and bodyarmour are back. No more waiting behind cover for health to recover, instead you are encouraged to play aggressive. The game is extremely generous with healthpacks and even on the harder difficulties, offers little challenge.
Graphically Wolfenstein is great, it has some old textures but they make up for it with interesting environments and beautiful effects.
I can't really think of much negative stuff to say about the game, the only thing being a specific technical problem I occasionally encountered. After dying and loading, the game would sometimes put my GFX card to its knees and slow down to 1-2 frames per second, while normally running at a silky smooth framerate. The problem fixed itself after rebooting the game.
MachineGames made a bold move when they decided to ship an FPS game without a multiplayer mode. They wanted to focus on making a kickass singleplayer campaign and they succeeded, kudos.
Personally I can't wait for their next game.
- Gunplay
- Stealth
- Characters (Frau Engel & Bubi, Deathshead, B.J.)
- The world
- Health system
- Soundtrack
- Length
- Occasional framedrop problem after dying.
