One of the things that I am sort of disappointed in is when they released the EL update, they said it would help new players start easier (no tech tree, better balanced gameplay, even the starter SMGs and plasmas are great if used correctly.) so I made a new account and found out that you start off with 0 robits. You have to grind singleplayer until you get to level 10 and then you can go into all the other gamemodes. Since the matchmaking is a little off you get paired with "seal clubbers," aka people who fit legendary weapons (ion distorter, goliathon, leviathan, LOML, flak) and this makes it so the game is unfair to newer players.
Some of the things I really like about RC is the fact that the graphics and the gameplay are good for a free game. The amount of weapons and what they do also means you can have a lot of versatility in what you build. It's the same in the movement also.
Overall I think that this is a very good game even with its flaws. I wish they made it a little easier to start out (having some robits) and not having seal clubbers. if you can overlook those minor things then this is a great game and I can easily recommend it to you.

I'm giving this a thumbs up because it's a great game. The huge seamless maps with battles everywhere is loads of fun. The XP system for spotting, repairing, medic work etc. is outstanding.
But I dont have much fun playing it. It's been out long enough, and the player base is good enough, that you will die repeatedly over and over again. No matter what class, and no matter what you do, and no matter where you go, or how well you try to hide. Everyone has better weapons, and everyone already knows just where to camp on the map to farm kills. Most vet players play a dedicated class; they do the same thing overa and over again ad infinitum. The most lop sided part of the game against noobs is air combat, which by the way is almost exclusively the realm of keyboard and mouse. Trying to plug in your flight sticks will just give you a headache. This is an arcade flyer, and none of your sim expierence means anything here.
The catch is if you have lots of friends playing all the time or a clan, you'll usually roll over other people. If you're playing alone, you'll get rolled over. That's not a downside IMO, but it's a point worth making.
I'm not ragging on it either. It's a great game that does well what it does (massed clan combat). But you will have to put serious, serious time into it to not feel like a hopeless noob. I'm not bad at FPS's in general, and I've got 34 hours in this at this review, and while I might have some good runs as infantry, I spend most of my time in an infinite respawn loop. Step outside of camping as infantry at a cap point to try a run in a tank, or even worse flying, and the deaths seem to come quicker. Every clever flank move you try, the vets already know you're trying it.
Yes, this a rage review, but it's honest. If you're not willing to make this the one game you play all of the time, or if you want to play many different classes constantly, you had better be happy with a .5 or lower KDR. If you're fine with that, give it a go.

Let's start off with this, Pay 2 Win, that's what this is. You can argue that all you want but there is a large amount of guns that can only be unlocked by purchasing them with Station Cash, which is like the premium credit microstransaction for this game. Those weapons also happen to be substantially better than the ones you can get through playing, see how long I've been playing, I have yet to get enough certification points to purchase a new weapon (I could have gotten a new sniper that was equal to the one you start with, but I wouldn't have been able to get as many upgrades as I have) Also upgrades don't transfer between classes, each item you upgrade, it will only be upgraded for that class. When you start the game you'll be prompted to pick a faction and then choose a server, you cannot change factions and you cannot change servers. You have 3 "character" spots (the "character" is the faction and server you chose), so if you want to go to a different server, you'll have to make a new "character" and you will start at level 1, that's right, your rank isn't tied to your account, it's tied to your character, as are upgrades and the like. The game isn't "the next big thing", it's like your standard FPS, just with a horrid user interface, which the developers pride themselves on, never heard of a company that prides themselves on not being able to make a proper UI. Oh and with all poorly built games, just because you have the exact same equipment and upgrades as another person, doesn't mean you'll win a gunfight if you start shooting first, the lag (maybe cheats?) makes sure of that. Tip though, hold shift when using a sniper to hold your breath when zoomed in, otherwise you wobble like you're drunk. The game doesn't tell you this.

In every human enterpreneaurship there is this subtly need for aestethics, in a work like this, a game, filled already with the need of it, its easy to blurry the lines between a game and a interactive timeless masterpiece of art.

If you are out for some casual fun, play this game. If your out for interesting and "revolutionary" gameplay, look elsewhere.
now, I'm about to inform you on one of the most effective ways to kill a game.
I've been playing since closed beta, with 580 hours on record (I didn't use steam for a long while) and the game and its concepts are wonderful on paper, horrid in excution. I've acutally stopped playing in recent months because the developers have repeatedly changed what the games core concepts where about.
When I started in open beta, the game was about squad or platoon tatics. The lattice system wasn't in place so the map offered alot of tatical options for how you wanted to take on the enemy. However, this lead to a problem for the devs, because big groups of players would simply go around eachother, with only skirmishes on the edges. So they introduced the alert system. The alert system is fantastic! it allowed us to play skimish-y when we wanted and we could all gather for a mega zerg when alerts come up.
that was the best stage in the game, and I would've kept play had it been that way, but the devs decided that planet side 2 wasn't about a whole bunch of smaller battles , with bigger batles tossed in here and there. Planet side 2 was about mega zerging all the time, with small battles being a rarity. So they introduced the lattice system.
basically, the lattice system prevented you from going around an enemy force, you HAD to defeat them, which made quickly explotable tank forces nigh impossible to besige , you simply couldn't get around them. This made the game filled with mega zergs all the time.
The problem with a mega zerg is that you can't be tatical with it, you have to be tatical within it. I was part of the max clan, and we pulled in a full platoon most nights, sometimes 2 platoons on fridays, and before the lattice system, we had power. We could affect the map and make a differance for the NC. When the lattice brought mega zergs, we lost alot of our power, we didn't even make up half the population of the zerg. If we wanted to do something tatical we had to hope that our OWN faction of disorginized players in the zerg, would act in our favour. Often times we would get screwed by our own zerg, or simply be unable to make a dent in the enemy zerg because we were too small.
put aside all the balance issues with the game, but aside the map design, all the bugs  and all the little nit-picky things , all those could be fixed. But what will never be fixed, is the games ability to make a community of gamers feel absoutly powerless.
50 guys all in comms, a team speak heirchy giving flawess comms within squads and within platoons.
20 guys are in the air, 6 liberators and 12 revers
20 guys in armour , 12 in tanks, 5 in harrassers and 3 supporting sundies
10 guys on on the ground, engies keeping the tanks rolling
but we need more boots on the ground to protect us from infantry, and what does the zerg of randoms do? they spawn a horde of tanks, our force can't get through, its a traffic jam, the enemy attacks, we can't return fire because were choked by friendlies , our ground force is wiped and then our air follows suite when we have no counter for the enemy AA.
50 guys made useless by the mega zerg.
thats how you kill a game.

For anyone coming from CS: from the little amount of games (+10 hours) I have played against "elite" ranked players, the games skill ceiling ends at MG1 / DMG in CS. If you rekt them too much they come out with either a noobtube character (nader) or a tank with much HP. Nothing you can't counter with headshots.
It's very fun, casual can be frustrating when medics don't revive, or skyhammers ask for their airstrikes either on their position, killing themselves, or inside a building, where bombs obviously can't boomala boombala, but it's casual after all, expect newbies.
The ranked matchmaking reminds me a bit of CS, duoqueuers just teamkilling with no consequences, the only punishment you can give them as a player is type /p to punish, that will take away some points off their total game score, but that's it. Can't kick because they are never alone, and can't report because there is no griefing option.
Overall is a fun game, still in beta, with alpha features, but it has a bright future, even more now that the developers have bought themselves out of the horrible publisher that was Nexon.
If you are into shooters but CS is too hardcore, try it out, it's very fun, even more with friends.

A giant, frustrating, impressive, hardware-killing MMOFPS that can serve as a reminder for future game developers to NEVER EVER AGAIN enable friendly fire in an MMO-ish game where you can kill somebody by driving over him.
+ More than two years after release, the servers are still densely populated.
+ Almost glitch-free if you don't provoque it.
+ Complex battles with infantry, vehicles and air combat.
+ Nice-looking.
+ Skill beats money (which is rare in an F2P).
+ Good long-time motivation if you keep your individual sessions shorter than 3 hours.
+ well balanced, with regular balance patches keeping it this way. (Though many people disagree with me here)
+ Can become highly strategic if you're playing in an organized platoon.
+ Starting weapons are competitive, you don't have to purchase different ones just to have a chance.
- Very demanding when it comes to your hardware, especially for a 2 year old game.
- Can become extremely frustrating when you repeatedly die without accomplishing anything.
- No fun at all if your faction is getting significantly overpopped (Other faction has more players online).
- Community can be annoying at times.
- Unbearable lag if you have a weak computer or internet connection. (although this is no minus for the game, it is worth mentioning)
- Weapons and equipment are ridiculously overpriced (About 7€ for ONE WEAPON)
Looks: 4/5
Gameplay: 3.5/5
F2P System: 3/5

Robocraft used to be great, I spent many enjoyable hours designing, fighting, perfecting robots. Grinding isn't exactly fun, but it was fun to try to improve the average amount of money I won each game by optimizing my robot. I always hoped they would fix comms so that teams could coordinate better like other team games I played. Instead, they went another way.
They added new modes that many including myself found boring, and then took out the old modes so that we wouldn't play them, taking the attitude that they new better than the players how to have fun. Then they took away the good looking blocks with the cool tints, and replaced them with black and white then asked you to re-pay to change colors again. then they took away the old earning system and replaced it with crates and make you craft junk into what you need (dont make a mistake and craft something you need, since theres no real way to organize your inventory) what a waste of time. There is an annoying lady that repetitively chatters loudly at you telling you, essentially, that things are happening. Since these things always happen unless nobody is playing, she is always chattering.
Oh, then they repriced premium so it costs way more. everything costs more.  Do not trust these devs, every dev changes the game, but what robocraft pulls is on a different level. When they revalued premium, they had to do some things to not get sued, but effectively they still devalued any money you put in their system before the changes. Not talking about depreciation of already bought items, but the potential utility of any credits you have. Thats on an objective level, not taking into account that the game subjectively sucks more too. Maybe some other devs dont listen, but they are consistent and don't pull the rug out from under players every other month. This is on a whole 'nother level. I really loved this game but these devs, they seem to want to win a notorious dev award or something. Like the kind where nobody will buy one of your games again because you are untrustworthy and capricious.

If you've read any of the other recent reviews, you would know that Robocraft USED to be a great game. It really was. But somewhere around the aeroflak update it has just kept going downhill.
The biggest blunder by far is the lootcrate system. It's just like one of those cheap mobile games that tempt you into spending money on a bunch of worthless crap. Except Robocraft's system is even worse. Instead of buying specific parts or some kind of exchangable tokens, you can buy high tier lootcrates. However, you have absolutely no clue what you're going to get, and your chances of getting something actually useful are hardly better than the standard low tier crates. It is essentially gambling. You might as well play some slots at an actual casino, because your chances of winning are so much higher.
To be honest, the crates wouldn't be an issue if they also supplied you with a decent amount of "robits" (the in-game currency), or if you could actually sell those random parts for a decent price. But instead, you have to sell parts for 25% of their value. This makes acquiring the parts you actually want so much harder, especially if you want to use SMGs or Plasmas whose low tiers are only useful if you have a lot of them. I had enough cubes saved up from before the update to build my bots, but I can't even fathom the grinding noobs have to do just to be able to build a single competitive bot. An active player used to be able to build a completely new robot every other day or so with the old economy system.
I'm not even going to get started on the "you get loot based on your performance" system, because I lack the adjectives to describe how utterly terrible it is. The price of premium (which is used to unlock the extra parts dangled in front of your face during lootcrate opening) also falls under this category. I'm confident that these two system are merely a way to force players to spend money, essentially a cash grab.
The saddest part about the new updates is that the dev's have no intention of changing them. I'm not sure if it's ignorance, pride, greed, or a combination of all three, but it's safe to say robocraft will only get worse from here on out. From what I can tell, the dev's "attempts" at involving the community are nothing but a facade to cover up the bigger issues. It's only a matter of time until we need to start carving the tombstone.
It's a shame, really. As much as I used to love Robocraft, it just seems rotten now.

I decided recently to return after a longer hiatus for some simple and fun action with this game. Or that's what I planned to do. I wondered the 'mixed' review-rating and after some digging I found that things had changed. Quite a bit, it seemed.
I ignored these warnings, choosing to base my conclusions on my own observations. Once I entered the game I noticed that part-acquiring system had changed, once again. Nothing too dramatic, nothing I could not learn again, I though. But after some investigation a realization dawned upon me, that a large part of these mechanics had been changed to force more money out of the player. Robocraft had met the ultimate among grim fates for F2P-games, economics.
Perhaps the old premium system did not provide enough income to sustain Freejam's operations, an understandable cause for these changes, but the game felt cold and dead to me now. I came to the conclusion that new setup purposefully made life unconfortable and clunky for non-paying players, wrangling their patience to compete against their wallet. This is a market tactic I absolutely despise and boycott without exception on principle. Perhaps this creation could be still saved. Perhaps I should fight on. But no, I shall not. My principles stand above all, untouched and sacred, and shall not be shaken by old fond memories.
So I say:
Do not download, do not play. The show is over and the fun has ended.
Prayers might save this lost soul, but I urge you to abandon it to decay. Who knows how deep this corruption runs, who knows where we'll end up in eons to come if we silently approve this sort of forceful milking.

The crate system really destroyed how I earn in game cash. It used to be if you do well in a battle, you get an amount of money determined by how well you did. But now you could be the very best on your team, and if your team loses, you get crappy stuff in a silver crate. Yeah sure, there's a chance something good may be in there, but take it from me, in the last 20 hours I've played (give or take), and no matter what crate I got, I never recieved more than 1,000 robits exept for maybe 4-5 times. I would have totally recommended this game some time ago, but now, it could be a lot better. What I think would be a much better system for the crates is to replace protonium, diamond, gold, etc... with a point system. Based on how well you do in a single match, regardless of weather your team wins or loses, you earn a certian amount of points. Those points can be used to purchase crates with a set type of item in there. For instance, you earn some amount of points and you spend it on an epic crate, you can expect to earn epic items. That way it's not down to chance, but by skill, and that is how you climb the MOBA ladder, skill.

Dirty Bomb is just good enough to be frustrating, because it has a lot of good elements that don't quite manage to make up for the bad ones.
-Good selection of characters and maps
-Gameplay is fast and fun
-Extremely poor matchmaking systems
-Unlocking characters and weapons is painfully slow without spending $
-Noticable but not extreme stability problems
It has a surprisingly good selection of different characters, a small but functional variety of maps, and some cool game modes. When everything's going well, the action is fast and fun, and it's easy to have a great time. Most of the time, though, a host of major issues turned the game into a frustrating slog.
That's when everything's going well, though. The unranked matchmaking mode has a depressing tendency to set up teams that are wildly unbalanced. It's not uncommon to see games where the lowest scoring person on the winning team has more points than the highest scoring person on the losing team. The game's focus on teamwork means that how your team is playing makes a huge impact on how well you can do. I've seen the same player get a 3 to 1 k/d score on a leading team, and reverse it to a 1/3 when the stack turned the other way. It's painful.
The ranked matchmaking isn't much help, either. I'm probably pretty average in terms of overall FPS skills, and it took me about 16 hours to qualify for the ladder. Once I got there, though, I'd spend more time waiting in the matchmaking queue than actually playing rounds, and would end up playing in supposedly skill-matched games against people with 10x my playtime. There just don't seem to be enough people playing the game on ranked, even during peak hours.
Unfortunately, the community for this game is filled with a lot of awful people. Most matches had a few people spitting out racist/sexist/homophobic slurs, or just shouting profanity over the mic. The game got noticably better after I just started muting everyone, which is a shame, because it can't have helped with the teamwork aspect of things. A lot of this might just be because the game leaves a lot of people feeling frustrated.
The game uses a microtransactions system where you can unlock new characters, equipment, and special abilitiies for your characters through either in-game currency or by spending real money. You earn in-game cash by completing nifty little challenges that refresh every few hours, which is nice, but the money drip is pretty slow. Expect to probably play for a two to three weeks in order to unlock a new character, plus weeks more to get their upgraded loadouts. Everyone gets the same two basic characters for free, plus 3-4 characters on an open rotation that changes every two weeks or so.
Finally, the game has some stability issues and tends to crash to desktop in the middle of gameplay maybe once every two hours or so. The game servers will also crash occasionally, dumping everyone playing back to the main menu. It wasn't enough to be a major problem on its own, but whenever the game crashed in the middle of one of the few-and-far-between good matches, I'd feel soured on the game for days.

Oh my, this is a blast from the past. But in a highly enjoyable way, bringing back the glory days of CRT monitors, trackball mice, and 256/512 MB hard drives.
This game is a classic and still very much an awesome experience. I highly recommend purchasing this item if you have the means to. This game and others like it defined the RTS genre.
For those that dont know anything about this game, you can play the in-depth campaigns, which cover a number of historical periods and battles, allowing the player to get a very simplified version of what happened and what could have happened. For me though, multiplayer and skirmish are my bread and butter, and skirmish allows you to set up the game, from what civs, how big the map is, what type of map, so on and so forth. The game will begin with your town center with a few villagers and a scout. Typically you would use the scout to explore the map, finding the enemy and more resources. At the same time you have the few villagers start to collect resources, mostly wood and food at first. You would want to then pump out a few more villagers, building housing as needed, all to accelerate resourse collection. After a sizable amount has been stored and the right conditions are met, you can then advance ages, which unlocks more options for building your town and armies. Anyone that has not played this game is missing out on what I think is a crucial piece of RTS gaming history.
And if you havent figured it out yet, I really like this game. So much so that my first copy way back in CD-ROM days was burnt right through by my old computer's disc drive. Thats how much I played this game.

First, I must say this is easily one of the most perfect games I have ever been lucky enough to play. I used to play it all the time before the disc broke when I was younger, and my recent return to its beauty is a warm welcome. The HD graphics "update" doesn't really stand out to me, as it looks nearly the exact same. However, the exact same is good enough for me. The music fits the game like a hand in a glove, and if you're one who cares as much as I do about in-game soundtracks, this is THE most memorable music I have ever heard while playing a game. It stands out with its really unique approach to the how a game should sound, and listening to the entire 30 minute long epic (and that's only the base game soundtrack) while outmaneuvering enemy players is a dream come true.
The game itself still holds up extremely well in terms of variability even to this day. Its many different civilizations all offer something slightly different, both in terms of playing style and building style. The expansions for the game add on an almost ungodly amount of additional civilizations, which only furthers its flexibility. The game modes are relatively straightforward, and all very fun in their own way. My all-time favorite will forever be conquest, in which you must conquer all enemy players completely and decisively in order to win. The resource system in the game is perfectly executed, in my opinion. I believe it found just the perfect balance between simplicity and depth, as it is very simple to learn, but very difficult to master, hence the appeal from a shallow learning curve. The different branches of research are much more difficult to master, as they are plentiful and all useful in certain situations. You need to decide what is most vital at the moment, and work towards it (ex. advancing villager resource gathering speed or troop strength) while also juggling however many other tasks you can in order to keep a fluid overall movement and pace as the game progresses.
The workshop implementation for this game is simply a joy to browse through, as this game was just begging for it from the start. The map creator tool in game makes it possible for custom maps to be posted and downloaded by anyone, and the more open-ended game files allow for easier modding. Right now whenever i play the game, I am treated to the game of thrones soundtrack at the title screen as a result of a simple download from the workshop. Various available texture packs caringly created by the workshop members are really nice to try out, as they can add entirely different feels to the game as you play it. Beyond this, I can't think of much more to add about it, other than the fact that it greatly furthers this game's life expectancy in my games library.
Overall, I can tell you that this game, no, this MASTERPIECE, is well worth the buy, and the constant discounts it offers should only entice you further to snatch this baby up.

Build robots. Drive robots. Fight Robots.
Hence - Build. Drive. Fight.
Robocraft is a creative game which involves constructing armed vehicles to fight down against enemy front lines in an online MOBA. The building mechanics are fluent and easy to use, and the gameplay enjoyable - easy for anyone used to FPS, and also easy for anyone used to more strategic combat style games.
The rewards system has recently taken a huge hit, making it harder for players to gain good high-end weaponry, which makes the game last longer, and gives the developers more room to add new content, which usually occurs on a monthly basis. This is why people have recently been posting negative reviews, because they see the new reward system as "cheap" and "unintuitive" for veteran users who are used to gaining high-end material almost every match.
Honestly, the game is indeed awesome. You build robots in any shape or form, which is already enough to enjoy. It's sort of a mix between League of Legends, Minecraft, War of Tanks, and Kerbal Space Program, all in one.
Still, they should change their slogan from "Build. Drive. Fight." to:
Build. Laugh. Explode.
10/10 would build suicide penguin again.

I first heard of this game from a few of my friends, and being enticed by the advertised mechanics I hopped on. Since
recommended this game along with warframe, one of my favorite games, I thought it would be easy to progress without spending anything. So far, I have avoided all the usual traps to pay for progression, and boy is it a grind. I am used to grinding for items, but this is another level. See, to get items, you either get them through crates or you use ingame currency to buy them. Sounds good right? Well, that's the issue. You can open any crates you earn for free (thank god), which gives you some items, but there's a catch, the rarer and more useful items are locked behind the premium rank, which isn't a one time payment, you pay for a certain amount of time, that counts down even when you are offline. Now you must be thinking, well you can always just buy the items with ingame currency right? Well, the problem here is that to get that currency you need to sell items you have, which has a really bad sell value compared to the price of the stuff in the shop, no it isn't selling for half the amount in the shop of even a third, it is selling for 1/5 to 1/10 the value, which makes it terrible to buy rarer items. The crates would be no problem, as the devs need to make money somehow right? Wrong. When you score highest in a winning team, you get a protonium crate, the supposed best crate in the game,  but you don't HAVE to score highest, or even play for that matter, you can simply BUY the crates, which is pretty much buying wins. Another problem I have encountered is the lack of a tutorial, which is really annoying, as I had to literally BEG on the forums for help, only to be mocked, so I aqcuired a guide in another game forums, which pretty much gives you an idea about the community. You can indeed argue that I have too little time in this game to already write a review, but that's the problem, the new player experience is just terrible, and will probably turn away the less resilient or ensnare the spoiled. I am currently putting more time into this game, and I might even change my review, but for now, it just doesn't live up to the praise, or deserves any money. I would rate it at 5/10, a glorified freemium mobile game

This game has a lot of potential to it that I felt has been slowly squandered. I really enjoyed the set up that this game had when it first launched. It really made the game heavily dependant on team work and strategy as well as skill because of the vast options and openness that the original territory capture system had. Granted it had it's issues (ghost capping in particular) but it wasn't unfixable. I felt there was a good way to tweak the system to obliterate the issue while still maintaining the openness and options that the system had, but SOE missed it by a mile.
I had a lot of fun until SOE decided to dumb down the game and went way too far in restricting strategic options. This new system of funneling all the players into very specific capture lines has completely changed the game, and not for the better. Now capturing territory all boils down to numbers (of who has the most players on their side) where strategy and teamwork has gone out the window. Playing this game as a numbers game is not fun for me.
Because of all this, Planetside 2 has become boring, repetative, and makes your personal contribution to the fight feel completely pointless. It was good at one time, but not anymore.

I've played Deathside 2 for quite some time (only recently began to play it through steam to count how many hours I've wasted) and I can tell you this:
Deathside 2, much like the original Deathside, is a fantastic game to die in. Now, some people have managed to have few deaths. Vanu is smiling upon them and giving them good grace to live. Every war needs champions, but the majority in Auraxis will die in every way known to man.  If you've never played this game, then you should do so to die for Vanu's enjoyment. It's free to play! What's not to like? But, here's a list of spoilers in how you'll die:
- You hit Instant Action to send you into battle. You come down in in a drop pod, it opens, you're see this beautiful world only for it all to be ripped away as a tank runs you over a second later.
- You respawn in a base, you die from a grenade immediately
- You spawn on a deployed Sunderer, you exploded from another grenade
- You respawn on same said Sunderer, an aircraft just shot you
- For some reason you respawn on said Sunderer for a third time believeing "three times a charm" method.  It explodes as soon as you spawn, debris goes everywhere, and you think "I live, I live!" and then you die from a knife.
- You're defending a control point, you get shot in the back of the head. A medic sits there staring at your lifeless body and contemplates the meaning of life instead of reviving you.
- You respawn, you run out of the spawn room and get run over by a cloaked ATV. Didn't even see it coming.
- You go to leave the spawn again only to be sniped in the head the moment you're leaving.
- You decide to play Infiltrator, you find a nice hill, you begin shooting enemies. This is working out well! Oh wait, you just got shot by a tank from long distance.
- You jump into your own tank thinking this will go much better than being on foot. Then you get bombed by a Liberator gunship.
- You're in an open field on foot because you're out of resources for vehicles and no one will give you a ride. As you run, you fall through the ground.  And you fall, and fall, and fall, and fall, and fall, falling, still falling, keep falling, more falling. At this point you realized you've entered purgatory and Vanu is laughing at your pain. This is why you're given one single grenade. There's only one way out of this.
- You spawn on a Sunderer, Sunderer kills you a millisecond later.
- You decide to spawn an aircraft thinking being up above and away from the crazy people will make you safe and the moment you do you are kamikazied by another aircraft.
Glorious times of death. Oh, did I meantion this was all friendly fire? It's totally worse when you actually begin to fight another empire. Expect worse when it's a three-way fight. This is only a small list of what's happened. The rest you must find out on your own!
Just remember one thing: Shoot your enemies and avoid your allies. Both will kill you.

WARNING: While the minimum system requirements are reasonable, this game is HORRIBLY unoptimized. That being said, if you have a decent GPU this will be one of the best looking games you can play.
The basic idea is fairly uncreative and boring: Three factions fight endelessly to control the four continents of Auraxis.
The GAMEPLAY, on the other hand, can be glorious. Imagine an entire army of bombers and gunships descending upon the unsuspecting enemy base, launch troops with jetpacks, mech suits, and all manner of explosizes and shooty things. The enemy reacts with AA guns and tanks firing skyward, but are ultimately defeated.
So then what?
Well, here's where my critisisms come in. The objectives are so watered down that there is no real reason to do anything. "PROTECT ______ TECH PLANT!" "Why?" "I don't know, this game has no backstory, plot, NPCs, or any sense of life to it, so go shoot things to earn monies!"
"What do I do with my monies?" Well, first of all, you're going to have to accept that experienced players will rekt you, not necessarily because they are more skillful (although that is almost always true), but because more certs (monies) = more advanced armor, weapons, grenades (which noobs don't get at all), and flashy neon camo patterns (which increase your coolness by -300%).

-Throughout the game you will attempt to capture "territories" for your faction

-Amerish (A bit of a combonation)

-Indar (Desert Area)
-Esamir (Winter Area)
Each Faction has faction-specific weapons and vehicles which i will discuss later.
-Pros-
-Massive Scale
-Variety of Weaponary
-General variety across the game (Vehicles to landscapes)
-Social system
-Large scale attacks
-Cons-
-Pay to Win (Kinda)
-Alot of grinding
-Balance
-Unfriendly to new players

-More Description on the given Pros and Cons-
(Feel free to skip this part, this part is simply me explaining why i think something)
-Pros-
=Massive Scale=
You are 1 solider of thousands fighting on four huge worlds
=Variety of Weaponary=
The game roaster has a large set of different weapon types.
=General Variety=
Each Faction is different, each class is different, etc. Everything feels unique, and not a slightly different verison of the others.
=Social system=
The game allows players to create or join outfits, or squads/platoon. Throughout these groups, people can plan and execute massive scale attacks, or covert operations.
=Large Scale Attacks=
You are riding in the gunner's seat of a vehicle you arrive at your destination jump out and rush the enemy with 200 other people, need I say more?
-Cons-

You can obtain everything without spending a dollar except cosmetics.
=Grinding=
Everyone loves grinding in games, right? You will be grinding, no doubt, nevertheless you still have fun during the time.
=Unfriendly to new players=
This game is extremly harsh to new players. It is a tough learning curve to adapt to the game. When you first start playing you are given a short tutorial then dropped straight into the largest battle currently happening! My Pros and Cons Of Planetside 2
Pros:
-Extremely massive battles, with lots of chaos
-4 different continents, each with its unique flora and appearance
-6 classes that fit anyone's play style
-Teamwork is key in this game, and really urges you to interact with your teamates, with things like healing, revives, and repairs, and actually awards you with XP for doing these things!
-cool weapons, with a wide variety of attachments
-3 empires, that have their own beliefs on how to rule
-Has a great setting, the planet of Auraxis
-for a game that can feature 2,000 people on 1 continent, is has little to no netcode issues.
Cons:
-since its F2P, Sony had to make money somehow. So, they implemented Cert points and Station Cash into the game. Cert points takes a while to build up a good amount to buy yourself an attachment,camo, or Cosmetic. Station cash can only be bought.
-Game includes some low res textures for things like rocks
-Non-members of the game are constantly reminded they are non-members, by the game showing you potential earnings you could have if you were a member. the game always tries to urge you to spend money to become a member, and if you don't want to, it can get pretty annoying.
-this game is a bit P2W since people who are willing to pay money on cert points gets better gear, attachments, and weapons.
even with some of the pretty hideous cons, I do recommend this game. If I had to give a score out of a ten, I would probably choose an 8/10. good game, with massive, chaotic battles, but the cert points, and member crap kinda kills it for me.

If you do not want to read a lengthy review, here are some pros, cons, and ratings to start with:
:
+ Unique gameplay.
+ Fun classes.
+ Well-designed maps.
+ Quick match-making.
+ Optional server browsing.
+ Not pay to win, everything can be earned.
+ Parkour.
+ Unique and fun card-collection loadout system.
+ Welcomes a variety of playstyles.
+ Not many bugs (in my experience).
+ Features a class rotation system where you can try certain classes for free before even buying them.
+ No optimization issues (that I could tell on my rig, anyway).
:
- Sometimes laggy players.
- Can feel a bit grindy once daily missions are complete.
- Very few maps.
- Not many modes.
- Mic-spamming children can be found.
- Match-making sometimes fails to create balanced teams.
- Balance is only good in the early game. Once you're level 6, you'll be pitted against level 30s or higher. The second this happens, matches being won is entirely ruled by who has the highest level, or who has gold/cobalt cards, regardless of what you do.
- Nobody works together to achieve anything in most cases. Once you get past level 5, it's just a bunch of people being farmed.
- The community is downright dreadful, ranging from kids who spam on chat, to people who will kick you for literally no reason whatsoever.
- Ridiculous grind.
- Grind is made additionally tedious through the things it makes you go through (terrible community, etc).
Now then, onto my thoughts on the game. Let's start off with...
At first glance, one might assume this is just yet another MMOFPS game, with more shooty shooty pew pew that is little more than "free CoD". These initial assumptions will prove inaccurate, however, as the game quickly shows how different its experience truly is. The game isn't exactly "revolutionary", as it does still maintain a lot of the basic core mechanics of your typical FPS game, however, this is what you'll find different:
The game features multiple classes, very similar to how TF2 does. However, each class has two special abilities all their own, which, more often than not, are intended to be used in organized team play rather than helping you do all the things by yourself. Another difference from TF2 lies in the fact that classes tend to not have their own weapons per se, but they are nonetheless restricted to specific weapons (Aura, for example, only has shotguns and SMGs as primaries). However, the way you equip said weapons is not how you would expect, as rather than purchasing weapons individually, you receive cards that contain a specific loadout. These range from various levels of rarity, with cobalt being the highest. Every loadout contains a primary, secondary, and melee weapon, as well as a series of little bonuses, like reloading while sprinting. Since these cards last with you forever, it's more a matter of collecting the cards for the classes you like and figuring out which ones best suit your playstyle, rather than collecting a ton of random weaponry.
Now then, onto...
The gameplay in this game is easily summarized as "addicting" at first, put purely unbalanced and frustrating later on. While the maps are limited in number, the few we do have are fun to play on and tend to not get stale. This is aided by the fact that the game does not encourage solo gameplay... Unless you're level 30 or higher. If you run off to "hardcore wreck some noobs", you're just going to die and bring your team down with your lack of effort to work with them, that is, until later where no matter what you do, you'll die even if you use teamwork, because the enemy has a level 30+. At first, you'll only have losses due to a bad team, but once you're level 6 or higher, you will have losses simply because the enemy has an outright advantage over you through level.
Another cause of losses is the match-making's tendancy to stack all the really good players against all the really bad players. It could definitely use some tweaks in how it handles team balancing.
This will bring you down, as whether you try or don't, the outcome will remain the same. Even in just the very small amount of time I've played, I've already had a number of moments where it honestly felt like it didn't matter if I sat still and did nothing or actually went out and tried. In this game, level 30+ players are the main characters, and everyone else is the random trash mobs to be killed effortlessly. When they get bored of you, they'll just call up a kick for no reason, even if you said nothing and did nothing wrong.
At the very least, all playstyles are welcome here. You want to snipe? Every map welcomes it. You want to support your team with healing and revives? You'll be the hero of your team. You want to be an assassin and sneak up behind the enemy with a sword? You can do that too! Whatever your playstyle is, you likely won't find yourself having to stray too far from it to find your place in a team. That is, until your playstyle stops mattering.
However, with the teamwork aspect in mind...
The community on this absolutely dreadful in every way imaginable, fun players who are very friendly are limited to the early game only, after that it's onto the stereotypical mic-spamming 12 year olds who seem to have a vocabulary consisting of nothing but profanity, and other kids who, as I mentioned, kick you without cause or warning. To emphasize my already emphasized point, even when you ask them why they're opening up a kick for you, they will not offer a single reason. This is not a rare problem either, you will encounter this frequently.
That said, not often does the team actually work together, but when they do it's amazing. I highly suggest having friends to play this with so that you may team up and have more guaranteed good experiences... Or at least until you face the already mentioned level 30's, who guarantee victory anyway.
And so...
All in all, the game can offer you a fun, original, and memorable experience at first, but then it will change to just another terrible game where skill is absolutely meaningless. If you can tolerate losing and winning only because a high level was on your team, are willing to subject yourself to horrible grind, and don't care if your actions are entirely meaningless to the actual outcome, this is the game for you.

These are my first impressions of the game. As of this writing I'm only 4 hours in. I'm gonna write a proper bulleted review once I get some more hours in.
Wow.
I was not expecting this game to be so good. Especially considering it's free, and from Nexon.
Although yes, some of the mercs (Dirty Bomb's version of Overwatch's heroes) seem to have better weapons and equipment than others, you can do just fine with the two default classes.
Using the default medic class, considered one of the weakest classes in the game AFAIK, I can get to the top of the scoreboard pretty regularly. What I'm saying is that it all comes down to skill in the end.
Also all of the things that are actually useful i.e mercs and loadout cards, you can buy with either in-game credits or USD. Yes, there's XP/currency boosters you can buy with USD (and only USD), but that's really only useful for if you're a completionist and you want to get every merc in the game (which, again, isn't necessary).
The gunplay itself is very good too. All weapons are accurate when hipfired, the ADS function is only for zoom for if you're trying to shoot at range. And unlike most games, pistols are actually useful.
The game is also very nicely optimized. I'm getting more than 100 FPS on max settings with a GTX 760.
The community is pretty toxic, unfortunately. It's almost as bad as CSGO. Within these first 4 hours I had various insults slung at me for being a bad medic, and I also saw multiple instances of &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥team,♥♥♥♥♥♥game". That doesn't faze me though.
The only real problem I have with this game is the grind. New mercs cost 50K credits, new loadouts go for around 20K. You usually earn about 300 credits per game, though once it got up to 600 credits. So it obviously takes a very long time to get new loadouts, even longer for new mercs.
But honestly, this game is really, really, really good. Somehow it's better than most AAA shooters that I've played, and it's free. This is going to keep me entertained for a very long time. Splash Damage & Nexon may have a masterpiece on their hands.
You have nothing to lose. Get. This. Game.

As far as I can tell, Planetside is a great game for teaming up with large groups of friends to take on enemies and work together in groups to make an experience where the skill of the individual is equally important as the teamwork between the players. This concept has been tried again, and again, but planetside offers a whole new look on this idea, with much, much larger servers to accomadate tons of players. This makes it more fun the play because your individual skrimishes seem more important and rewarding when the huge objective is completed.
That being said, I spent the first (and last) two hours of playing this game running around, not knowing what at all is going on. The two minute tutorials gave the player a general sense of how the average fps works without explaining the game at all. You are spawned into a giant hub where you press another button to be transported to who knows where, only to find yourself killed by some tank or aircraft camping your spawnpoint. After a few minutes, your team will do all of the work, causing you to either win or lose. Regardless, after that match is over, the whole thing will start all over again, throwing you into another viscious loop in which everyone blames you for being useless, (which of course, you are) but will not be willing to help you learn.
The mentoring system is a good step, but no game should force you look up help on the wiki or youtube videos just to be able to understand what is going on.
I am sure Planetside 2 is a great game, and I will keep playing for now, it looks like it may have quite a bit of potential, but I am sure that I am not the only one with such struggles. I can only assume that Planetside's poor introductory system is a insurmountable obstacle to people new to the game.
I am looking forward to understanding this game better so that I can write a more accurate and insightful reveiw.

Dirty Bomb is an interesting objective-based online-multiplayer First Person Shooter. There is a progression system which allows you to level up, and the more you play the more you get the chance to improve the quality of the team of mercenaries you use in the missions (you can recruit new ones, and give passive skills to the ones you have - nothing dramatic, thus avoiding the trap of having more experienced players owning super-strong characters at the expenses of newbies). The variety of mercenaries and weapons is OK.
While the game is good fun when played with friends (I played 22 hours so far, some of my friends played up to 60), the game lacks in maps variety. After a while, you end up playing the same thing over and over again (the train one! Canary Wharf! Escort the EV! Defend the Pylon!), and it gets repetitive. The game could certainly use more maps to increase its longevity. But even in its current state (it's April 2016), you can sink a decent amount of hours into it and have fun.

EDIT: As of the entirety of 2017 I have been questioning the decisions Freejam has been making. I still care for the game, but instead of because I really enjoy the game, it's now because I am hanging from a thread trying to hold on to the few reasons why I still love the game. It can be broken down into just one: No other game has movement mechanics as complicated, yet simply executed as Robocraft. Right now it is the only reason I play, and no other game has anything like it to my knowledge.
Other than that, if you know nothing about this game then just understand one thing: the game has a few very unique features that are very satisfying and fun to mess around with, but other than that it's not very wholesome. The devs used to prioritze bug fixes and patches over content releases, now they focus too much on content releases and give off the assumption that they ignore their issues. The devs need to wake up, or sell the game to another parent company with common sense in order for it to succeed.
I would reccomend this game for people to try out, but how long they stay in the game is up to them.

I've written a formal letter to FreeJam in the Robocraft Sub-Reddit, which I will link to, however, I'd like to outline some feelings I've had toward this game. I understand it's in Early Access, and I understand this is only one 'phase' of many. Who knows? Maybe in the future, I'll end up wiping this review and posting another one, but here are some finer key points of my letter, and the reasoning behind those points.
TL;DR Game used to be good, now the balance sucks, and the economy is worse. Wrote a letter, here's some points and clarification.
*Lock On Missile Launcher
This point was my first. In real life, Flak shells are used as Anti-Aircraft weaponry, because the shells can be fired high into the air and explode, leaving shrapnel to tear planes apart.
However, in Robocraft, the 'AeroFlak Cannon' (aptly named so as to make you believe that it should be used against airborne targets) instead causes significant damage with those same shrapnel explosions to anything not connecting with the ground, whether they're meters in the air, or a few centimeters off the ground. These explosions hit all blocks within the explosion radius and can potentially destroy a bot in as little as three well placed shots.
Not only that, but if the shells don't explode and connect with a player directly, they do their standard explosion damage, though given in a smaller radius. Mind you, the AeroFlak Cannon is a high-powered weapon. The damage is does is very significant, and you're likely to take massive damage, even if you're hit directly. With this in mind, you'd think that the trade-off would be either a very low rate of fire, or a higher power consumption (more on that in a moment). Surpisingly, no. The Flak fires at a steady pace of roughly once a second, however, add more guns, and you're firing more often. Roughly twice a second.
Now, regards towards power. Each robot has a power meter that goes from 100% to 0% and recharges over the course of ten seconds (or eight, if you have the optional Power Booster attached to your robot). Here's the problem that we face with the Flak cannon. It has only a power consumption rate of 10.8% per shot, allowing you to fire off at least 10 before needed to recharge (however, the power is recharging constantly, meaning you may face upwards of 11-13 shots before the enemy needs to recharge completely). Worse still, it does over 30,000 damage a shot, and your average armor cube has 2100 health, meaning at least 13 or 14 armor cubes are getting toasted. (The damage does fall off in the blast radius, thankfully, but not by much.)
But that's not all folks! These cannons are damn near indestructible, with over 130,000 points of health themselves. And, if you do not directly hit the weapon block, it doesn't take damage. The only exception to this is Plasma weaponry, which has a small explosion radius (roughly the size of a grenade), which leads into my next point, surprisingly.
And by golly, is that true! In a recent update Plasma weapons (or grenade launchers, as they could be considered) were actually REDUCED in damage, compared to their high powered counterparts. As a trade, they instead were given a higher blast radius and lower power consumption. But, there in lies a problem. If a player cannot do enough damage to destroy a high-powered weapon at short-to-medium distance (as is Plasma's intended purpose), then what use do they have on a player's robot? Now, understandably, higher tiered weaponry does do considerably more damage, but at that power consumption and fire rate trade off, the Plasmas were more balanced than the AeroFlak Cannon. Need proof? The second highest tiered Plasma, an Epic Quality item (just like the Flak, an Epic quality), has 40,000 health (roughly), does 38,000 points of damage (roughly) with a slower fire rate than the flak cannon, and a lower blast radius. So, while they do roughly the same amount of harm, the Plasma was balanced in such a way that it could be combated and successfully defended against, unlike the Flak cannon.
This was one of my biggest issues. The game expects players to have an understanding of physics when it comes to building flying robots, as in where to put wings and how much force required to get a vehicle off the ground. Yet, I don't believe even the developers do. The engines in this game are vastly underpowered, requiring usually no less than five to get someone off the ground. The smaller engine tiers hardly provide any lift at all and I wonder why they're still relevant. Now, I'm going to point out, the robot in reference here has 6 of the highest tier and two of the next tier down pushing it forward, and the acceleration and lift are absolutely meager. I'm surprised the damn robot flies at all.

God, bored of this review yet? Oh wait, points... So! The economy in the game drastically shifted with the introduction of Epic Loot, because gone were the days of battling for currency, instead now you battled for parts that dropped in a random crate after each battle. The better you did, the better the crate (from Rusted to Protonium). However, you'd be led to believe that Protonium crates would offer higher tiered items, the Epic and Legendary ones. Yet after testing players have shown a very low drop rate for these items. Players would often hope for Movement or Weapon parts, but would frequently receive cosmetics instead, these cosmetics "recycling" for a very low currency count. (I.E. a 10,000 robit flag resold at 750 robits.)
"At this point, this is not a game I wish to see to completion, it's really not. Because if the current 'meta' is to stand in a similar fashion... ...then there will never be any balance... New players will come in, get rekt, pack up and leave... I've never been one to complain... ...I now understand why people are so upset." As an avid supporter of the game, I've not only poured time into it, but money as well. Originally, I thought my funds were well placed, but I suppose I was wrong.

So, Robocrap recently went into "BETA" (about time, it only took them three years of Alpha testing) and so I decided to go on to check what's changed and this is my oppinion of it.
Robocraft......is a joke. I mean it has to be, there is no other rational explanation as to how or why a company would make a good proof of concept game, only to ruin it over the course of three years. This "Beta test" is the final evoloution of the seething mass of excrement that this game has become, just none of this makes any logical sense. Just how are freejam this incompitant?
First I'll talk about the matchmaking system they added since my last review. Freejam removed league battles and instead made it so that players had an ELO score (those who played league before this update kept their ELO rank, everyone else started at zero) . Players gain  a little ELO score when they win a match and lose a staggeringly huge amount when you lose a game, if you get in a bad team, then you're going to be padleing merilly down ***t creek with your hands today. This system has its flaws, but in a 1v1 game it could work, but robocraft is a game where you're in teams, currently me and many other vetren players are stuck at 0 ELO because of this rediculously flawed MM system. How does Freejam defend this you ask? Here is what one employee said when we complained about it (read in an insultingly dismissive voice) "The matchmaking rating is based off team performance because Robocraft is a team game." "unfortunatly we cannot force players to work as a team." (anyone else see the contradiction in the first two statements?) "The game needs more time to gather sufficient data (Total BS)."
And now we get on to fun part, the actual BETA, what have Freejam done? First, they reduce the team sizes from 8v8 to 5v5, you won't have any massive fun battles anymore, no, instead you'll be playing hide and seek and if even one player on your team disconnects or is in an inferior bot, then you can kiss your ELO ranking goodbye.
The Maps: The map size has been decreased to acomodate the lack of players, now maps are much smaller and more compact, which plays hell with balence. On one hand, since the aps are so compact and cover is closer together, ion distorters rule, meanwhile the railgun now has the range to see and fire on the entire map on most maps, if positioned correctly.
The Mode: And now we get to my favourate part. As flawed as battle arena was, it was still quite a bit of fun and at least required strategy, capping the towers, defending them and forming up for a large assault on the enemy's crystal was all rather fun. But battle arena is gone, now you simply go over to a flat pad, wait for a few seconds for it to change to your team's colour, then you go and do the same to another pad and do the same again, once you have these two pads, you simply defend them and wait for a timer to count up (A TIMER! ARE YOU KIDDING ME?). sounds fun right?

This includes overpowered weapons that 1 shot new players, impossibly large sums of money required to get anything at all, premiums get twice as many items from crates as non-premiums, playing in a match with a premium doesn't give you additional money like it used to, I could go on for hours.
The largest problem I've encountered is players attaching a really OP weapon to their robot but nothing else and lowering their cpu enough to get into new players' matches, meaning that they'll always win and gain easy loot. This mainly occurs with the new AeroFlak Cannon which, in early games, destroys any ground targets, even though the weapon was designed to be an anti aircraft gun.
Secondly the insane cost of items. So you play a match, come first in the team and win, gaining a protonium crate, and gain some stuff you dont want, so you sell it and gain maybe 300 money. Now you want to buy something...oh wait, you can't...because even the cheapest gun costs 400 and selling items gets you less than a tenth of what you can buy it for in some cases. So, you play another match...but there's someone with an AeroFlak, by the way did I mention that the AeroFlak costs 75,000 to buy?But thats not even the most expensive item there is, the lock on rocket launcher (another commonly used cheat weapon) costs 125,000 to buy, and I bet that leaves you wondering "but how do I get that?" well the sad answer is... you don't... or at least without spending MORE MONEY.Anyway you obviously loose and get a rusty case and inside you find... some more junk.
This has basically described what the game feels like for non-premiums...but wait, what if you are a premium? Well other than costing a TON of money (a single day costs £1) it is very good, access to all the paints (yes thats only for premiums), twice the items from crates, custom profile pic ect. Dirty bomb has a good, fast-paced combat system that, while occasionally frustrating, can be immensely rewarding. Graphics are good, maps are generally big and varied enough to be enjoyable without overdoing it, and have enough variability and verticality to make it interesting (and provide nice wall-jumping opportunities).
The available mercs each have a unique skill, which can range from support to healing to pure combat-oriented, which gives most characters an interesting role.
Weapons are shared between groups (so a merc that uses smgs will be able to use any of the smgs, and so on), and are handed out via loadout cards, which you get as drops. The system works well and allows for long-term tweaking of playsyles.
The market for the game seems pretty good, the game has no major flaws - worth trying.

What this means is that there is no game lobby, the "matches" is the fight for the base, and if you take the base you sweep the stragglers and go to the next base, but if you lose taking the base most likely you will be pushed back even more. If you go into it expecting the same game, merely updated to be playable on a modern machine, you'll definitely be getting what you want.  If you are doing it for the nostalgia... wait for a sale, or you'll probably feel you overpayed.  And, again, I'd definitely suggest getting the 'Forgotten' campaings, too.

The “Whoooaaaaaaa, Dude!” Award
I’m going to be honest, the description for this one was super vague and frankly there’s other games more deserving of this one than my nomination, but again they’ve already been nominated for being awesome in more specific ways. There’s all kinds of ways a game can blow your mind: The scenery and sound in Sovngarde is legendary, the violence in DOOM has been distilled to an art form and that bit in Undertale where the game directly mocks you for save-scumming out of a bad decision freaked me out completely. But Portal 2 isn’t without its moments and also manages to impress on a regular basis, both in terms of its ingenious puzzles, nefarious gags, delicious lore and the climactic pinch that sends you literally off the face of the planet. Portal 2 was exactly what I wanted to see happen when Valve took the seedling that was the original Portal and injected a digital empire’s worth of creative energy into fleshing it out. It’s just a shame Valve still haven’t gotten over their fear of the number three.

A well built, fast paced, free to play FPS.  The devs, Splash Damage, took what went wrong with Brink (their previous game), and not only fixed it, but made it better.
Classed based, with a strong reliance on teamwork.  No one class can do everything.  And no one player can do everything.
While all gamemodes are objective based, they are both fast paced games and can stretch out time quite a bit.  Each map is well done, with multiple paths and side objectives each team can exploit to gain the upper hand.  Only downside is the lack of a protected spawn area, meaning you run the risk of being spawn killed by dominating enemies.
All the Mercs (different classes similar to a MOBA, or other objective based shooters such as TF2 or Overwatch) are different in their abilities, although some are of course going to be similar.  Whether you are a tank mowing down enemies with a mingun, and fire support specialist calling in airstrikes, or an objective specialist completing them quickly and laying down mines to defend it, there are classes that will fit your style.  And each has both their advantages and flaws.  Some are glass cannons, some are slower than a turtle, some only rock shotguns, some only rock marksman rifles.
Each match requires teamwork.  A team that doesn't work together is one that is going to struggle to win.  Heal your allies, pass around ammo, watch their backs, and you'll get through.
Every merc (with the exception of two that are used for training) will go through a period of being free to use, similar to how most MOBAs do their characters.  All are purchasable in two ways, with ingame currency earned by playing it, or with real cash (as this is a Free To Play game.  The devs need to earn money).  Every merc also has a varity of loadouts, which are different weapons, skins, and passive perks to boost your playstyle (such as lessened fall damage, lessened self explosive harm, or faster melee attack).  Loadouts are earned through cases and can be traded up in quality, or traded in for a card for a different merc.  Cases are earned after a match, purchasable with ingame currency, or bought with real money (again same principle as the Mercs)
There is NO CONTENT LOCKED BEHIND A REAL MONEY PAY WALL (with the exception of Event based loadouts, which are just varients of different loadout cards, usually based off of gold or silver cards)

After playing this game for about a week or two now, I can say that I enjoy this game. It feels like a good FPS in MMO form. It's great for anyone who wants to join in massive combined arms battles against players from all arround the world. Finding  people to play with is easy, and the in game chat feature (which I read was horrible at first) works very well. There is never any shortage of challenge or prople to play with (Though you may need to switch characters every now and again). So I absolutly recomend this game. It has great combat, great community, and is all arround good fun.
All that being said, this game has some horrible flaws that desperatly need to be fixed. First of all, the tutorial is laughably short and uninformitave. It teaches you the basics of movement and combat. By basics, I mean that it only teaches you how to move your character, shoot the badguys, and interact with the environment. And that's it. There's a brief driving lesson, but it doesn't teach you about anything other than summoning the vehicle, and  driving it arround. There is absolutly no backstory whatsoever. Everything you know about the three factions is what you read in the description about them. So there's no reason to really care about the factions, and no attachment. F2P players will quickly get frustrated at the slow rate of in-game currency, and the high price of every decent upgrade and new weapon (some of which require real world money to buy). Customization is limmited at character creation, and expensive after creation. All armor customizations (Helmets, colors, camo, etc) other than what you start with cost station cash (real world money).
So, with all those cons, how am I able to recomend this game? Easy, It's still fun to play despite how much grinding you'll need to do. if you just want to shoot people, drive tanks, fly interesting aircraft, and talk to people, this is the game for you. But for a more sirious MMO, you're better off with almost any other MMO. If you want a good shooter, CoD, BF4, and TF2 are all better choices. I keep playing this game because it has a good community, and I don't have to spend a dime on it.

A well built, fast paced, free to play FPS.  The devs, Splash Damage, took what went wrong with Brink (their previous game), and not only fixed it, but made it better.
Classed based, with a strong reliance on teamwork.  No one class can do everything.  And no one player can do everything.
While all gamemodes are objective based, they are both fast paced games and can stretch out time quite a bit.  Each map is well done, with multiple paths and side objectives each team can exploit to gain the upper hand.  Only downside is the lack of a protected spawn area, meaning you run the risk of being spawn killed by dominating enemies.
All the Mercs (different classes similar to a MOBA, or other objective based shooters such as TF2 or Overwatch) are different in their abilities, although some are of course going to be similar.  Whether you are a tank mowing down enemies with a mingun, and fire support specialist calling in airstrikes, or an objective specialist completing them quickly and laying down mines to defend it, there are classes that will fit your style.  And each has both their advantages and flaws.  Some are glass cannons, some are slower than a turtle, some only rock shotguns, some only rock marksman rifles.
Each match requires teamwork.  A team that doesn't work together is one that is going to struggle to win.  Heal your allies, pass around ammo, watch their backs, and you'll get through.
Every merc (with the exception of two that are used for training) will go through a period of being free to use, similar to how most MOBAs do their characters.  All are purchasable in two ways, with ingame currency earned by playing it, or with real cash (as this is a Free To Play game.  The devs need to earn money).  Every merc also has a varity of loadouts, which are different weapons, skins, and passive perks to boost your playstyle (such as lessened fall damage, lessened self explosive harm, or faster melee attack).  Loadouts are earned through cases and can be traded up in quality, or traded in for a card for a different merc.  Cases are earned after a match, purchasable with ingame currency, or bought with real money (again same principle as the Mercs)
There is NO CONTENT LOCKED BEHIND A REAL MONEY PAY WALL (with the exception of Event based loadouts, which are just varients of different loadout cards, usually based off of gold or silver cards)

Returned to Robocraft after a year to find many changes - many of which initially excited me, but then after a number of games realized that balance of weapons is still sorely lacking. I read how the developers want to move to a "horizontal progression" scheme, and while I agree with this move in theory, in practice it still amounts to a grind to attain what are currently the "best" weapons.
Previously, the game had a kind of rock/paper/scissors balance between different types of bots, but they recently changed it so that you can use multiple types of weapons on a single bot. In theory, this should be exciting, but there were many balances that had been calibrated by the previous 2 years of development that were trampled on by this change. Despite the developer saying that they wanted to balance weapons, making even lower quality weapons effective depending on player design, in practice they are not.
Matches now are dominated by users with long range missiles and close range shotguns, both of which cost an arm and  leg in terms of play time to acquire. Every other weapon is of such reduced value that most of my previous builds were rendered virtually ineffective. Despite having played over 200 hours of this game in the past, acquisition of the new weapons looks to be very tedious - too tedious to hold my interest in returning to the game.

If your looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie

Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Want a free FPS with aircraft, tanks, 4wheelers and jetpacks?!?  This is the game for you.  Mix Tribes, Battlefield, and Team Fortress together and you have Planetside 2.  Working as a team is a MUST in this game to really make a difference.  Take an army of tanks, jets, or infantry into many different types of buildings and environments to capture sections of the map.  If you don't feel like playing in the group, feel free to pull out a sniper rifle and pick people off from the mountain adjacent of the fortress being attacked.  The game offers a wide variety of types of FPS gameplay, from Run-n-gun to sniping to barging in the front door with a fully loaded MAX unit blowing everything up that comes into your sight.
Yes the game is free, and yes there are in-game purchases.  The advantage that this game has over other "free-to-play" games is you can get all of the "pay for" items that actually increase your gameplay through in game currency called "Certs" that you get for killing enemies and capturing buildings.  You never HAVE to pay for anything that would make you a "better player", but you sure can fork out the cash to get it quicker if you want.  You never feel extremely overwhelmed by seasoned players who may own all the cool guns, as you start with a fair arsenol and most of your outcome depends on how tactical you are and how well you play as a team.

If your looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie

Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Here's a shooter that's fast, fun, competitive and doesn't have too many crutches for low skill players.
Unlike a lot of popular shooters, you rarely see people calling out people use certain weapons for being too overpowered. Sure there are some broken balancing, but what game doesn't?
Netcode, hitreg, map designs and character designs are great. Unless you purposely join a server with over 100 ping, you'll almost never experience rubberbanding, getting hit when you've reached cover long ago or hits not registering because you died before the latency catched up.
Dirty Bomb operates smoothly, the game mechanics are fun and that's what's important in multiplayer first-person shooters.
The F2P aspect of this game is of no concern either. You can buy the mercs with money, but it takes only 1-3 of playing to get enough in-game credits to buy a new merc. Loadouts can be bought with the same credits and they're even acquired randomly when playing the game. You can increase the chances of getting a high rarity card which is purely cosmetic by buying a different case. There is no P2W in Dirty Bomb.

First of all:
-Yes the loadout cards give SMALL advantages that are no match to actual skill.
-To get best possible advantage out of loadout cards you only need bronze cards and those are fairly easy to obtain.
-The loadout cards beyond bronze are nothing more than a different skin.
-Each merc is fairly balanced, before you say he is over powered search for a way to deal with him.
-The mercs that you are given for free from the start are very powerful.
-There is always rotation of 3 mercs that you can play without buying them and it updates every 2 weeks.
-You can get credits pretty fast for a free game, you can roughly get 10 to 20k credits per day if you complete most challenge the game offers you.
-TF2 mixed with Unreal Tournament gameplay.
-This is a fast paced team play game that requires you to be as good at movement as much as at shooting even if you play slowest merc, yet you shouldn't rush all the time and think what you're doing.
-Each merc features a unique ability that makes him more interesting to play.
-Despite ability to aim with iron sight you shouldn't use it too much as it slows you down a lot and makes you an easy target. You can fire from hip with a fairly reliable accuracy allowing you to both avoid damage and deal it.
-The concept of support class aka medics was executed as good as possible, it's fun to play support mercs in this game.
-A lot of voice commands and taunts for every merc.
-Frequent events, give aways and updates.
-Wall jumps, each merc can do 2 wall jumps in a row, it's a small touch of agility that allows you to reach more places and dodge more easily, yet it's fairly hard to master.
-Long jumps, another interesting movement addition, remember the jumping module from half life? (if you played it)
Works exactly the same, to perform one you must sprint crouch and jump at the same time, takes time to get used to.
It's defianetly worth your time.
